# Sets, relations and topology {#sec-sets-relations-topology}

Mathematics starts with sets and the maps between them, continues with the two ways of building new sets, by
gluing elements together and by pairing them, and reaches geometry when a set is given enough structure to speak
of nearness: a topology. This chapter contains those first steps, in five sections. Sets and maps fixes the
vocabulary of elements, images, injective, surjective and bijective maps and inverses. Relations, quotients and
products introduces composition, equivalence relations and quotient sets, and Cartesian products. Topological
spaces defines open sets, continuity and homeomorphisms, and the subspace and quotient topologies. Compact and
connected spaces adds the three global properties, Hausdorff, compact and connected, that the spaces of the later
chapters all share. Metric spaces gives these topologies a concrete form through a distance, defines convergent and
Cauchy sequences and complete spaces, proves that compact metric spaces and the coordinate spaces are complete, and
ends with the contraction mapping theorem, which solves equations by iteration.
Every definition, theorem and proposition is followed by ten examples of increasing complexity and ten exercises of
increasing difficulty, each exercise with a hidden solution worked by hand and in SageMath. The reader who knows this
material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; every notion used later is defined here first, and every
counting statement is proved. The sources are @lee2013introduction [App. A], @keskivakkuri2022mathematical
[Secs. 2.3, 4.1] and the problem book @cheung2024metric, with the further texts named at the start of each section; the
examples are drawn from the circle, the sphere, spin configurations and simple mechanical systems, which recur
throughout the book.

## Sets and maps {#sec-sets}

A set is a collection of things, a map a rule assigning to each thing of one set a thing of another. The six
notions of this section, sets, maps, injective, surjective and bijective maps, and inverse maps, are the vocabulary
in which every later definition is phrased. Each definition is followed by ten examples, from the simplest
instances to cases from physics and to the limits of the notion, and by ten exercises of increasing difficulty
with hidden solutions; the counting results of the section are collected in a proposition after the definition of
the inverse map.

For more on this topic, see @chirivi2020selected [Theory Ch. 1-2], @komjath2006problems [Ch. 1, Ch. 3], @radozycki2020solving [Ch. 1-2], @keskivakkuri2022mathematical [Sec. 2.3], @starkovichStructuresMathematicalPhysics2021 [Secs. 1.1, 1.3] and @lee2013introduction [App. A].

### Sets

Before anything can be counted, mapped or given a shape, one has to say what a collection of objects is and when
one collection sits inside another. The picture to keep in mind is a bag of labelled items, with no order and no
repetition, together with the smaller bags that can be taken out of it. The first definition fixes this vocabulary,
the two symbols, membership and inclusion, that recur on every page of the book, and the three ways of combining
two subsets.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-set}
#### Set

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, its **elements**; $x \in X$ means that $x$ is an element of $X$. A
set $Y$ is a **subset** of $X$, written $Y \subseteq X$, if every element of $Y$ is an element of $X$. The set with
no elements is the **empty set** $\emptyset$, and $|X|$ denotes the number of elements of a finite set. For subsets
$A, B \subseteq X$, the **union** $A \cup B$, the **intersection** $A \cap B$ and the **difference** $A \setminus B$
are the sets of elements of $X$ that lie in $A$ or in $B$, in both, and in $A$ but not in $B$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest sets are those whose elements can be written out in full, so that the size is a matter of counting.
The three sets below are of this kind, and the last of them, the six rotations of a hexagon, is the first
appearance of a set of symmetries, the kind of set on which the groups of later chapters are built.

::: {#exm-set-finite}
#### Finite sets

$\{1, 2, 3\}$ has three elements; $\{0, 2, 4\}$ is a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$; the set of six rotations of a
regular hexagon by multiples of $60^\circ$ has $|X| = 6$.
:::

The smallest sets deserve a name of their own, because they are the edge cases of every later statement. The empty
set is a subset of every set, since it has no element that could fail to lie in the other set, and a set with a
single element is not the same thing as that element.

::: {#exm-set-empty-singleton}
#### The empty set and singletons

$\emptyset \subseteq X$ for every set $X$, and $X \subseteq X$. A **singleton** $\{p\}$ has exactly one element:
$\{0\}$ is the coordinate space $\mathbb{R}^0$ of dimension zero [@lee2013introduction, Example A.6]. The set
$\{\emptyset\}$ has one element, the empty set, so $|\{\emptyset\}| = 1$ while $|\emptyset| = 0$.
:::

Union, intersection and difference are best seen first on sets small enough to list. The example combines two
sets of integers and two intervals, and it shows that the difference, unlike the other two operations, depends on
the order of the two sets.

::: {#exm-set-operations}
#### Union, intersection and difference

For $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $B = \{3, 4, 5\}$: $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$, $A \cap B = \{3, 4\}$,
$A \setminus B = \{1, 2\}$ and $B \setminus A = \{5\}$. For intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: $[0, 2] \cup [1, 3] = [0, 3]$,
$[0, 2] \cap [1, 3] = [1, 2]$ and $[0, 2] \setminus [1, 3] = [0, 1)$. Two sets with empty intersection, such as the
even and the odd integers, are called **disjoint**.
:::

The subsets of a set form a new set, and this construction is the first way of producing a larger set from a
smaller one. Its size doubles with every element added, a count proved among the exercises below.

::: {#exm-set-power-set}
#### The power set

The **power set** of $X$ is the set of all subsets of $X$. For $X = \{a, b\}$ it is $\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\},
\{a, b\}\}$, with $4 = 2^2$ elements; the power set of $\emptyset$ is $\{\emptyset\}$, with one element. A
collection of subsets of $X$ is itself a subset of the power set [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 4.1.1].
:::

Most sets of analysis and physics cannot be listed element by element. The familiar number systems are the standard
infinite sets, and they come with inclusions among them that will be taken for granted throughout; the lists of $n$
real numbers are the coordinate spaces in which the points of curves and surfaces are labelled.

::: {#exm-set-numbers}
#### Number sets

$\mathbb{Z}$ (integers), $\mathbb{R}$ (real numbers), $\mathbb{C}$ (complex numbers) and $\mathbb{R}^n$ (lists of
$n$ real numbers) are infinite sets, with $\mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C}$.
:::

A set can also be specified by a condition on the points of a larger set. The same expression $X^2 + Y^2$, compared
with $1$ in three ways, cuts out three different subsets of the plane, and @fig-plane-sets draws them side by side.

::: {#exm-set-discs}
#### Discs and the circle

The **open unit disc** $\{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : X^2 + Y^2 < 1\}$, the circle $S^1 = \{X^2 + Y^2 = 1\}$ and the
**closed unit disc** $D = \{X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1\}$ satisfy $D = \{X^2 + Y^2 < 1\} \cup S^1$, a union of two disjoint
sets. In $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ the same conditions give the open and closed unit balls and the $n$-sphere $S^n$; the
$0$-sphere $S^0 = \{-1, 1\}$ has two points [@lee2013introduction, Example A.8].

![The open unit disc, the unit circle and the closed unit disc in the plane; the dashed edge of the first is not
part of it.](figures/plane_sets.svg){#fig-plane-sets width=80%}
:::

The circle and the sphere are described by equations in a coordinate space, and this is how they will be handled
throughout the book. The example lists them, cut out by one equation each, and a circle in space cut out by two.

::: {#exm-set-geometric}
#### Geometric sets

The circle $S^1 = \{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : X^2 + Y^2 = 1\}$ and the sphere $S^2 = \{(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 :
X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1\}$ are subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ cut out by one equation. The equator
$\{(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1, Z = 0\}$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ cut out by two
equations, a circle in space.
:::

In quantum physics a system is described first by the set of its possible states. A spin-$\tfrac12$ particle
measured along the $z$-axis has two outcomes, and a row of several such spins has as many configurations as there
are lists of outcomes.

::: {#exm-set-spin-states}
#### Spin configurations

The set of outcomes of one spin is $\{\uparrow, \downarrow\}$. The configurations of three spins in a row are the
lists $\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow$, $\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow$, ..., $\downarrow\downarrow\downarrow$, a set of
$2^3 = 8$ elements. The configurations with exactly one spin down, $\{\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow,
\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow, \uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\}$, form a subset of three elements.
:::

The bound states of the hydrogen atom are labelled by three integers, and the labels belonging to one energy level
form a finite set whose size is the degeneracy of that level. Listing the set for the first two levels shows the
pattern $n^2$, which an exercise below confirms for every level.

::: {#exm-set-hydrogen-labels}
#### Hydrogen labels

The labels $(n, l, m)$ of hydrogen have $n \geq 1$, $0 \leq l \leq n - 1$ and $-l \leq m \leq l$. For $n = 1$ the
set is $\{(1, 0, 0)\}$; for $n = 2$ it is $\{(2, 0, 0), (2, 1, -1), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1)\}$, with $4 = 2^2$
elements.
:::

Two remarks mark the limits of the definition. A set is determined by its elements alone, so order and repetition
in a list are invisible; and not every collection that can be described in words is a set.

::: {#exm-set-limits}
#### What a set is not

$\{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\} = \{1, 1, 2\}$: the three lists describe one set with two elements. The collection of all sets
that are not elements of themselves cannot be a set: if it were a set $R$, then $R \in R$ would hold exactly when
$R \notin R$ (Russell's paradox). Axiomatic set theory rules such collections out; the sets of this book, built from
numbers, coordinate spaces and their subsets, are never of that kind.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the full inventory of subsets of a three-element set, including the empty set and the
set itself. Doing it by hand shows where the count $2^3$ comes from, and the Sage check introduces the enumeration
style that recurs in the counting exercises of this section.

::: {#exr-set-subsets}
#### Subsets of a small set

List all subsets of $\{a, b, c\}$ and count them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A subset is fixed by deciding, for each of the three elements, whether it is in or out, so there are $2 \cdot 2
\cdot 2 = 2^3 = 8$ subsets: $\emptyset$, $\{a\}$, $\{b\}$, $\{c\}$, $\{a, b\}$, $\{a, c\}$, $\{b, c\}$, $\{a, b, c\}$.

## SageMath

Sage lists the subsets of $\{a, b, c\}$ and counts them.

```{.python .sage}
X = Set(["a", "b", "c"])
subs = sorted((sorted(s) for s in X.subsets()), key=lambda s: (len(s), s))
for s in subs: print(s)
print("number of subsets:", len(subs), "; equal to 2^3:", len(subs) == 2^3)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[]
['a']
['b']
['c']
['a', 'b']
['a', 'c']
['b', 'c']
['a', 'b', 'c']
number of subsets: 8 ; equal to 2^3: True
```
::::
:::

The three operations of @def-set are now applied by the reader to two small sets. The exercise checks each
definition element by element, and asks for both differences, which differ.

::: {#exr-set-operations-compute}
#### Computing with two sets

For $A = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ and $B = \{3, 5, 7, 9\}$, find $A \cup B$, $A \cap B$, $A \setminus B$ and
$B \setminus A$, and check that $A \cup B$ is the union of the three disjoint sets $A \setminus B$, $A \cap B$ and
$B \setminus A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$A \cup B = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9\}$, $A \cap B = \{3, 5\}$, $A \setminus B = \{0, 1, 2, 4\}$ and $B \setminus A
= \{7, 9\}$. Every element of $A \cup B$ lies in $A$ only, in both, or in $B$ only, and in exactly one of these
cases, so the three sets are disjoint with union $A \cup B$; the sizes add up, $4 + 2 + 2 = 8$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the four sets with Python's set operations and checks the decomposition.

```{.python .sage}
A = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; B = {3, 5, 7, 9}
print("A u B =", sorted(A | B), "; A n B =", sorted(A & B))
print("A - B =", sorted(A - B), "; B - A =", sorted(B - A))
parts = [A - B, A & B, B - A]
print("union of the parts is A u B:", set().union(*parts) == A | B, "; sizes", [len(p) for p in parts], "sum to", len(A | B))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A u B = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9] ; A n B = [3, 5]
A - B = [0, 1, 2, 4] ; B - A = [7, 9]
union of the parts is A u B: True ; sizes [4, 2, 2] sum to 8
```
::::
:::

Inclusions between sets are the first relations that need checking rather than assuming, and each failed inclusion
is witnessed by a single element. This exercise runs through the chain of number systems and then through the
circle and the two discs of @exm-set-discs, where the question becomes whether a boundary belongs to a region.

::: {#exr-set-inclusions}
#### Inclusions among familiar sets

Decide which inclusions hold among $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$, the circle
$S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, the closed disc $D = \{X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1\}$ and the open disc.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, each inclusion
strict ($-1 \notin \mathbb{N}$, $\tfrac12 \notin \mathbb{Z}$, $\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}$, $i \notin \mathbb{R}$). The
open disc is a subset of the closed disc, and the circle is a subset of the closed disc but disjoint from the open
one: $S^1 \subseteq D$, $S^1 \cap \{X^2 + Y^2 < 1\} = \emptyset$, since a point cannot have $X^2 + Y^2$ equal to $1$
and less than $1$. No inclusion holds between a set of numbers and a set of points of the plane.

## SageMath

Sage tests the four witnesses of strictness and three sample points of the plane against the three conditions.

```{.python .sage}
print("-1 in ZZ but not NN:", -1 in ZZ and not (-1 > 0), "; 1/2 in QQ, not ZZ:", (1/2) in QQ and (1/2) not in ZZ)
print("sqrt(2) rational:", sqrt(2) in QQ, "; I real:", I in RR)
for p in [(0, 0), (3/5, 4/5), (1, 1)]:
    r = p[0]^2 + p[1]^2
    print(p, "open disc:", r < 1, " circle:", r == 1, " closed disc:", r <= 1)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
-1 in ZZ but not NN: True ; 1/2 in QQ, not ZZ: True
sqrt(2) rational: False ; I real: False
(0, 0) open disc: True  circle: False  closed disc: True
(3/5, 4/5) open disc: False  circle: True  closed disc: True
(1, 1) open disc: False  circle: False  closed disc: False
```
::::
:::

Intervals of the real line are combined in the same way as finite sets, but the endpoints need care. Whether an
endpoint belongs to a union or a difference depends on which of the two intervals contains it.

::: {#exr-set-interval-ops}
#### Operations on intervals

Find $[0, 2) \cup (1, 3]$, $[0, 2) \cap (1, 3]$, $[0, 2) \setminus (1, 3]$ and $\mathbb{R} \setminus (0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A number lies in the union when $0 \leq x < 2$ or $1 < x \leq 3$, that is $0 \leq x \leq 3$: the union is $[0, 3]$.
It lies in the intersection when $1 < x < 2$: the intersection is $(1, 2)$. It lies in the difference when $0 \leq x
< 2$ and not $1 < x \leq 3$, that is $0 \leq x \leq 1$: the difference is $[0, 1]$, closed at $1$ because $1 \notin
(1, 3]$. Finally $\mathbb{R} \setminus (0, 1) = (-\infty, 0] \cup [1, \infty)$.

## SageMath

Sage's `RealSet` computes the four sets.

```{.python .sage}
A = RealSet.closed_open(0, 2); B = RealSet.open_closed(1, 3)
print("union:", A.union(B), "; intersection:", A.intersection(B))
print("difference:", A.difference(B), "; complement of (0, 1):", RealSet.open(0, 1).complement())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
union: [0, 3] ; intersection: (1, 2)
difference: [0, 1] ; complement of (0, 1): (-oo, 0] ∪ [1, +oo)
```
::::
:::

Cutting a set out by two conditions at once is intersecting two sets, and the result can be much smaller than
either. The exercise intersects the circle and the sphere with a plane, where the same slicing has very different
outcomes in two and in three dimensions; the circles of latitude obtained here return when the sphere is given
coordinates.

::: {#exr-set-circle-line}
#### A set cut out by two equations

Describe the set of points of the circle $S^1$ that lie on the line $Y = \tfrac12$, and the set of points of the
sphere $S^2$ with $Z = \tfrac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

On the circle, $Y = \tfrac12$ gives $X^2 + \tfrac14 = 1$, so $X = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$: the intersection is the
set of two points $(\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tfrac12)$. On the sphere, $Z = \tfrac12$ gives $X^2 + Y^2 = \tfrac34$: the
intersection is a circle of radius $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ in the plane $Z = \tfrac12$, a set with infinitely many
elements.

## SageMath

Sage solves the two equations of the circle and substitutes $Z = \tfrac12$ in the equation of the sphere.

```{.python .sage}
X, Y, Z = var("X Y Z")
print("circle and the line Y = 1/2:", solve([X^2 + Y^2 == 1, Y == 1/2], [X, Y]))
print("sphere and the plane Z = 1/2:", (X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 - 1).subs(Z=1/2), "= 0, a circle of radius", sqrt(3/4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
circle and the line Y = 1/2: [
[X == -1/2*sqrt(3), Y == (1/2)],
[X == 1/2*sqrt(3), Y == (1/2)]
]
sphere and the plane Z = 1/2: X^2 + Y^2 - 3/4 = 0, a circle of radius 1/2*sqrt(3)
```
::::
:::

The hydrogen labels of @exm-set-hydrogen-labels are counted here level by level. The count is the degeneracy of the
level, and the exercise asks for the formula and for the total over the first few levels.

::: {#exr-set-hydrogen-count}
#### Counting hydrogen labels

Show that the set of labels $(n, l, m)$ with a fixed $n$ has $n^2$ elements, and count the labels with $n \leq 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For each $l$ there are $2l + 1$ values of $m$, so the level $n$ has $\sum_{l=0}^{n-1} (2l + 1) = 2 \cdot
\tfrac{(n-1)n}{2} + n = n^2$ labels. For $n \leq 4$ the total is $1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30$.

## SageMath

Sage builds the set of labels with $n \leq 4$ and counts it level by level.

```{.python .sage}
labels = [(n, l, m) for n in range(1, 5) for l in range(n) for m in range(-l, l + 1)]
print("labels per level:", [len([t for t in labels if t[0] == n]) for n in range(1, 5)])
print("total for n <= 4:", len(labels), "; equal to 1 + 4 + 9 + 16:", len(labels) == 30)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
labels per level: [1, 4, 9, 16]
total for n <= 4: 30 ; equal to 1 + 4 + 9 + 16: True
```
::::
:::

Equality of sets is proved in practice by two inclusions, one in each direction. The exercise states this
principle and uses it once on a set given by an equation.

::: {#exr-set-equality-double-inclusion}
#### Equality by two inclusions

Show that $A = B$ exactly when $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$, and use it to prove $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 - 3x
+ 2 = 0\} = \{1, 2\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A set is determined by its elements (@def-set), so $A = B$ means that every element of $A$ is in $B$ and every
element of $B$ is in $A$, which are the two inclusions. For the example, let $S$ be the solution set. $1 - 3 + 2 = 0$
and $4 - 6 + 2 = 0$, so $\{1, 2\} \subseteq S$. Conversely, $x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2)$, and a product of real
numbers vanishes only if a factor does, so $x \in S$ gives $x = 1$ or $x = 2$: $S \subseteq \{1, 2\}$.

## SageMath

Check on the quadratic: Sage factors it, solves it, and compares the solution set with $\{1, 2\}$.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
p = x^2 - 3*x + 2
S = {s.rhs() for s in solve(p == 0, x)}
print("factorisation:", p.factor(), "; solution set:", sorted(S), "; equal to {1, 2}:", S == {1, 2})
```

```{.text .sage-output}
factorisation: (x - 1)*(x - 2) ; solution set: [1, 2] ; equal to {1, 2}: True
```
::::
:::

Complements turn unions into intersections and intersections into unions. The exercise proves these two rules, De
Morgan's laws, which are used whenever a condition is traded for its negation.

::: {#exr-set-de-morgan}
#### De Morgan's laws

For subsets $A, B$ of a set $X$, prove $X \setminus (A \cup B) = (X \setminus A) \cap (X \setminus B)$ and $X
\setminus (A \cap B) = (X \setminus A) \cup (X \setminus B)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $x \in X$: $x \in X \setminus (A \cup B)$ means that $x$ is neither in $A$ nor in $B$, that is $x \in X \setminus
A$ and $x \in X \setminus B$; this proves the first law by two inclusions (@exr-set-equality-double-inclusion).
Likewise $x \in X \setminus (A \cap B)$ means that $x$ is not in both, that is $x \notin A$ or $x \notin B$, which is
$x \in (X \setminus A) \cup (X \setminus B)$.

## SageMath

Check on all pairs of subsets of $X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$: Sage tests both laws for each of the $16 \cdot 16$ pairs.

```{.python .sage}
X = Set([1, 2, 3, 4])
subs = list(X.subsets())
law1 = all(X.difference(A.union(B)) == X.difference(A).intersection(X.difference(B)) for A in subs for B in subs)
law2 = all(X.difference(A.intersection(B)) == X.difference(A).union(X.difference(B)) for A in subs for B in subs)
print("pairs tested:", len(subs)^2, "; first law:", law1, "; second law:", law2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
pairs tested: 256 ; first law: True ; second law: True
```
::::
:::

The power set of @exm-set-power-set doubles in size with every new element. The exercise asks for a proof of the
formula $2^n$ by induction on the number of elements.

::: {#exr-set-power-set-count}
#### The size of the power set

Prove that a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $n = 0$ the only subset of $\emptyset$ is $\emptyset$, and $2^0 = 1$. Suppose every set with $n$ elements has $2^n$
subsets, and let $X$ have $n + 1$ elements; pick $p \in X$ and put $X' = X \setminus \{p\}$, with $n$ elements. A
subset of $X$ either does not contain $p$, and is then a subset of $X'$, or contains $p$, and is then $A' \cup \{p\}$
for exactly one subset $A' \subseteq X'$. Each kind has $2^n$ members, so $X$ has $2^n + 2^n = 2^{n+1}$ subsets.

## SageMath

Check on the sets $\{1, \dots, n\}$ for $n = 0, \dots, 7$: Sage counts the subsets and compares with $2^n$.

```{.python .sage}
counts = [Subsets(range(1, n + 1)).cardinality() for n in range(8)]
print("numbers of subsets:", counts)
print("equal to 2^n:", counts == [2^n for n in range(8)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
numbers of subsets: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
equal to 2^n: True
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines the spin configurations of @exm-set-spin-states with the subsets of a finite set.
Choosing which spins point up is choosing a subset of the positions, so the counts of the two problems agree.

::: {#exr-set-spin-configurations}
#### Spins and subsets

Four spin-$\tfrac12$ particles sit at the positions $1, 2, 3, 4$. How many configurations have exactly two spins up
(total $S_z = 0$)? How many configurations are there in all, and how many have at least one spin up?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A configuration is fixed by the set of positions whose spin is up, a subset of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, and every subset
occurs exactly once. Two spins up means a subset with two elements: $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$, $\{2,3\}$,
$\{2,4\}$, $\{3,4\}$, so $6$ configurations. In all there are $2^4 = 16$ configurations (@exr-set-power-set-count),
and all but the one with no spin up, the empty subset, have at least one spin up: $15$.

## SageMath

Sage lists the configurations as strings of `u` and `d` and counts them.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
configs = ["".join(c) for c in product("ud", repeat=4)]
two_up = [c for c in configs if c.count("u") == 2]
print("all:", len(configs), "; two up:", len(two_up), two_up)
print("at least one up:", sum(1 for c in configs if "u" in c))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
all: 16 ; two up: 6 ['uudd', 'udud', 'uddu', 'duud', 'dudu', 'dduu']
at least one up: 15
```
::::
:::
::::

### Maps

With sets in place, the next notion is a rule that sends elements of one set to elements of another. The picture is
a set of arrows, exactly one leaving each point of the domain, and the two subsets attached to such a rule, the
values actually taken and the points sent into a given target region, are the objects in which continuity and
quotients are later phrased.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-map}
#### Map

A **map** $f : X \to Y$ assigns to every element $x$ of the **domain** $X$ exactly one element $f(x)$ of the
**codomain** $Y$. The **image** of $f$ is the subset $\{f(x) : x \in X\} \subseteq Y$ of values actually taken, and
the **preimage** of a subset $V \subseteq Y$ is $f^{-1}(V) = \{x \in X : f(x) \in V\}$. More generally, the image of
a subset $A \subseteq X$ is $f(A) = \{f(x) : x \in A\}$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When both sets are finite the map is a table, and its image and preimages are read off directly from that table.
The example also gives a first count, the number of all maps between two small sets, which is the first of the
counts collected at the end of the section.

::: {#exm-map-finite}
#### Maps between finite sets

$f : \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{x, y\}$ with $f(1) = f(2) = x$, $f(3) = y$ is a map with image $\{x, y\}$ and preimage
$f^{-1}(\{x\}) = \{1, 2\}$. There are $2^3 = 8$ maps from a three-element set to a two-element set, one choice of
value for each element.
:::

Every set carries a few maps that need no formula at all. They look trivial, but they are the maps against which
the properties of the following definitions are first tested.

::: {#exm-map-identity-constant}
#### Identity, inclusion and constant maps

The **identity** $\mathrm{id}_X : X \to X$, $x \mapsto x$, has image $X$. For a subset $A \subseteq X$, the
**inclusion** $A \to X$, $a \mapsto a$, has image $A$. A **constant map** $x \mapsto c$ has image $\{c\}$ when $X$ is
not empty, and the preimage of $V$ under it is $X$ if $c \in V$ and $\emptyset$ otherwise.
:::

A map between small finite sets is best drawn as arrows from the points of the domain to the points of the
codomain. @fig-map-diagram shows three such maps, and the next three definitions are read off from their
pictures.

::: {#exm-map-arrows}
#### Maps drawn as arrows

In the first map of @fig-map-diagram, from $\{1, 2\}$ to $\{x, y, z\}$, the image is $\{x, y\}$ and the preimage of
$\{z\}$ is empty. In the second, from $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to $\{x, y\}$, two arrows end at $x$, so $f^{-1}(\{x\}) = \{1,
2\}$. In the third, every point of $\{x, y, z\}$ receives exactly one arrow.

![Three maps between finite sets drawn as arrows: an injective map that is not surjective, a surjective map that is
not injective, and a bijection.](figures/map_diagram.svg){#fig-map-diagram width=85%}
:::

The functions of calculus are maps with the real line as domain, and their images are the ranges one learns to
compute. The second map of this example goes further: it wraps the line around the circle, so that its image is a
curve rather than an interval and its preimages are infinite sets of angles. This wrapping map is the model for
every parametrisation in the book.

::: {#exm-map-functions}
#### Functions and parametrisations

$\cos : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a map with image $[-1, 1]$. The map $\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$
from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ has image the circle $S^1$: it parametrises the circle, and the preimage of the
single point $(1, 0)$ is the set of multiples of $2\pi$.
:::

Preimages of intervals under a periodic function are unions of infinitely many intervals. @fig-preimage-sine
shows this for the sine, the set of angles at which a pendulum's horizontal displacement, measured in units of the
string length, exceeds one half.

::: {#exm-map-preimage-sine}
#### The preimage of an interval under the sine

The preimage of $(\tfrac12, 1]$ under $\sin : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is $\{x : \sin x > \tfrac12\} =
\bigcup_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (\tfrac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi, \tfrac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi)$, a union of infinitely many open intervals,
and the preimage of $\{2\}$ is empty.

![The graph of the sine, the band of values in $(\tfrac12, 1]$, and on the horizontal axis the intervals of its
preimage.](figures/preimage_sine.svg){#fig-preimage-sine width=90%}
:::

Image and preimage are not inverse operations: going down and back up can lose points, and going up and back down
can gain them. The squaring map shows both effects at once, and an exercise below proves the two
inclusions that always hold [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 2.3, Part A, Problem 17].

::: {#exm-map-image-preimage-rules}
#### Image of a preimage, preimage of an image

For $f(x) = x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$: $f(f^{-1}([-1, 4])) = f([-2, 2]) = [0, 4]$, strictly smaller than $[-1, 4]$, and
$f^{-1}(f([0, 1])) = f^{-1}([0, 1]) = [-1, 1]$, strictly larger than $[0, 1]$.
:::

Maps need not start from a line or a plane; the domain can itself be a curved set, or the codomain can be one. The
height function on the sphere forgets two of the three coordinates, while the spherical angles of geography produce
every point of the sphere, and both reappear in the exercises that follow.

::: {#exm-map-projection}
#### The height function and the spherical angles

The projection $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto Z$ from the sphere to $\mathbb{R}$ (the height function) has image $[-1, 1]$.
The map $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$, defined on the
pairs of real numbers with $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ and $0 \leq \varphi < 2\pi$, has image the whole sphere.
:::

A physical quantity is a map from the set of states to the real numbers, and the preimage of a value is the set of
states with that value. For the oscillator each energy is taken once; for hydrogen each energy is shared by a whole
set of labels.

::: {#exm-map-energy}
#### Energy as a map on states

The harmonic oscillator has levels $n \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ and the energy map $n \mapsto \hbar\omega(n +
\tfrac12)$, whose preimage of $\{\tfrac52\hbar\omega\}$ is $\{2\}$. For hydrogen the energy depends only on $n$: the
map $(n, l, m) \mapsto n$ from the labels of @exm-set-hydrogen-labels to $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$ has the preimage of
$\{n\}$ with $n^2$ elements, the degeneracy of the level.
:::

Projecting the circle onto a line is a map whose preimages change size from point to point. @fig-circle-shadow draws
the projection onto the $X$-axis, the shadow of the circle in light falling along the $Y$-direction.

::: {#exm-map-circle-shadow}
#### The shadow of the circle

The map $(X, Y) \mapsto X$ from $S^1$ to $\mathbb{R}$ has image $[-1, 1]$. The preimage of a value $u \in (-1, 1)$
is the pair $(u, \pm\sqrt{1 - u^2})$, that of $u = \pm 1$ the single point $(\pm 1, 0)$, and that of any $|u| > 1$
is empty.

![The circle and its shadow $[-1, 1]$ on the horizontal axis; a value $u$ inside has two preimages, one above and
one below.](figures/circle_shadow.svg){#fig-circle-shadow width=45%}
:::

A rule that gives no value, or several values, at some point is not a map. The last example collects three
familiar rules that fail the definition, and the way each is repaired.

::: {#exm-map-not-maps}
#### Rules that are not maps

$x \mapsto 1/x$ is not a map $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, since $0$ has no value; it is a map on $\mathbb{R}
\setminus \{0\}$. "$x \mapsto \pm\sqrt{x}$" gives two values to every $x > 0$; choosing the positive root gives a map
$[0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$. The angle of a point of the circle is defined only up to multiples of $2\pi$, so it is a
map to $\mathbb{R}$ only once a range such as $[0, 2\pi)$ is chosen.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks the reader to read images and preimages off an explicit table of values, as in
@fig-map-diagram. The point to notice is that a preimage can be empty, and that the preimage of a set of two values
collects everything sent to either of them.

::: {#exr-map-image-preimage}
#### Image and preimage of a finite map

For $f : \{1, 2, 3, 4\} \to \{a, b, c\}$ with $f(1) = f(3) = a$, $f(2) = c$, $f(4) = a$, find the image of $f$ and
the preimages of $\{a\}$, $\{b\}$ and $\{a, c\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The values taken are $a$ and $c$, so the image is $\{a, c\}$. The elements sent to $a$ are $1, 3, 4$, so $f^{-1}(\{a\})
= \{1, 3, 4\}$; nothing is sent to $b$, so $f^{-1}(\{b\}) = \emptyset$; every element is sent to $a$ or $c$, so
$f^{-1}(\{a, c\}) = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$.

## SageMath

Sage stores the map as a dictionary and computes the image and the three preimages.

```{.python .sage}
f = {1: "a", 2: "c", 3: "a", 4: "a"}
image = set(f.values())
preimage = lambda V: {x for x in f if f[x] in V}
print("image:", sorted(image))
for V in ({"a"}, {"b"}, {"a", "c"}): print("preimage of", sorted(V), ":", sorted(preimage(V)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
image: ['a', 'c']
preimage of ['a'] : [1, 3, 4]
preimage of ['b'] : []
preimage of ['a', 'c'] : [1, 2, 3, 4]
```
::::
:::

The maps of @exm-map-identity-constant have images and preimages that can be written down for every subset at once.
The exercise asks for them, and shows that a constant map has only two possible preimages.

::: {#exr-map-identity-inclusion}
#### Images and preimages of the simplest maps

For $X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, the subset $A = \{1, 2\}$ with its inclusion $\iota : A \to X$, and the constant map $c :
X \to X$ with value $3$, find $\iota^{-1}(\{2, 3\})$, $\mathrm{id}_X^{-1}(\{2, 3\})$, $c^{-1}(\{2, 3\})$ and
$c^{-1}(\{1, 2\})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The preimage under the inclusion keeps the elements of $A$ that lie in the set: $\iota^{-1}(\{2, 3\}) = A \cap \{2,
3\} = \{2\}$. The identity sends every set to itself, so $\mathrm{id}_X^{-1}(\{2, 3\}) = \{2, 3\}$. The constant map
sends everything to $3$, so its preimage of a set containing $3$ is all of $X$, and of a set not containing $3$ is
empty: $c^{-1}(\{2, 3\}) = X$ and $c^{-1}(\{1, 2\}) = \emptyset$.

## SageMath

Sage writes the three maps as dictionaries and computes the four preimages.

```{.python .sage}
X = [1, 2, 3, 4]
pre = lambda f, V: sorted(x for x in f if f[x] in V)
iota = {1: 1, 2: 2}; ident = {x: x for x in X}; const = {x: 3 for x in X}
print("iota^-1({2,3}) =", pre(iota, {2, 3}), "; id^-1({2,3}) =", pre(ident, {2, 3}))
print("c^-1({2,3}) =", pre(const, {2, 3}), "; c^-1({1,2}) =", pre(const, {1, 2}))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
iota^-1({2,3}) = [2] ; id^-1({2,3}) = [2, 3]
c^-1({2,3}) = [1, 2, 3, 4] ; c^-1({1,2}) = []
```
::::
:::

For a function on the real line, images and preimages are computed by solving inequalities rather than by reading a
table. The squaring map is the standard example in which the preimage of an interval splits into two pieces and the
preimage of a point can be empty.

::: {#exr-map-square}
#### Image and preimage of $x \mapsto x^2$

Find the image of $x \mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and the preimages of $[1, 4]$ and of $\{-1\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Every square is non-negative, and every $y \geq 0$ is the square of $\sqrt y$, so the image is $[0, \infty)$. $x^2 \in
[1, 4]$ means $1 \leq |x| \leq 2$, so the preimage is $[-2, -1] \cup [1, 2]$; the preimage of $\{-1\}$ is empty,
since no square is negative. A preimage can be empty, or larger than the set whose preimage it is.

## SageMath

Sage solves the inequalities $1 \leq x^2 \leq 4$ and the equation $x^2 = -1$ over the reals.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
print("1 <= x^2 <= 4:", solve([x^2 >= 1, x^2 <= 4], x))
print("real solutions of x^2 = -1:", [s for s in solve(x^2 == -1, x) if s.rhs().imag() == 0])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
1 <= x^2 <= 4: [
[-2 < x, x < -1],
[1 < x, x < 2],
[x == -2],
[x == -1],
[x == 1],
[x == 2]
]
real solutions of x^2 = -1: []
```
::::
:::

The floor function rounds a real number down to an integer, and its preimages are half-open intervals. The exercise
asks for a few of them, and the answer shows how the endpoints are decided by the rounding rule.

::: {#exr-map-floor}
#### Preimages under the floor function

The floor $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the largest integer $\leq x$. Find the image of $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor : \mathbb{R} \to
\mathbb{R}$ and the preimages of $\{0\}$, of $\{0, 1\}$ and of $[\tfrac12, \tfrac32]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The values are integers and every integer $k$ is the floor of itself, so the image is $\mathbb{Z}$. $\lfloor x \rfloor
= k$ means $k \leq x < k + 1$, so the preimage of $\{0\}$ is $[0, 1)$ and that of $\{0, 1\}$ is $[0, 1) \cup [1, 2) =
[0, 2)$. The only integer in $[\tfrac12, \tfrac32]$ is $1$, so its preimage is the preimage of $\{1\}$, namely $[1,
2)$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the floor on a grid of quarter steps in $[-1, 3)$ and prints the grid points of each preimage.

```{.python .sage}
grid = [k / 4 for k in range(-4, 12)]
pre = lambda V: [t for t in grid if floor(t) in V]
print("image on the grid:", sorted({floor(t) for t in grid}))
print("preimage of {0}:", pre({0}), "\npreimage of {0, 1}:", pre({0, 1}))
print("preimage of [1/2, 3/2]:", [t for t in grid if 1/2 <= floor(t) <= 3/2])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
image on the grid: [-1, 0, 1, 2]
preimage of {0}: [0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4]
preimage of {0, 1}: [0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1, 5/4, 3/2, 7/4]
preimage of [1/2, 3/2]: [1, 5/4, 3/2, 7/4]
```
::::
:::

The same questions make sense for the height function on the sphere, where the answers are regions of a surface
rather than subsets of a line. This exercise produces preimages that are caps, circles and the empty set, and the
circles of latitude among them are the level sets used later to give the sphere coordinates.

::: {#exr-map-height-cap}
#### Preimage of a cap

For the height function $h(X, Y, Z) = Z$ on the sphere, describe the preimages of the interval $(\tfrac12, 1]$, of
the point $0$ and of the interval $[2, 3]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$h^{-1}((\tfrac12, 1])$ is the set of points of the sphere with $Z > \tfrac12$: the open cap above the plane $Z =
\tfrac12$, including the north pole. $h^{-1}(0)$ is the set of points with $Z = 0$ and $X^2 + Y^2 = 1$, the equator,
a circle. $h^{-1}([2, 3])$ is empty, as $|Z| \leq 1$ on the sphere. The level sets $h^{-1}(c)$ for $-1 < c < 1$ are
the circles of latitude $X^2 + Y^2 = 1 - c^2$.

## SageMath

Sage samples points of the sphere in spherical angles and sorts them by their height.

```{.python .sage}
pts = [(sin(t) * cos(p), sin(t) * sin(p), cos(t)) for t in [k * pi / 6 for k in range(7)] for p in [0, pi / 2]]
cap = [P for P in pts if P[2] > 1/2]
equator = [P for P in pts if P[2] == 0]
print("points in the cap Z > 1/2:", cap)
print("points on the equator:", equator, "; points with Z in [2, 3]:", [P for P in pts if 2 <= P[2] <= 3])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
points in the cap Z > 1/2: [(0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1), (1/2, 0, 1/2*sqrt(3)), (0, 1/2, 1/2*sqrt(3))]
points on the equator: [(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)] ; points with Z in [2, 3]: []
```
::::
:::

The hydrogen energy map of @exm-map-energy is computed here on the first three levels. Its image is the set of
energies, and the size of each preimage is the degeneracy of the level.

::: {#exr-map-hydrogen-degeneracy}
#### The energy map of hydrogen

The energy of the label $(n, l, m)$ is $E_n = -R/n^2$, with $R \approx 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}$. On the labels with $n \leq
3$, find the image of the energy map and the preimage of each energy, with its size.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The energy depends on $n$ alone, so the image is $\{-R, -R/4, -R/9\}$. The preimage of $-R/n^2$ is the set of all
labels with that $n$, which has $n^2$ elements (@exr-set-hydrogen-count): $1$, $4$ and $9$ labels.

## SageMath

Sage computes the energies in units of $R$ and groups the labels by energy.

```{.python .sage}
labels = [(n, l, m) for n in range(1, 4) for l in range(n) for m in range(-l, l + 1)]
E = {t: -1 / t[0]^2 for t in labels}
for e in sorted(set(E.values())):
    pre = [t for t in labels if E[t] == e]
    print("E =", e, "R: preimage of size", len(pre), pre if len(pre) < 5 else "")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
E = -1 R: preimage of size 1 [(1, 0, 0)]
E = -1/4 R: preimage of size 4 [(2, 0, 0), (2, 1, -1), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1)]
E = -1/9 R: preimage of size 9
```
::::
:::

Preimages behave well under all three set operations, while images do not. The exercise proves this, which is why
conditions on maps are best phrased with preimages rather than images.

::: {#exr-map-preimage-operations}
#### Preimages preserve the set operations

For a map $f : X \to Y$ and subsets $V, W \subseteq Y$, prove $f^{-1}(V \cup W) = f^{-1}(V) \cup f^{-1}(W)$, $f^{-1}(V
\cap W) = f^{-1}(V) \cap f^{-1}(W)$ and $f^{-1}(V \setminus W) = f^{-1}(V) \setminus f^{-1}(W)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $x \in X$, $x \in f^{-1}(V \cup W)$ means $f(x) \in V$ or $f(x) \in W$, that is $x \in f^{-1}(V)$ or $x \in
f^{-1}(W)$. Replacing "or" by "and" gives the intersection, and by "and not" gives the difference. Each statement
is an equality of the conditions defining the two sets, hence an equality of sets.

## SageMath

Check on the map $x \mapsto x^2 \bmod 7$ from $\{0, \dots, 9\}$ to $\{0, \dots, 6\}$: Sage tests the three rules on
all pairs of subsets of the codomain.

```{.python .sage}
X = range(10); f = {x: x^2 % 7 for x in X}
pre = lambda V: frozenset(x for x in X if f[x] in V)
subs = [frozenset(S) for S in Subsets(range(7))]
ok = all(pre(V | W) == pre(V) | pre(W) and pre(V & W) == pre(V) & pre(W) and pre(V - W) == pre(V) - pre(W) for V in subs for W in subs)
print("pairs tested:", len(subs)^2, "; all three rules hold:", ok)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
pairs tested: 16384 ; all three rules hold: True
```
::::
:::

Images are less well behaved than preimages: they preserve unions but not intersections. The exercise proves the
rule for unions and the inclusion that replaces it for intersections, with an example where it is strict.

::: {#exr-map-image-intersection}
#### Images of unions and intersections

For $f : X \to Y$ and $A, B \subseteq X$, prove $f(A \cup B) = f(A) \cup f(B)$ and $f(A \cap B) \subseteq f(A) \cap
f(B)$, and show that the inclusion is strict for $f(x) = x^2$, $A = [-1, 0]$, $B = [0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$y \in f(A \cup B)$ means $y = f(x)$ for some $x$ in $A$ or in $B$, that is $y \in f(A)$ or $y \in f(B)$. If $y = f(x)$
with $x \in A \cap B$, then $y$ lies in $f(A)$ and in $f(B)$, which gives the inclusion. The converse fails because
$y \in f(A) \cap f(B)$ may come from different points of $A$ and of $B$: for the squaring map $A \cap B = \{0\}$, so
$f(A \cap B) = \{0\}$, while $f(A) = f(B) = [0, 1]$.

## SageMath

Check on the squaring map and the rational points of $A$ and $B$ with denominator $4$.

```{.python .sage}
A = {k / 4 for k in range(-4, 1)}; B = {k / 4 for k in range(0, 5)}
f = lambda S: {s^2 for s in S}
print("f(A n B) =", sorted(f(A & B)), "; f(A) n f(B) =", sorted(f(A) & f(B)))
print("f(A u B) == f(A) u f(B):", f(A | B) == f(A) | f(B))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f(A n B) = [0] ; f(A) n f(B) = [0, 1/16, 1/4, 9/16, 1]
f(A u B) == f(A) u f(B): True
```
::::
:::

The two inclusions of @exm-map-image-preimage-rules hold for every map. The exercise proves them and identifies
the points that make each one strict [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 2.3, Part A, Problem 17].

::: {#exr-map-image-preimage-inclusions}
#### Image of a preimage and preimage of an image

For $f : X \to Y$, $A \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq Y$, prove $A \subseteq f^{-1}(f(A))$ and $f(f^{-1}(V)) = V \cap
f(X)$, so that $f(f^{-1}(V)) \subseteq V$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $a \in A$, then $f(a) \in f(A)$, so $a \in f^{-1}(f(A))$. The first inclusion is strict when some $x \notin A$ has
the same value as a point of $A$. For the second, $y \in f(f^{-1}(V))$ means $y = f(x)$ with $f(x) \in V$, so $y \in V$
and $y \in f(X)$; conversely, if $y \in V \cap f(X)$, write $y = f(x)$, then $x \in f^{-1}(V)$ and $y \in
f(f^{-1}(V))$. The inclusion $f(f^{-1}(V)) \subseteq V$ is strict exactly when $V$ contains values that are not taken.

## SageMath

Check on $f(x) = x^2$ from $\{-3, \dots, 3\}$ to $\{0, \dots, 9\}$ with $A = \{1, 2\}$ and $V = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$.

```{.python .sage}
X = range(-3, 4); f = {x: x^2 for x in X}
img = lambda S: {f[x] for x in S}; pre = lambda V: {x for x in X if f[x] in V}
A = {1, 2}; V = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
print("f^-1(f(A)) =", sorted(pre(img(A))), "contains A:", A <= pre(img(A)))
print("f(f^-1(V)) =", sorted(img(pre(V))), "; V n f(X) =", sorted(V & img(X)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f^-1(f(A)) = [-2, -1, 1, 2] contains A: True
f(f^-1(V)) = [0, 1, 4] ; V n f(X) = [0, 1, 4]
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines the height function of @exr-map-height-cap with the shadow map of @exm-map-circle-shadow,
lifted to the sphere. A region of the sphere described by one map turns out to be a preimage under the other.

::: {#exr-map-sphere-polar-caps}
#### Polar caps two ways

Let $p(X, Y, Z) = (X, Y)$ and $h(X, Y, Z) = Z$ on the sphere $S^2$. Show that $p^{-1}(\{X^2 + Y^2 \leq \tfrac14\}) =
h^{-1}([-1, -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}] \cup [\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, 1])$, the union of two polar caps, and that the preimage
under $p$ of the open unit disc is the sphere minus the equator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

On the sphere $X^2 + Y^2 = 1 - Z^2$. So $X^2 + Y^2 \leq \tfrac14$ holds exactly when $Z^2 \geq \tfrac34$, that is
$Z \leq -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ or $Z \geq \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, and the two preimages are equal by
@exr-set-equality-double-inclusion. In the same way $X^2 + Y^2 < 1$ holds exactly when $Z \neq 0$, so the preimage of
the open disc is $S^2 \setminus h^{-1}(\{0\})$, the sphere minus the equator.

## SageMath

Check on a grid of points of the sphere in spherical angles: Sage compares the two conditions point by point.

```{.python .sage}
pts = [(sin(t) * cos(q), sin(t) * sin(q), cos(t)) for t in [k * pi / 12 for k in range(13)] for q in [0, pi / 3, pi]]
same = all(bool(P[0]^2 + P[1]^2 <= 1/4) == bool(P[2] <= -sqrt(3)/2 or P[2] >= sqrt(3)/2) for P in pts)
same_open = all(bool(P[0]^2 + P[1]^2 < 1) == bool(P[2] != 0) for P in pts)
print("points tested:", len(pts), "; caps agree:", same, "; open disc agrees:", same_open)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
points tested: 39 ; caps agree: True ; open disc agrees: True
```
::::
:::
::::

Of the maps seen so far, some lose information, sending two points to the same value, and some do not. The first of
the three properties of a map singles out the ones that do not: the picture is a set of arrows with no two
arrowheads meeting, and the equivalent statement in terms of preimages, at most one point over each value, is the
form that will be used in proofs.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-injective}
#### Injective map

A map $f : X \to Y$ is **injective** (one-to-one) if distinct elements have distinct values: $f(x) = f(x')$
implies $x = x'$. Equivalently, every point of $Y$ has at most one preimage.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For maps between finite sets injectivity can be settled by inspection, and the first map in @fig-map-diagram is the
model. The second half of the example is the pigeonhole principle in its simplest form: a set with more elements
cannot be mapped injectively into a set with fewer, which is one of the counts collected at the end of the section.

::: {#exm-injective-finite}
#### On finite sets

The first map of @fig-map-diagram, $1 \mapsto x$, $2 \mapsto y$ into $\{x, y, z\}$, is injective. No map from a
three-element set to a two-element set is injective, because three elements cannot have three distinct values among
two.
:::

The maps of @exm-map-identity-constant settle the question at once. The identity and the inclusions never merge
two points, while a constant map merges all of them.

::: {#exm-injective-identity}
#### Identity, inclusions and constants

$\mathrm{id}_X$ and the inclusion $A \to X$ of a subset are injective. A constant map on a set with at least two
elements is not injective; on a set with one element every map is injective.
:::

For functions on the real line, injectivity is the question whether a horizontal line can meet the graph twice.
Exponential and square give the two possible answers, and the square's failure, two arguments with the same value,
is the obstruction that later forces coordinates on a sphere to be restricted.

::: {#exm-injective-exp}
#### The exponential

$\exp : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is injective, since $e^{x} = e^{x'}$ forces $x = x'$; $x \mapsto x^2$ is not,
since $(-1)^2 = 1^2$.
:::

Affine functions are the simplest functions with a formula, and for them the question has a one-line answer. The
slope decides everything.

::: {#exm-injective-affine}
#### Affine functions

$x \mapsto ax + b$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is injective exactly when $a \neq 0$: $ax + b = ax' + b$ gives $a(x - x') = 0$, so
$x = x'$ if $a \neq 0$, while for $a = 0$ the map is constant.
:::

The horizontal-line test of @exm-injective-exp can be drawn. @fig-horizontal-line-test compares a function whose
graph every horizontal line meets at most once with one whose graph a line meets four times.

::: {#exm-injective-horizontal-line}
#### The horizontal-line test

$x \mapsto x + \tfrac12 \sin x$ is injective on $\mathbb{R}$: since $|\sin a - \sin b| \leq |a - b|$ (the chord of the
unit circle between the angles $a$ and $b$ is shorter than the arc), $a \neq b$ gives $|f(a) - f(b)| \geq |a - b| -
\tfrac12|a - b| > 0$. $\sin$ is not: on $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ it takes the value $\tfrac12$
four times.

![The line $y = \tfrac12$ meets the graph of $\sin x$ four times on $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ and the graph of $x + \tfrac12
\sin x$ once.](figures/horizontal_line_test.svg){#fig-horizontal-line-test width=90%}
:::

The wrapping map of @exm-map-functions is not injective on the whole line, since an angle is only determined up to
multiples of $2\pi$, but it becomes injective once the domain is restricted to an open interval of length $2\pi$.
This restriction is what makes the angle a coordinate on an arc of the circle.

::: {#exm-injective-chart}
#### The angle on an arc

$\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is injective on the interval $(0, 2\pi)$, where distinct angles give
distinct points, but not on all of $\mathbb{R}$, where $\varphi$ and $\varphi + 2\pi$ give the same point.
Coordinates are always restricted in this way, to a piece on which they label points uniquely.
:::

Whether a measured quantity is injective on the states decides whether its value identifies the state. The energy
does so for the oscillator but not for hydrogen, and the failure is the degeneracy of @exm-map-energy.

::: {#exm-injective-energy}
#### Energies that label states

$n \mapsto \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac12)$ is injective: each oscillator energy belongs to one level. On the hydrogen
labels the energy $(n, l, m) \mapsto -R/n^2$ is not: $(2, 0, 0)$ and $(2, 1, 1)$ have the same energy. Recording the energy together with the angular momentum
numbers $l$ and $m$ gives an injective map, which is why the three numbers together label the states.
:::

Placing distinguishable particles on sites, at most one per site, is an injective map from particles to sites. This
is how an exclusion rule appears in counting, and the count is a product of decreasing factors.

::: {#exm-injective-particles}
#### Particles on sites with exclusion

An assignment of three distinguishable particles $1, 2, 3$ to five sites with at most one particle per site is an
injective map $\{1, 2, 3\} \to \{1, \dots, 5\}$; there are $5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 60$ of them. Without the exclusion
rule all $5^3 = 125$ maps are allowed.
:::

Three maps out of the sphere show how injectivity depends on what a map remembers. The inclusion remembers
everything, the shadow on the plane forgets the sign of $Z$, and the stereographic projection of
the north pole remembers everything except at one point, where it is not defined.

::: {#exm-injective-sphere-maps}
#### Maps out of the sphere

The inclusion $S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is injective. The map $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto (X, Y)$ is not: $(0, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 0,
-1)$ have the same image. The stereographic projection $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto (X, Y)/(1 - Z)$ on $S^2 \setminus \{(0, 0,
1)\}$ is injective, as an exercise on bijections shows.
:::

On infinite sets injectivity behaves in a way that finite intuition does not prepare for. A set can be mapped
injectively onto a proper part of itself, and whether a rule is injective depends on the domain chosen for it.

::: {#exm-injective-limits}
#### Limits of injectivity

$n \mapsto n + 1$ is an injective map from $\mathbb{N}$ to itself whose image $\mathbb{N} \setminus \{1\}$ misses a
point: no finite set has such a map. $x \mapsto x^2$ is injective on $[0,
\infty)$ but not on $\mathbb{R}$, so injectivity is a property of the rule together with its domain.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader is now asked to settle injectivity for three maps given by their lists of values, and then to count all
injective maps between two small sets. The count is the first instance of the falling factorial, each value having
to avoid the ones already chosen, a count that holds for sets of any size.

::: {#exr-injective-finite-check}
#### Deciding injectivity

Which of the maps $\{1, 2, 3\} \to \{a, b, c, d\}$ given by $(a, b, c)$, $(a, a, b)$, $(d, c, b)$ (the values of
$1, 2, 3$ in order) are injective? Count all the injective maps from a three-element set to a four-element set.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The first and third are injective (distinct values), the second is not ($1$ and $2$ share the value $a$). An
injective map chooses a value for $1$ among $4$, then for $2$ among the $3$ remaining, then for $3$ among $2$:
$4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 24$ injective maps.

## SageMath

Sage tests the three lists of values and counts the injective maps by enumeration.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
maps = {"(a,b,c)": ("a", "b", "c"), "(a,a,b)": ("a", "a", "b"), "(d,c,b)": ("d", "c", "b")}
inj = lambda vals: len(set(vals)) == len(vals)
for k, v in maps.items(): print(k, "injective:", inj(v))
print("injective maps from 3 to 4 elements:", sum(1 for vals in product("abcd", repeat=3) if inj(vals)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(a,b,c) injective: True
(a,a,b) injective: False
(d,c,b) injective: True
injective maps from 3 to 4 elements: 24
```
::::
:::

Three functions of the line are tested next, one affine, one with an absolute value and one restricted to half the
line. Each answer needs either a one-line proof or a single pair of points with equal values.

::: {#exr-injective-affine-check}
#### Three functions of the line

Decide whether $x \mapsto 3x - 2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto |x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $x \mapsto x^2$ on $[0,
\infty)$ are injective.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$3x - 2 = 3x' - 2$ gives $x = x'$, so the first is injective (@exm-injective-affine). $|{-1}| = |1|$, so the second
is not. For $x, x' \geq 0$, $x^2 = x'^2$ gives $(x - x')(x + x') = 0$; if $x + x' = 0$ then $x = x' = 0$, and
otherwise $x = x'$: the third is injective.

## SageMath

Sage solves $f(x) = f(x')$ for the affine map, lists the arguments in $\{-1, 1\}$ with $|x| = 1$, and factors $x^2 - x'^2$.

```{.python .sage}
x, xp = var("x xp")
print("3x - 2 = 3x' - 2:", solve(3*x - 2 == 3*xp - 2, xp))
print("|x| = |x'| at x = 1:", [s for s in [-1, 1] if abs(s) == abs(1)])
print("x^2 - x'^2 =", (x^2 - xp^2).factor(), "; x + x' = 0 with x, x' >= 0 forces x = x' = 0")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
3x - 2 = 3x' - 2: [
xp == x
]
|x| = |x'| at x = 1: [-1, 1]
x^2 - x'^2 = (x + xp)*(x - xp) ; x + x' = 0 with x, x' >= 0 forces x = x' = 0
```
::::
:::

Multiplication by a fixed number on the remainders modulo $n$ is injective for some multipliers and not for others.
The exercise decides two cases, which return in the counts at the end of the section.

::: {#exr-injective-mod}
#### Multiplication on remainders

On the set $\mathbb{Z}_n = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ of remainders modulo $n$, with arithmetic modulo $n$, decide
whether $k \mapsto 3k$ is injective for $n = 7$, and
whether $k \mapsto 2k$ is injective for $n = 6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Modulo $7$ the values of $3k$ for $k = 0, \dots, 6$ are $0, 3, 6, 2, 5, 1, 4$, all distinct: injective. Modulo $6$,
$2 \cdot 0 = 0 = 2 \cdot 3$, so $k \mapsto 2k$ is not injective.

## SageMath

Sage lists the values in `Integers(n)` and tests whether they are distinct.

```{.python .sage}
for n, a in ((7, 3), (6, 2)):
    R = Integers(n); vals = [a * R(k) for k in range(n)]
    print("n =", n, "a =", a, ":", vals, "injective:", len(set(vals)) == n)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n = 7 a = 3 : [0, 3, 6, 2, 5, 1, 4] injective: True
n = 6 a = 2 : [0, 2, 4, 0, 2, 4] injective: False
```
::::
:::

A strictly increasing function cannot take the same value twice, which makes monotonicity the practical test for
injectivity on the line. This exercise applies the test to two cubics, one that passes and one that fails at three
points, and lets Sage find the roots that witness the failure.

::: {#exr-injective-monotone}
#### A strictly increasing function is injective

Show that $f(x) = x^3 + x$ is injective on $\mathbb{R}$, and that $g(x) = x^3 - x$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$f(x') - f(x) = (x' - x)(x'^2 + x'x + x^2 + 1)$, and $x'^2 + x'x + x^2 + 1 = (x' + \tfrac{x}{2})^2 + \tfrac34 x^2 + 1 >
0$, so $x < x'$ gives $f(x) < f(x')$: $f$ is strictly increasing, and equal values force equal arguments.
For $g$, $g(-1) = g(0) = g(1) = 0$: three arguments with the same value.

## SageMath

Sage factors $f(x') - f(x)$ and finds the roots of $g$.

```{.python .sage}
x, xp = var("x xp")
f = lambda t: t^3 + t; g = x^3 - x
print("f(x') - f(x) =", (f(xp) - f(x)).factor())
print("roots of g:", solve(g == 0, x))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f(x') - f(x) = -(x^2 + x*xp + xp^2 + 1)*(x - xp)
roots of g: [
x == -1,
x == 1,
x == 0
]
```
::::
:::

The exclusion rule of @exm-injective-particles is counted here for six sites. Comparing with the count without
exclusion shows how strongly the rule restricts the configurations.

::: {#exr-injective-count-placements}
#### Placing particles with exclusion

Three distinguishable particles are placed on six sites. Count the placements with at most one particle per site,
and the placements without restriction; what fraction obeys the exclusion rule?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A placement with exclusion is an injective map from the three particles to the six sites: $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 = 120$
of them, each particle choosing among the sites left free. Without restriction there are $6^3 = 216$ maps. The
fraction is $120/216 = 5/9$.

## SageMath

Sage enumerates all maps from three particles to six sites and keeps the injective ones.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
allmaps = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=3))
inj = [m for m in allmaps if len(set(m)) == 3]
print("all:", len(allmaps), "; injective:", len(inj), "; fraction:", QQ(len(inj)) / len(allmaps))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
all: 216 ; injective: 120 ; fraction: 5/9
```
::::
:::

The restriction that rescued the circle parametrisation in @exm-injective-chart has a two-dimensional analogue for
the sphere. Spherical coordinates are injective on an open rectangle of angles but collapse an entire edge of the
closed rectangle to the north pole; the exercise locates the collapse precisely, and that is why spherical
coordinates leave out the poles.

::: {#exr-injective-sphere-parametrisation}
#### Where spherical coordinates are injective

Is $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$ injective on the pairs
with $0 < \theta < \pi$, $0 < \varphi < 2\pi$? On the pairs with $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$, $0 \leq \varphi < 2\pi$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

On the open range it is: $\cos\theta$ determines $\theta$ in $(0, \pi)$, where the cosine is strictly
decreasing, and then $\sin\theta > 0$ lets $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ determine $\varphi$ in $(0, 2\pi)$
(@exm-injective-chart). On the closed range it is not: every $(0, \varphi)$ is sent to the north pole $(0, 0, 1)$, so
the pole has infinitely many preimages. Spherical coordinates label points uniquely only away from the poles.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the map at $\theta = 0$ for three values of $\varphi$, and at two distinct interior points.

```{.python .sage}
th, ph = var("th ph")
P = lambda t, p: (sin(t) * cos(p), sin(t) * sin(p), cos(t))
print("theta = 0:", [P(0, p) for p in (0, pi / 2, pi)])
print("interior points:", P(pi / 3, pi / 4), "and", P(pi / 3, 3 * pi / 4), "differ:", P(pi / 3, pi / 4) != P(pi / 3, 3 * pi / 4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
theta = 0: [(0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1)]
interior points: (1/4*sqrt(3)*sqrt(2), 1/4*sqrt(3)*sqrt(2), 1/2) and (-1/4*sqrt(3)*sqrt(2), 1/4*sqrt(3)*sqrt(2), 1/2) differ: True
```
::::
:::

Injectivity can be read off preimages of images: a map is injective exactly when it never adds points on the way
down and back up. The exercise proves this criterion, which sharpens the inclusion of
@exr-map-image-preimage-inclusions.

::: {#exr-injective-preimage-criterion}
#### Injectivity through preimages of images

Prove that $f : X \to Y$ is injective if and only if $f^{-1}(f(A)) = A$ for every subset $A \subseteq X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The inclusion $A \subseteq f^{-1}(f(A))$ always holds (@exr-map-image-preimage-inclusions). If $f$ is injective and $x
\in f^{-1}(f(A))$, then $f(x) = f(a)$ for some $a \in A$, so $x = a \in A$: equality holds. Conversely, if equality
holds for every $A$ and $f(x) = f(x')$, take $A = \{x'\}$: then $x \in f^{-1}(f(\{x'\})) = \{x'\}$, so $x = x'$.

## SageMath

Check on two maps of $\{0, \dots, 5\}$, $k \mapsto 5k \bmod 6$ (injective) and $k \mapsto k^2 \bmod 6$ (not): Sage
tests the condition on all $64$ subsets.

```{.python .sage}
X = range(6)
def criterion(f):
    pre = lambda V: {x for x in X if f[x] in V}
    return all(pre({f[a] for a in A}) == set(A) for A in Subsets(X))
for name, f in (("5k mod 6", {k: 5 * k % 6 for k in X}), ("k^2 mod 6", {k: k^2 % 6 for k in X})):
    print(name, ": injective", len(set(f.values())) == 6, "; criterion holds", criterion(f))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
5k mod 6 : injective True ; criterion holds True
k^2 mod 6 : injective False ; criterion holds False
```
::::
:::

Images of intersections were only contained in intersections of images in @exr-map-image-intersection. The
exercise shows that equality for all pairs of subsets is again equivalent to injectivity.

::: {#exr-injective-intersection-criterion}
#### Injectivity through images of intersections

Prove that $f : X \to Y$ is injective if and only if $f(A \cap B) = f(A) \cap f(B)$ for all $A, B \subseteq X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The inclusion $f(A \cap B) \subseteq f(A) \cap f(B)$ always holds (@exr-map-image-intersection). If $f$ is injective
and $y \in f(A) \cap f(B)$, then $y = f(a) = f(b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$; injectivity gives $a = b \in A \cap B$,
so $y \in f(A \cap B)$. Conversely, if $f(x) = f(x')$ with $x \neq x'$, take $A = \{x\}$, $B = \{x'\}$: $f(A \cap B) =
f(\emptyset) = \emptyset$ but $f(A) \cap f(B) = \{f(x)\}$, so equality fails.

## SageMath

Check on $k \mapsto k^2 \bmod 5$ on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$, which is not injective: Sage finds a pair of subsets where
equality fails.

```{.python .sage}
X = range(5); f = {k: k^2 % 5 for k in X}
img = lambda S: {f[x] for x in S}
bad = [(sorted(A), sorted(B)) for A in Subsets(X) for B in Subsets(X) if img(set(A) & set(B)) != img(A) & img(B)]
print("injective:", len(set(f.values())) == 5, "; failing pairs:", len(bad), "; first:", bad[0])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
injective: False ; failing pairs: 240 ; first: ([1], [4])
```
::::
:::

An injective map between finite sets cannot have a smaller codomain than domain. The exercise proves this
inequality, the pigeonhole principle.

::: {#exr-injective-pigeonhole}
#### The pigeonhole principle

Prove that if $f : X \to Y$ is injective and $X$, $Y$ are finite, then $|X| \leq |Y|$. Deduce that among any
$n + 1$ integers two have the same remainder on division by $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_k\}$ with the $x_i$ distinct, injectivity makes $f(x_1), \dots, f(x_k)$ distinct elements of
$Y$, so $Y$ has at least $k = |X|$ elements. The remainder map from $n + 1$ given integers to $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$
goes from a set of $n + 1$ elements to a set of $n$ elements, so it is not injective: two of the integers have the
same remainder.

## SageMath

Check on $n = 6$: Sage draws seven random integers, computes their remainders and finds a repeated one.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(1)
nums = [ZZ.random_element(-1000, 1000) for _ in range(7)]
rem = [a % 6 for a in nums]
print("integers:", nums, "\nremainders:", rem, "; a remainder repeats:", len(set(rem)) < 7)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
integers: [-794, -385, 627, 430, 585, 71, -251]
remainders: [4, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 1] ; a remainder repeats: True
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines injectivity with the image of @def-map and the geometric sets of @exm-set-geometric.
Archimedes' projection sends the sphere minus the poles horizontally onto the cylinder around it, and is the map
behind his theorem on the area of a spherical zone.

::: {#exr-injective-archimedes}
#### Archimedes' projection

Let $C = \{(X, Y, Z) : X^2 + Y^2 = 1\}$ be the unit cylinder. Show that $a(X, Y, Z) = (X/r, Y/r, Z)$, with $r =
\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, is an injective map from $S^2 \setminus \{(0, 0, 1), (0, 0, -1)\}$ to $C$, and find its image.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Away from the poles $r = \sqrt{1 - Z^2} > 0$, and $(X/r)^2 + (Y/r)^2 = 1$, so $a$ maps into $C$. If $a(X, Y, Z) =
a(X', Y', Z')$, the third coordinates give $Z = Z'$, hence $r = r'$, and then $X = X'$, $Y = Y'$: $a$ is injective.
The third coordinate of $a(P)$ is $Z \in (-1, 1)$, and every $(U, V, W) \in C$ with $-1 < W < 1$ is the image of
$(rU, rV, W)$ with $r = \sqrt{1 - W^2}$, which lies on the sphere. So the image is the open cylinder $\{(U, V, W) \in
C : -1 < W < 1\}$.

## SageMath

Check on the point $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$ of the sphere: Sage maps it to the cylinder and back.

```{.python .sage}
P = vector([1/2, 1/2, 1/sqrt(2)])
r = sqrt(P[0]^2 + P[1]^2)
Q = vector([P[0] / r, P[1] / r, P[2]])
back = vector([sqrt(1 - Q[2]^2) * Q[0], sqrt(1 - Q[2]^2) * Q[1], Q[2]])
print("P on the sphere:", bool(P * P == 1), "; a(P) =", Q, "on the cylinder:", bool(Q[0]^2 + Q[1]^2 == 1))
print("recovered P:", back == P)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
P on the sphere: True ; a(P) = (sqrt(1/2), sqrt(1/2), 1/2*sqrt(2)) on the cylinder: True
recovered P: True
```
::::
:::
::::

The second property of a map looks at the other end of the arrows: whether every point of the codomain is reached.
The picture is that no element of the target is left without an incoming arrow, and the condition is simply that
the image, defined in @def-map, is the whole codomain.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-surjective}
#### Surjective map

A map $f : X \to Y$ is **surjective** (onto) if its image is all of $Y$: every $y \in Y$ equals $f(x)$ for at
least one $x$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a finite set, surjectivity is checked by seeing whether every target value appears in the table, and the second
map of @fig-map-diagram shows the typical case. Counting the surjective maps among the eight maps from three
elements to two is a matter of excluding the constant maps, a count that the exercises extend.

::: {#exm-surjective-finite}
#### On finite sets

The second map of @fig-map-diagram, $1, 2 \mapsto x$, $3 \mapsto y$, is surjective onto $\{x, y\}$. Of the eight
maps from a three-element set to $\{x, y\}$, six are surjective, all but the two constant maps.
:::

The maps of @exm-map-identity-constant answer the question as simply as they answered the question of
injectivity, but with the roles changed. The inclusion of a proper subset is injective and not surjective.

::: {#exm-surjective-identity}
#### Identity, inclusions and the image

$\mathrm{id}_X$ is surjective. The inclusion $A \to X$ is surjective only when $A = X$. Every map $f : X \to Y$ is
surjective onto its image, viewed as a map $X \to f(X)$: surjectivity depends on the declared codomain.
:::

For functions on the real line, surjectivity onto $\mathbb{R}$ asks whether every horizontal line meets the graph
at least once. The cube, the square and the exponential give three different images, and comparing them with
@exm-injective-exp shows that injectivity and surjectivity are independent properties.

::: {#exm-surjective-cube}
#### Polynomials

$x \mapsto x^3$ is surjective onto $\mathbb{R}$ (every real number has a cube root); $x \mapsto x^2$ is not (its
image misses the negative numbers); $\exp$ is not (its image is the positive numbers).
:::

Maps between the integers and the real line give simple examples in both directions. Rounding down reaches every
integer, while doubling an integer reaches only the even ones.

::: {#exm-surjective-floor}
#### Floor and doubling

The floor $x \mapsto \lfloor x \rfloor$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is surjective, since $\lfloor k \rfloor = k$.
$k \mapsto 2k$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is not, its image being the even integers, but $x \mapsto 2x$ from
$\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is, with $y = 2 \cdot \tfrac{y}{2}$.
:::

Projections forget coordinates, and whether they are surjective depends on the set they start from. The shadow of
the circle in @fig-circle-shadow covers only a segment of the line, while the shadow of the plane covers all of it.

::: {#exm-surjective-projection}
#### Projections

$(X, Y) \mapsto X$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is surjective. Restricted to the circle it is not surjective
onto $\mathbb{R}$, but it is surjective onto $[-1, 1]$ (@exm-map-circle-shadow).
:::

The wrapping map onto the circle and the spherical angles onto the sphere reach every point of their targets, so
they are surjective even though neither is injective. Every point of the sphere has a latitude and a longitude,
which is the content of the second statement.

::: {#exm-surjective-orbit}
#### Parametrisations

$\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is surjective from $\mathbb{R}$ onto the circle. The spherical angles
of @exm-map-projection are surjective onto the sphere: a point $(X, Y, Z)$ has $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ with $\cos\theta
= Z$, and then $\sin\theta = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$ and an angle $\varphi$ of the point $(X, Y)$ of the plane.
:::

The energy maps of @exm-map-energy are surjective onto the spectrum but not onto the real line. In physics this is
the statement that a measurement of the energy returns only these values.

::: {#exm-surjective-energy}
#### Spectra as images

$n \mapsto \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac12)$ is surjective onto the set $\{\tfrac12\hbar\omega, \tfrac32\hbar\omega, \dots\}$
of oscillator energies, and not onto $\mathbb{R}$. The map $(n, l, m) \mapsto n$ on the hydrogen labels is surjective
onto $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$, since $(n, 0, 0)$ is a label for every $n$.
:::

An assignment of particles to energy levels is surjective when every level is occupied. Counting such assignments
needs the exclusion of the maps that miss a level, the same step as in @exm-surjective-finite.

::: {#exm-surjective-occupation}
#### Every level occupied

Three distinguishable particles are put into two levels. Of the $2^3 = 8$ assignments, those that leave a level
empty put all three particles in the same level, so $8 - 2 = 6$ assignments occupy both levels.
:::

Restricting the domain of a map can destroy surjectivity, or keep it, depending on how much is removed. The cosine
on two intervals of different length shows both outcomes.

::: {#exm-surjective-restriction}
#### Restricting the domain

$\cos$ restricted to $[0, \pi]$ is still surjective onto $[-1, 1]$; restricted to $[0, \tfrac\pi2]$ its image is $[0,
1]$. The wrapping map restricted to $[0, \pi]$ has image the upper half of the circle, so it is no longer
surjective onto $S^1$.
:::

On a finite set with as many elements in the domain as in the codomain, surjective and injective are the same
property, as an exercise below proves. On infinite sets this fails in both directions, and two maps of $\mathbb{N}$
to itself show it.

::: {#exm-surjective-infinite}
#### Surjective but not injective on $\mathbb{N}$

$n \mapsto \lceil n/2 \rceil$, the smallest integer $\geq n/2$, sends $1, 2, 3, 4, \dots$ to $1, 1, 2, 2, \dots$: it is
surjective onto $\mathbb{N}$ but not injective. The shift $n \mapsto n + 1$ of @exm-injective-limits is injective but
not surjective.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise decides surjectivity for three maps given by formulas. In each case either a preimage is found
for every target value, or one target value without a preimage is named.

::: {#exr-surjective-check}
#### Deciding surjectivity

Decide whether $k \mapsto k + 5$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, $k \mapsto 3k$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ and
$x \mapsto x^2$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $[0, \infty)$ are surjective.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Every integer $m$ equals $(m - 5) + 5$, so the first map is surjective. $1$ is not a multiple of $3$, so the second
is not. Every $y \geq 0$ equals $(\sqrt y)^2$, so the third is surjective onto $[0, \infty)$.

## SageMath

Sage looks for preimages of the integers $-3, \dots, 3$ under the first two maps among the integers $-10, \dots, 10$.

```{.python .sage}
targets = range(-3, 4); dom = range(-10, 11)
print("k + 5 reaches:", [m for m in targets if any(k + 5 == m for k in dom)])
print("3k reaches:", [m for m in targets if any(3 * k == m for k in dom)])
print("x^2 = 7 at x =", solve(var("x")^2 == 7, var("x")))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k + 5 reaches: [-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]
3k reaches: [-3, 0, 3]
x^2 = 7 at x = [
x == -sqrt(7),
x == sqrt(7)
]
```
::::
:::

Whether a map is surjective depends on the codomain declared for it, not on the rule alone. This exercise asks for
the images of two familiar functions and then for the codomains onto which they are surjective, making the point
of @exm-surjective-identity that any map becomes surjective once its codomain is shrunk to its image.

::: {#exr-surjective-sin}
#### The image of a function

Find the image of $\sin : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and of $x \mapsto x^2 + 1$; onto which codomains are they
surjective?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|\sin x| \leq 1$, and every $y \in [-1, 1]$ is $\sin(\arcsin y)$, so $\sin$ has image $[-1, 1]$: it is surjective
onto $[-1, 1]$ but not onto $\mathbb{R}$. $x^2 + 1 \geq 1$, and every $y \geq 1$ is the value at $\sqrt{y - 1}$, so
the image is $[1, \infty)$. Each map is surjective onto any codomain equal to its image, and onto no larger one.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the sine at its critical points, the minimum of $x^2 + 1$, and a preimage of a sample value of each image.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
print("critical points of sin in [0, 2 pi]:", [pi / 2, 3 * pi / 2], "; values:", sin(pi / 2), sin(3 * pi / 2))
print("sin(arcsin(1/3)) =", sin(arcsin(1/3)), "; x^2 + 1 at sqrt(4 - 1):", (x^2 + 1).subs(x=sqrt(3)), "; minimum of x^2 + 1:", (x^2 + 1).subs(x=0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
critical points of sin in [0, 2 pi]: [1/2*pi, 3/2*pi] ; values: 1 -1
sin(arcsin(1/3)) = 1/3 ; x^2 + 1 at sqrt(4 - 1): 4 ; minimum of x^2 + 1: 1
```
::::
:::

Surjections are harder to count than arbitrary maps, because the maps that miss a value have to be excluded. The
exercise does this for two small cases, one by excluding the constant maps and one where surjective turns out to
mean bijective, and an enumeration in Sage displays the maps behind each count.

::: {#exr-surjective-count}
#### Counting surjections

How many of the $2^4 = 16$ maps from $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ to $\{x, y\}$ are surjective? And how many maps from a
three-element set to a three-element set are surjective?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A map to $\{x, y\}$ fails to be surjective exactly when it misses $x$ or misses $y$, that is when it is constant: all
but the two constant maps are surjective, $16 - 2 = 14$. From three elements to three, a surjective map takes three
distinct values on three elements, so it is also injective, hence a bijection; there are $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6$.

## SageMath

Sage enumerates the maps as lists of values and keeps those that take every value.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
```
