```{.python .sage}
def hausdorff(T, X):
    return all(any(a in U and b in V and not (U & V) for U in T for V in T) for a in X for b in X if a < b)
for X in ([1, 2], [1, 2, 3]):
    T = topologies(X); h = [t for t in T if hausdorff(t, X)]
    print("points:", len(X), "topologies:", len(T), "Hausdorff:", len(h), "discrete:", all(len(t) == 2^len(X) for t in h))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
points: 2 topologies: 4 Hausdorff: 1 discrete: True
points: 3 topologies: 29 Hausdorff: 1 discrete: True
```
::::
:::

The separating balls of @exm-hausdorff-rn are computed for two concrete points of the plane. The exercise also checks
that a smaller radius would do, but a larger one would not.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-separate-points}
#### Separating two points of the plane

For $p = (0, 0)$ and $q = (3, 4)$, give disjoint balls around $p$ and $q$, and show that the balls of radius $3$ around
them meet.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$d = |q - p| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, so $B_{5/2}(p)$ and $B_{5/2}(q)$ are disjoint by the triangle inequality, as in
@exm-hausdorff-rn; any radius $r \leq 5/2$ works as well. The midpoint $m = (3/2, 2)$ has $|m - p| = |m - q| = 5/2 < 3$, so
it lies in both balls of radius $3$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $d$ and tests the points of a fine grid for membership in both balls of each radius.

```{.python .sage}
p = vector(QQ, [0, 0]); q = vector(QQ, [3, 4])
d = (q - p).norm(); print("d =", d)
grid = [vector(QQ, [i / 8, j / 8]) for i in range(-8, 33) for j in range(-8, 41)]
for r in [5/2, 3]:
    both = [x for x in grid if (x - p).norm() < r and (x - q).norm() < r]
    print("radius", r, ": grid points in both balls:", len(both))
m = (p + q) / 2; print("midpoint", m, "distances", (m - p).norm(), (m - q).norm())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
d = 5
radius 5/2 : grid points in both balls: 0
radius 3 : grid points in both balls: 139
midpoint (3/2, 2) distances 5/2 5/2
```
::::
:::

On the circle the separating open sets can be chosen as arcs, and for two points a quarter turn apart they can be cut out
by one linear inequality each. The exercise asks for them and checks that they are open in the subspace topology.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-circle-arcs}
#### Separating two points of the circle

Show that $U = S^1 \cap \{u > v\}$ and $V = S^1 \cap \{v > u\}$ are disjoint open sets of $S^1$ containing $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$,
and describe them by angles.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The half-planes $\{u > v\}$ and $\{v > u\}$ are open, as preimages of $(0, \infty)$ under the continuous functions $u - v$ and
$v - u$ (@exm-continuous-level-sets), and disjoint; their traces on $S^1$ are open in $S^1$ (@def-subspace-topology) and
disjoint. $(1, 0)$ has $u > v$ and $(0, 1)$ has $v > u$. With $(u, v) = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$, $\cos\varphi - \sin\varphi =
\sqrt2\cos(\varphi + \pi/4)$, so $U$ is the arc $-3\pi/4 < \varphi < \pi/4$ and $V$ the arc $\pi/4 < \varphi < 5\pi/4$.

## SageMath

Sage checks the identity for $\cos\varphi - \sin\varphi$ and the side of each point.

```{.python .sage}
phi = var("phi")
print("cos - sin - sqrt(2) cos(phi + pi/4) =", (cos(phi) - sin(phi) - sqrt(2) * cos(phi + pi / 4)).expand_trig().simplify_full())
side = lambda P: sign(P[0] - P[1])
print("side of (1, 0):", side((1, 0)), "; side of (0, 1):", side((0, 1)))
print("ends of U:", [(cos(a), sin(a)) for a in (-3 * pi / 4, pi / 4)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
cos - sin - sqrt(2) cos(phi + pi/4) = 0
side of (1, 0): 1 ; side of (0, 1): -1
ends of U: [(-1/2*sqrt(2), -1/2*sqrt(2)), (1/2*sqrt(2), 1/2*sqrt(2))]
```
::::
:::

The first proof exercise is the consequence of the definition used most often: points are closed. The proof assembles
the complement of a point from the neighbourhoods that separate it from every other point.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-points-closed}
#### Points are closed

Prove that in a Hausdorff space every single point $\{p\}$ is a closed set, and show that the converse fails.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For each $q \neq p$ choose disjoint neighbourhoods $U_q \ni q$ and $V_q \ni p$; then $p \notin U_q$. The union of all $U_q$ is
open (@def-topological-space) and equals $X \setminus \{p\}$, so $\{p\}$ is closed. The converse fails: in the cofinite
topology on an infinite set every point is closed, but the space is not Hausdorff (@exm-hausdorff-cofinite).

## SageMath

Check on the $29$ topologies of three points: Sage counts those in which every point is closed and those that are
Hausdorff, and tests that the second are among the first.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import combinations
F = frozenset; X = [1, 2, 3]
subs = [F(c) for r in range(4) for c in combinations(X, r)]
tops = [T for T in ({subs[i] for i in range(8) if m >> i & 1} for m in range(256))
        if F() in T and F(X) in T and all(A | B in T and A & B in T for A in T for B in T)]
closed_pts = [T for T in tops if all(F(X) - {p} in T for p in X)]
haus = [T for T in tops if all(any(a in U and b in V and not U & V for U in T for V in T) for a in X for b in X if a < b)]
print("topologies:", len(tops), "; points closed:", len(closed_pts), "; Hausdorff:", len(haus))
print("Hausdorff ones have closed points:", all(T in closed_pts for T in haus))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
topologies: 29 ; points closed: 1 ; Hausdorff: 1
Hausdorff ones have closed points: True
```
::::
:::

The Hausdorff property passes from a space to all its subsets, which is what made @exm-hausdorff-subspace immediate. The
exercise asks for the proof in general, for any Hausdorff space and any subset.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-subspace}
#### Subspaces of Hausdorff spaces

Prove that every subset $Y$ of a Hausdorff space $X$, with the subspace topology, is Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $p \neq q$ in $Y$. As points of $X$ they have disjoint open sets $U \ni p$, $V \ni q$ of $X$. Then $U \cap Y$ and $V \cap Y$
are open in $Y$ (@def-subspace-topology), contain $p$ and $q$, and are disjoint since $(U \cap Y) \cap (V \cap Y) \subseteq U
\cap V = \emptyset$.

## SageMath

Check on the circle: for the points at angles $1$ and $1 + 1/10$, Sage samples the circle and finds no point within half
their distance of both.

```{.python .sage}
a, b = 1, 1 + 1/10
P = lambda t: vector(RDF, [cos(t), sin(t)])
d = (P(a) - P(b)).norm(); print("distance:", round(d, 6))
both = [k for k in range(2000) if (P(2 * pi * k / 2000) - P(a)).norm() < d / 2 and (P(2 * pi * k / 2000) - P(b)).norm() < d / 2]
print("sample points of the circle in both traces:", len(both))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
distance: 0.099958
sample points of the circle in both traces: 0
```
::::
:::

The unique limit of @exm-hausdorff-limits is proved here for every Hausdorff space. The proof compares the late terms of
the sequence with two disjoint neighbourhoods of the two candidate limits.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-limits-unique}
#### Uniqueness of limits

Prove that in a Hausdorff space a sequence converges to at most one point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $x_k$ converges to $p$ and to $q \neq p$. Take disjoint neighbourhoods $U \ni p$, $V \ni q$. There are indices
$K_1$, $K_2$ with $x_k \in U$ for $k \geq K_1$ and $x_k \in V$ for $k \geq K_2$ (@exm-hausdorff-limits). For $k = \max(K_1,
K_2)$ the point $x_k$ lies in $U \cap V = \emptyset$, which is impossible.

## SageMath

Check on $x_k = 1/k$ in $\mathbb{R}$: for the candidate limits $0$ and $q = 1/5$, Sage finds from which index the terms
stay in $B_{q/2}(0)$, and that from then on none lies in $B_{q/2}(q)$.

```{.python .sage}
q = 1/5; r = q / 2
x = [1 / k for k in range(1, 200)]
K = min(k for k in range(1, 200) if all(abs(t) < r for t in x[k - 1:]))
print("terms in B_r(0) from index", K)
print("terms from index K in B_r(q):", [t for t in x[K - 1:] if abs(t - q) < r])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
terms in B_r(0) from index 11
terms from index K in B_r(q): []
```
::::
:::

The definition separates a point from one other point at a time, but finitely many separations can be combined. The
exercise asks for the separation of a point from a finite set, using finite intersections of open sets.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-point-finite-set}
#### A point and a finite set

In a Hausdorff space, let $p \notin \{q_1, \dots, q_m\}$. Show that there are disjoint open sets $U \ni p$ and $V \supseteq
\{q_1, \dots, q_m\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For each $i$ choose disjoint open $U_i \ni p$ and $V_i \ni q_i$. Put $U = U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_m$, open as a finite
intersection and containing $p$, and $V = V_1 \cup \dots \cup V_m$, open and containing every $q_i$. A point of $U \cap V$
lies in some $V_i$ and in $U_i$, which are disjoint; so $U \cap V = \emptyset$.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{R}$ with $p = 0$ and the set $\{1, 2, -3\}$: Sage takes balls of half the distances and verifies on a
grid that $U$ and $V$ do not meet.

```{.python .sage}
p = 0; qs = [1, 2, -3]
rs = [abs(q - p) / 2 for q in qs]
U = lambda x: all(abs(x - p) < r for r in rs)
V = lambda x: any(abs(x - q) < r for q, r in zip(qs, rs))
grid = [k / 100 for k in range(-500, 501)]
print("radius of U:", min(rs), "; grid points in U and V:", [x for x in grid if U(x) and V(x)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
radius of U: 1/2 ; grid points in U and V: []
```
::::
:::

A continuous injective map into a Hausdorff space pulls the Hausdorff property back to its domain. The exercise asks for
the proof and applies it to the quotient of the line that is the circle of angles.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-continuous-injective}
#### Pulling back the separation

Let $f : X \to Y$ be continuous and injective, with $Y$ Hausdorff. Prove that $X$ is Hausdorff, and deduce that the
quotient $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ is Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $p \neq q$ in $X$, $f(p) \neq f(q)$ by injectivity, so there are disjoint open $U \ni f(p)$, $V \ni f(q)$ in $Y$. Their
preimages are open (@def-continuous-map), contain $p$ and $q$, and are disjoint, since $f^{-1}(U) \cap f^{-1}(V) = f^{-1}(U \cap
V) = \emptyset$. The map $[\varphi] \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ from $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ to $S^1$ is continuous
and injective (@exm-quotient-circle-top) and $S^1$ is Hausdorff (@exm-hausdorff-subspace), so $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$
is Hausdorff.

## SageMath

Check on the classes of $\varphi = 1$ and $\varphi = 1 + \pi$: Sage computes their images on the circle and verifies that
the preimages of the two separating balls contain no common angle in a sample.

```{.python .sage}
f = lambda t: vector(RDF, [cos(t), sin(t)])
a, b = 1, 1 + pi
d = (f(a) - f(b)).norm(); print("distance of the images:", round(d, 6))
common = [k for k in range(4000) if (f(4 * pi * k / 4000) - f(a)).norm() < d / 2 and (f(4 * pi * k / 4000) - f(b)).norm() < d / 2]
print("sampled angles in both preimages:", len(common))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
distance of the images: 2.0
sampled angles in both preimages: 0
```
::::
:::

The line with two origins of @exm-hausdorff-line-two-origins is examined in detail. The exercise asks both for the
failure of the Hausdorff property and for the local resemblance to the line, which together show that the two
properties are independent.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-two-origins}
#### The line with two origins

Take two copies $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}'$ of the line, and identify $x \sim x'$ for all $x \neq 0$. Show that the quotient
is not Hausdorff, and that every point has an open neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open interval.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $\pi$ be the quotient map. An open set $W$ containing the origin $0$ has an open preimage containing $0 \in \mathbb{R}$,
hence an interval $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ of the first copy, so $W$ contains the classes of all $x$ with $0 < |x| <
\varepsilon$. The same holds for a neighbourhood $W'$ of $0'$ with some $\varepsilon'$, and both contain the class of $x =
\min(\varepsilon, \varepsilon')/2$; so $0$ and $0'$ have no disjoint neighbourhoods. The image $\pi(\mathbb{R})$ of the
first copy is open, since its preimage is $\mathbb{R} \cup (\mathbb{R}' \setminus \{0'\})$, and $\pi$ restricted to the first
copy is a continuous bijection onto it whose inverse is continuous, as an open set of $\mathbb{R}$ maps to an open set; so
every point other than $0'$ has the neighbourhood $\pi(\mathbb{R})$ homeomorphic to the line, hence to an open interval
(@exm-homeomorphism-interval), and $0'$ likewise with the second copy.

## SageMath

Sage models the classes by pairs (value, copy) and checks, for given radii around the two origins, that the class of half
the smaller radius lies in both neighbourhoods.

```{.python .sage}
def cls(x, copy):
    return (x, 0) if x != 0 else (0, copy)            # copies 0 and 1 agree away from the origin
print("origins distinct:", cls(0, 0) != cls(0, 1))
for e1, e2 in [(1, 1), (1/10, 1/1000), (1/1000, 1/2)]:
    x = min(e1, e2) / 2                                   # the class of x lies in both neighbourhoods
    print("radii", e1, e2, ": class of", x, "in both:", cls(x, 0) == cls(x, 1) and abs(x) < e1 and abs(x) < e2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
origins distinct: True
radii 1 1 : class of 1/2 in both: True
radii 1/10 1/1000 : class of 1/2000 in both: True
radii 1/1000 1/2 : class of 1/2000 in both: True
```
::::
:::

The last exercise folds the line onto a half-line by identifying each number with its negative. The quotient is
Hausdorff, and the pull-back criterion of @exr-hausdorff-continuous-injective proves it with the absolute value.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-quotient-absolute}
#### Folding the line

Let $x \sim y$ on $\mathbb{R}$ iff $y = \pm x$. Show that the quotient $\mathbb{R}/{\sim}$ is Hausdorff, using the map $[x]
\mapsto |x|$ to $[0, \infty)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The map $g([x]) = |x|$ is well defined, since $|{-x}| = |x|$, and injective, since $|x| = |y|$ means $y = \pm x$. It is
continuous because its composition with the quotient map is the continuous function $x \mapsto |x|$
(@def-quotient-topology). Its target $[0, \infty)$ is Hausdorff as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ (@exm-hausdorff-subspace), so
$\mathbb{R}/{\sim}$ is Hausdorff by @exr-hausdorff-continuous-injective; $g$ is in fact a bijection onto $[0, \infty)$.

## SageMath

Check on the classes $[3]$ and $[-1]$: Sage separates $3$ and $1$ by balls of radius $1$ and pulls them back to sets of
real numbers that are unions of classes.

```{.python .sage}
a, b = 3, -1
r = abs(abs(a) - abs(b)) / 2
U = lambda x: abs(abs(x) - abs(a)) < r; V = lambda x: abs(abs(x) - abs(b)) < r
grid = [QQ(k) / 20 for k in range(-100, 101)]
print("r =", r, "; preimage of U is symmetric:", all(U(x) == U(-x) for x in grid))
print("grid points in both preimages:", [x for x in grid if U(x) and V(x)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
r = 1 ; preimage of U is symmetric: True
grid points in both preimages: []
```
::::
:::
::::

### Compact spaces

The second global property replaces finiteness for infinite spaces: whatever can be done with finitely many open sets
can be done on the whole space. The definition phrases this through open covers, and the picture for subsets of a
coordinate space is a closed and bounded set, with the consequence that continuous functions on it attain their
extremes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-compact}
#### Compact space

An **open cover** of a topological space $X$ is a family of open sets whose union is $X$; a **subcover** is a subfamily
that still covers. The space is **compact** if every open cover has a finite subcover, and a subset is compact if it is
compact in the subspace topology. For subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ this is equivalent to being closed and bounded (the
**Heine-Borel theorem**), and a continuous real function on a compact space is bounded and attains its maximum and
minimum; both facts are proved in the exercises below.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Finite spaces are compact whatever their topology, because a cover of finitely many points needs only finitely many of
its sets. This is the case that compactness generalises [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.3, Part A, Problem 1].

::: {#exm-compact-finite}
#### Finite spaces

If $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_m\}$ and $\{U_\alpha\}$ is an open cover, choose for each $i$ one set $U_{\alpha_i}$ containing $x_i$;
the $m$ sets $U_{\alpha_1}, \dots, U_{\alpha_m}$ cover $X$. So every finite space, and every finite subset of any space, is
compact.
:::

An interval with its endpoints and one without are the first pair to compare, and only the first is compact.
@fig-open-cover shows a finite cover of the closed interval and the cover of the open interval that cannot be reduced.

::: {#exm-compact-interval}
#### Closed and open intervals

$[0, 1]$ is compact, by the Heine-Borel theorem. $(0, 1)$ is not: the open intervals $(1/n, 1)$, $n \geq 2$, cover it, but
finitely many of them lie in the one with the largest $n$ and miss $(0, 1/n]$. Since a homeomorphism carries open sets
to open sets (@exr-homeomorphism-invariance), and hence open covers to open covers, an open interval is not
homeomorphic to a closed one.

![Top, four open intervals covering $[0, 1]$. Bottom, the intervals $(1/n, 1)$ for $n = 2, \dots, 12$: they cover
$(0, 1)$ together with all larger $n$, but each finite family misses the points near $0$.](figures/open_cover.svg){#fig-open-cover width=75%}
:::

A sequence that accumulates at a point gives a non-compact set, and adding the point repairs it. The pair is the
simplest illustration of how closedness enters [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.3, Part A, Problems 3-4].

::: {#exm-compact-sequence-set}
#### $\{1/n\}$ with and without $0$

$S = \{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ is not compact: the intervals $(1/n - 1/(2n^2), 1/n + 1/(2n^2))$ cover $S$, each containing
exactly one point of it, and no finite subfamily covers. $S \cup \{0\}$ is compact: a set of a cover containing $0$
contains $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, hence all $1/n$ with $n > 1/\varepsilon$, and finitely many more sets catch the
rest.
:::

An infinite discrete set is never compact, because its points can be covered one by one. The integers in the line are
of this kind, and so are the sites of an infinite lattice [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.3, Part A, Problem 2].

::: {#exm-compact-integers}
#### The integers

$\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is not compact: the intervals $(n - \tfrac12, n + \tfrac12)$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, cover it and
each contains one integer. The same cover, scaled by $a > 0$, shows that the sites $x = na$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, of an infinite
one-dimensional lattice form a non-compact subset of the line.
:::

The circle, the sphere and the torus are closed and bounded in their coordinate spaces, so they are compact. Ellipses
and the other closed curves of the plane follow in the same way [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.4, Part A, Problems
1-2].

::: {#exm-compact-spheres}
#### Spheres and tori

$S^1 = \{u^2 + v^2 = 1\}$ and $S^2$ are closed, as level sets of continuous functions (@exm-continuous-level-sets), and
bounded, hence compact. So are the ellipse $\{u^2/a^2 + v^2/b^2 = 1\}$ and the torus $T^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ of
@exm-subspace-torus, a level set of $(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} - 2)^2 + z^2$ inside the ball of radius $3$.
:::

The configuration space of a pendulum is a circle, hence compact, and so its potential energy attains a maximum and a
minimum. The phase space is a cylinder, which is not compact, since the momentum is unbounded.

::: {#exm-compact-pendulum}
#### The pendulum

On the configuration circle $\{x^2 + y^2 = \ell^2\}$ the potential $V = mgy$ is continuous
(@exm-continuous-pendulum-energy), so it attains its minimum $-mg\ell$ at the bottom and its maximum $mg\ell$ at the top.
The phase space $S^1 \times \mathbb{R}$ is not compact, the momentum being unbounded, but the states with energy at most
$E_0$ form a closed and bounded subset of it, hence a compact one.
:::

Whether a particle can escape depends on whether the region its energy allows is bounded. The example compares a
potential well with walls on both sides with one that flattens out at infinity.

::: {#exm-compact-potential-well}
#### Bounded and unbounded wells

For $V(x) = x^2$ the allowed region $\{V(x) \leq E\}$ is $[-\sqrt E, \sqrt E]$ for every $E \geq 0$, compact: the particle is
trapped. For $V(x) = -e^{-x^2}$ and $-1 < E < 0$ the region is $[-\sqrt{-\ln(-E)}, \sqrt{-\ln(-E)}]$, compact, but for $E \geq
0$ it is all of $\mathbb{R}$, closed and unbounded, and the particle can escape to infinity.
:::

The harmonic oscillator and the double pendulum give two more compact spaces of physics. One is a region of phase space
cut out by the energy, the other a product of two circles.

::: {#exm-compact-oscillator-torus}
#### The oscillator and two angles

The states of the oscillator with $p^2/2m + kx^2/2 \leq E_0$ form a closed elliptical disc (@exm-open-oscillator-energy),
closed and bounded, hence compact, and so is its edge, the orbit. The configuration space $S^1 \times S^1 \subset
\mathbb{R}^4$ of a double pendulum is closed and bounded, $|x|^2 = 2$ on it, hence compact.
:::

Unbounded sets and sets missing part of their edge are the two ways to fail compactness in a coordinate space. The
example lists the standard cases [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.4, Part A, Problems 3-8].

::: {#exm-compact-plane}
#### Non-compact subsets of coordinate space

$\mathbb{R}^n$, the half-line $[0, \infty)$, the parabola $\{v^2 = u\}$, the hyperbola $\{u^2 - v^2 = 1\}$ and the cylinder
$\{x^2 + y^2 = 1\} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ are closed but unbounded; the open disc and the open upper half-circle are
bounded but not closed. None is compact.
:::

The criterion "closed and bounded" belongs to $\mathbb{R}^n$, not to compactness in general. Inside the half-line $(0,
\infty)$ the set $(0, 1]$ is closed and bounded, and still not compact [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.4, Part A,
Problem 9].

::: {#exm-compact-relative-closed}
#### Closed and bounded is not enough

In the space $X = (0, \infty)$ the subset $(0, 1] = X \cap [-1, 1]$ is closed (@def-subspace-topology) and bounded. It is
not compact: the open sets $(1/n, 2)$, $n \geq 1$, cover it, and finitely many of them miss the points close to $0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the non-compactness of the open interval claimed in @exm-compact-interval by an explicit
cover. Its second part asks why the same cover is of no use on the closed interval.

::: {#exr-compact-proof}
#### A cover without a finite subcover

Show that the open interval $(0, 1)$ is not compact by exhibiting an open cover with no finite subcover, and explain why
the same family is not a cover of $[0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The sets $U_n = (1/n, 1)$, $n \geq 2$, are open and cover $(0, 1)$, since $x > 1/n$ once $n > 1/x$. A finite subfamily
$U_{n_1}, \dots, U_{n_k}$ is contained in $U_N$ with $N = \max n_i$ and misses $1/(2N) \in (0, 1)$. On $[0, 1]$ the family
misses $0$ and $1$, so it is not a cover; any cover of $[0, 1]$ has a set containing $0$, hence an interval $[0,
\varepsilon)$, and this is what makes finitely many sets enough there.

## SageMath

Sage takes a finite subfamily with indices $2, 5, 17, 40$ and finds a point of $(0, 1)$ that it misses.

```{.python .sage}
ns = [2, 5, 17, 40]; N = max(ns); x = 1 / (2 * N)
print("x =", x, "; in some (1/n, 1):", any(1 / n < x < 1 for n in ns))
print("x lies in (1/n, 1) for n =", next(n for n in range(2, 1000) if 1 / n < x))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
x = 1/80 ; in some (1/n, 1): False
x lies in (1/n, 1) for n = 81
```
::::
:::

The compact set $\{1/n\} \cup \{0\}$ of @exm-compact-sequence-set is covered here by a specific family, and the finite
subcover is computed. The set around $0$ does most of the work, and only a few points are left over for the others.

::: {#exr-compact-sequence-subcover}
#### A finite subcover by hand

Cover $K = \{0\} \cup \{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ by $U_0 = (-1/10, 1/10)$ and the sets $U_n = (1/n - 1/(2n^2), 1/n + 1/(2n^2))$.
Find a finite subcover with as few sets as possible.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$U_0$ contains $0$ and every $1/n$ with $n \geq 11$. The points $1, 1/2, \dots, 1/10$ are not in $U_0$, and each $U_n$ contains
exactly one of them, $1/n$, since the gap between $1/n$ and $1/(n \pm 1)$ is larger than $1/(2n^2)$. So $\{U_0, U_1,
\dots, U_{10}\}$ is a subcover, and none of its $11$ sets can be dropped.

## SageMath

Sage lists the points of $K$ outside $U_0$ and, for each $U_n$, the points of $K$ it contains.

```{.python .sage}
K = [0] + [1 / n for n in range(1, 400)]
U0 = lambda x: -1/10 < x < 1/10
Un = lambda n, x: 1 / n - 1 / (2 * n^2) < x < 1 / n + 1 / (2 * n^2)
left = [x for x in K if not U0(x)]; print("outside U0:", left)
print("each U_n, n <= 10, holds one point of K:", all(len([x for x in K if Un(n, x)]) == 1 for n in range(1, 11)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
outside U0: [1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/7, 1/8, 1/9, 1/10]
each U_n, n <= 10, holds one point of K: True
```
::::
:::

Compactness guarantees that a continuous function attains its maximum and minimum, and the exercise shows the guarantee
and its failure on an open interval. The function is a parabola, so the extremes can be found by completing the square.

::: {#exr-compact-extremes}
#### Extremes on a compact set

Find the maximum and minimum of $f(x) = x(2 - x)$ on $[0, 2]$, and explain why $f$ has a maximum but no minimum on the
open interval $(0, 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$f(x) = 1 - (x - 1)^2$, so $f \leq 1$ with equality only at $x = 1$: the maximum is $1$, attained inside $(0, 2)$ as well.
On $[0, 2]$, $(x - 1)^2 \leq 1$, so $f \geq 0$, with $f(0) = f(2) = 0$: the minimum is $0$, at the endpoints. On $(0, 2)$,
$f > 0$, and $f(1/k) = 2/k - 1/k^2$ is as small as we please, so the infimum $0$ is not attained. Compactness of $[0, 2]$
guarantees attained extremes; without it they may be missing.

## SageMath

Sage completes the square and evaluates $f$ near the ends of the interval.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x"); f = x * (2 - x)
print("f - (1 - (x-1)^2) =", (f - (1 - (x - 1)^2)).expand())
print("f(0), f(1), f(2) =", f(x=0), f(x=1), f(x=2))
print("f(1/k) for k = 10, 100, 1000:", [f(x=1/k) for k in (10, 100, 1000)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f - (1 - (x-1)^2) = 0
f(0), f(1), f(2) = 0 1 0
f(1/k) for k = 10, 100, 1000: [19/100, 199/10000, 1999/1000000]
```
::::
:::

The Heine-Borel theorem starts from the compactness of a closed interval, and the exercise asks for it. The proof walks
along the interval as far as finitely many sets of the cover reach, and the least upper bound of the real numbers
ensures that the walk gets to the end.

::: {#exr-compact-closed-interval}
#### Closed intervals are compact

Prove that $[a, b]$ is compact, by considering $s = \sup\{x \in [a, b] : [a, x]$ is covered by finitely many sets of the
cover$\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $[a, b]$; by @def-subspace-topology each $U_\alpha$ is $W_\alpha \cap [a, b]$ with
$W_\alpha$ open in $\mathbb{R}$. The set $A$ of $x \in [a, b]$ with $[a, x]$ covered by finitely many $U_\alpha$ contains $a$ and
is bounded by $b$, so $s = \sup A$ exists and $a \leq s \leq b$. Some $W_\beta$ contains $s$, hence an interval $(s - \delta, s +
\delta)$. There is $x \in A$ with $x > s - \delta$; finitely many sets cover $[a, x]$, and adding $U_\beta$ covers $[a, \min(s +
\delta/2, b)]$. So $\min(s + \delta/2, b) \in A$, which forces $s = b$ and then $b \in A$: finitely many sets cover $[a, b]$.

## SageMath

Check on the cover of $[0, 1]$ by the intervals $(x - (1 + x)/8, x + (1 + x)/8)$, $x \in [0, 1]$: Sage walks along the interval
as in the proof, each time taking the set centred at the current point, and counts the sets needed.

```{.python .sage}
r = lambda x: (1 + x) / 8
s, used = QQ(0), []
while True:
    used.append(s)
    if s + r(s) > 1:
        break
    s = s + r(s) / 2
print("sets used:", len(used), "; centres:", [float(round(c, 3)) for c in used])
print("consecutive sets overlap:", all(c + r(c) > d - r(d) for c, d in zip(used, used[1:])))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sets used: 11 ; centres: [0.0, 0.062, 0.129, 0.199, 0.274, 0.354, 0.439, 0.529, 0.624, 0.726, 0.834]
consecutive sets overlap: True
```
::::
:::

From intervals one passes to rectangles, and then to boxes in any dimension. The exercise asks for the rectangle; the
argument first covers each vertical segment by finitely many sets and then uses the compactness of the horizontal side.

::: {#exr-compact-box}
#### Rectangles and boxes are compact

Prove that $R = [a, b] \times [c, d] \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is compact, and explain why every box $[a_1, b_1] \times \dots \times
[a_n, b_n]$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $\{W_\alpha\}$ be open sets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ covering $R$ (a cover by open sets of $R$ is of this form). Fix $x \in [a, b]$.
Each $(x, y)$, $y \in [c, d]$, lies in some $W_\alpha$ together with an open square $(x - \delta, x + \delta) \times (y - \delta, y
+ \delta)$ (@def-open-set). The intervals $(y - \delta, y + \delta)$ cover $[c, d]$, so finitely many do
(@exr-compact-closed-interval); with $\delta_x$ the smallest of their $\delta$, the strip $(x - \delta_x, x + \delta_x) \times
[c, d]$ is covered by finitely many $W_\alpha$. The intervals $(x - \delta_x, x + \delta_x)$ cover $[a, b]$, so finitely many
do, and the finitely many sets attached to them cover $R$. For boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ the same argument, with $[c, d]$
replaced by a box in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ known to be compact, gives the result by induction on $n$.

## SageMath

Check on $[0, 1]^2$ covered by the open discs of radius $1/5$ centred at all points: Sage takes the centres on a grid of
step $1/8$, which a finite argument of this kind produces, and verifies that a fine sample of the square is covered.

```{.python .sage}
cs = [(QQ(i) / 8, QQ(j) / 8) for i in range(9) for j in range(9)]
pts = [(QQ(i) / 50, QQ(j) / 50) for i in range(51) for j in range(51)]
ok = all(any((x - u)^2 + (y - v)^2 < (1/5)^2 for u, v in cs) for x, y in pts)
print("discs used:", len(cs), "; sample covered:", ok)
print("worst case: half-diagonal of a grid cell =", sqrt(2) / 16, "<", 1/5, ":", bool(sqrt(2) / 16 < 1/5))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
discs used: 81 ; sample covered: True
worst case: half-diagonal of a grid cell = 1/16*sqrt(2) < 1/5 : True
```
::::
:::

A closed subset of a compact space is compact, and the exercise asks for the proof, which adds the complement of the
subset to any cover. With the rectangle of @exr-compact-box this gives the compactness of the circle.

::: {#exr-compact-closed-subset}
#### Closed subsets of compact spaces

Prove that a closed subset of a compact space is compact, and deduce that the circle $\{u^2 + v^2 = 1\}$ is compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $C \subseteq X$ be closed and let $\{W_\alpha\}$ be open sets of $X$ whose traces cover $C$. Adding the open set $X
\setminus C$ gives an open cover of $X$; a finite subcover of $X$, with $X \setminus C$ removed, consists of finitely many
$W_\alpha$ whose traces cover $C$. The circle is closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (@exm-continuous-level-sets), hence in the square
$[-1, 1]^2$, which is compact (@exr-compact-box); so the circle is compact. The same argument applies to every sphere, a
closed subset of a cube.

## SageMath

Check on the cover of the square $[-1, 1]^2$ by the discs of radius $1/2$ at the grid points of step $1/2$, together with the
complement of the circle: Sage keeps the discs that meet the circle and checks that they cover a fine sample of it.

```{.python .sage}
cs = [(QQ(i) / 2, QQ(j) / 2) for i in range(-2, 3) for j in range(-2, 3)]
circ = [(cos(2 * pi * k / 400).n(), sin(2 * pi * k / 400).n()) for k in range(400)]
keep = [c for c in cs if any((x - c[0])^2 + (y - c[1])^2 < 1/4 for x, y in circ)]
print("discs meeting the circle:", len(keep), "of", len(cs))
print("they cover the sample:", all(any((x - u)^2 + (y - v)^2 < 1/4 for u, v in keep) for x, y in circ))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
discs meeting the circle: 20 of 25
they cover the sample: True
```
::::
:::

The two previous exercises combine into the Heine-Borel theorem stated in @def-compact. The exercise asks for both
directions; the converse uses covers by balls and the separation of points of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

::: {#exr-compact-heine-borel}
#### The Heine-Borel theorem

Prove that a subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $K$ is closed and bounded, it lies in a box $[-R, R]^n$, compact by @exr-compact-box, and is closed in it, so it is
compact by @exr-compact-closed-subset. Conversely let $K$ be compact. The balls $B_k(0)$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, cover $K$, and a
finite subfamily lies in the largest of them, so $K$ is bounded. For $p \notin K$, the sets $U_k = \{x : |x - p| > 1/k\}$ are
open and cover $K$; finitely many lie in one $U_N$, so $B_{1/N}(p)$ misses $K$. The complement of $K$ is thus open and $K$ is
closed.

## SageMath

Check on the closed disc and the open disc: Sage computes, for the cover of the open disc by the discs $\{|x| < 1 - 1/k\}$,
the largest radius reached by a finite subfamily, and the distance of the closed disc from a point outside it.

```{.python .sage}
ks = [2, 3, 10, 50]
print("radius covered by the finite subfamily:", max(1 - 1 / k for k in ks), "< 1, so points of the open disc are missed")
p = vector(QQ, [3, 4]); print("point outside the closed disc at distance", p.norm() - 1, "from it, a ball of that radius misses it")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
radius covered by the finite subfamily: 49/50 < 1, so points of the open disc are missed
point outside the closed disc at distance 4 from it, a ball of that radius misses it
```
::::
:::

Compactness is carried forward by continuous maps, which gives the extreme value statement of @def-compact. The exercise
asks for the image theorem and then for the existence of the maximum and minimum.

::: {#exr-compact-image}
#### Continuous images and extreme values

Prove that a continuous image of a compact space is compact. Deduce that a continuous $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ on a compact
$X$ is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $f : X \to Y$ be continuous and $\{W_\alpha\}$ open sets of $Y$ covering $f(X)$. The preimages $f^{-1}(W_\alpha)$ are open
and cover $X$, so finitely many do, and the corresponding $W_\alpha$ cover $f(X)$. For $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ the image $f(X)$ is
compact, hence bounded and closed (@exr-compact-heine-borel). Its least upper bound $M$ belongs to it: otherwise some
interval $(M - \varepsilon, M + \varepsilon)$ misses $f(X)$, by closedness, and $M - \varepsilon$ would be a smaller upper bound. So
$M = f(x_+)$ for some $x_+$, and likewise for the greatest lower bound.

## SageMath

Check on $f(u, v) = u + 2v$ on the circle: Sage samples the circle and compares the largest sampled value with the value
$\sqrt 5$ at the point $(1, 2)/\sqrt 5$.

```{.python .sage}
f = lambda u, v: u + 2 * v
vals = [f(cos(2 * pi * k / 1000).n(), sin(2 * pi * k / 1000).n()) for k in range(1000)]
print("sampled max, min:", round(max(vals), 5), round(min(vals), 5))
print("value at (1, 2)/sqrt(5):", f(1 / sqrt(5), 2 / sqrt(5)).simplify_full(), "=", round(sqrt(5).n(), 5))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sampled max, min: 2.23607 -2.23607
value at (1, 2)/sqrt(5): sqrt(5) = 2.23607
```
::::
:::

The cofinite topology, which is not Hausdorff (@exm-hausdorff-cofinite), is compact on every set. The exercise shows how
a single open set already covers all but finitely many points.

::: {#exr-compact-cofinite}
#### The cofinite topology is compact

Prove that every set with the cofinite topology (@exm-topology-cofinite) is compact. Is every compact subset of it closed?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $X$ and pick a non-empty $U_{\alpha_0}$. Its complement is finite, $\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}$,
and choosing $U_{\alpha_i} \ni x_i$ gives the finite subcover $U_{\alpha_0}, \dots, U_{\alpha_m}$. Every subset of $X$ is compact
by the same argument applied to its subspace topology, which is again cofinite; so on an infinite $X$ the compact subset
$X \setminus \{x\}$ is not closed, as its complement $\{x\}$ is not open.

## SageMath

Check on $X = \mathbb{Z}$, sampled as the integers from $-50$ to $50$, with the cover $U_0 = \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{1, 2, 3\}$ and
$U_k = \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{k + 3\}$: Sage picks $U_0$ and one set for each missing point.

```{.python .sage}
Z = set(range(-50, 51))
U = {0: Z - {1, 2, 3}}
U.update({k: Z - {k + 3} for k in range(1, 40)})
missing = sorted(Z - U[0])
pick = sorted({0} | {next(k for k in U if k != 0 and m in U[k]) for m in missing})
print("missing from U_0:", missing, "; subcover:", pick)
print("covers the sample:", set().union(*[U[k] for k in pick]) == Z)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
missing from U_0: [1, 2, 3] ; subcover: [0, 1]
covers the sample: True
```
::::
:::

The last exercise returns to physics with a particle in a double well. The region of phase space below a given energy is
shown to be compact, and the largest position reached is computed.

::: {#exr-compact-energy-region}
#### Phase space below an energy

For $H(q, p) = p^2/2 + (q^2 - 1)^2$ and $E > 0$, show that $K_E = \{H \leq E\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is compact, and find the
largest value of $q$ on it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$H$ is a polynomial, hence continuous (@exm-continuous-projections), so $K_E$ is closed (@exm-continuous-level-sets). On
$K_E$, $p^2 \leq 2E$ and $(q^2 - 1)^2 \leq E$, so $|p| \leq \sqrt{2E}$ and $q^2 \leq 1 + \sqrt E$; $K_E$ is bounded, hence compact
(@exr-compact-heine-borel). The function $q$ attains its maximum on $K_E$ (@exr-compact-image); since $q^2 \leq 1 + \sqrt E$
on $K_E$ with equality at $(\sqrt{1 + \sqrt E}, 0) \in K_E$, the maximum is $\sqrt{1 + \sqrt E}$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the largest $q$ with $H(q, 0) = E$ for three energies and checks that it lies on $K_E$.

```{.python .sage}
q = var("q")
for E in [1/4, 1, 4]:
    qmax = sqrt(1 + sqrt(E))
    print("E =", E, ": q_max =", qmax, "; H(q_max, 0) =", ((qmax^2 - 1)^2).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
E = 1/4 : q_max = sqrt(3/2) ; H(q_max, 0) = 1/4
E = 1 : q_max = sqrt(2) ; H(q_max, 0) = 1
E = 4 : q_max = sqrt(3) ; H(q_max, 0) = 4
```
::::
:::
::::

### Connected spaces

The third global property asks whether a space is in one piece. The definition phrases this negatively, through the
impossibility of splitting the space into two disjoint non-empty open sets, and the picture is of a set that cannot be
pulled apart; the components of the definition are the pieces when it can.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-connected}
#### Connected space

A topological space $X$ is **connected** if it is not the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets; such a pair, when
it exists, is a **separation** of $X$. A subset is connected if it is connected in the subspace topology. The maximal
connected subsets of $X$ are its **connected components**; they are disjoint and their union is $X$, as an exercise
below proves.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On small finite spaces connectedness can be decided by listing the open sets. A single point is connected, a discrete
space with two points is not, and the Sierpiński space, with too few open sets to split it, is connected.

::: {#exm-connected-finite-small}
#### Finite spaces

A one-point space is connected. A discrete space with at least two points is not: $\{p\}$ and its complement form a
separation, and its components are its points. The indiscrete topology is connected, and so is the Sierpiński space
$\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}\}$, whose only non-empty open sets $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 2\}$ meet.
:::

Removing a point from the line, or keeping only the rational numbers, gives sets that fall apart. In each case a single
cut point splits the set into the parts on its two sides [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.1, Part A, Problems 7 and
13].

::: {#exm-connected-real-subsets}
#### Subsets of the line that fall apart

$\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ has the separation $(-\infty, 0)$, $(0, \infty)$; so has $(0, 1) \cup (1, 2)$, with $(0, 1)$ and $(1,
2)$. The rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ have the separation $\mathbb{Q} \cap (-\infty, \sqrt2)$, $\mathbb{Q} \cap (\sqrt2, \infty)$, since
$\sqrt 2 \notin \mathbb{Q}$; the same cut at any irrational shows that the components of $\mathbb{Q}$ are its points.
:::

The intervals are exactly the connected subsets of the line. That intervals are connected rests on the least upper
bound of the real numbers, and that nothing else is connected is the cut argument of the previous example.

::: {#exm-connected-intervals}
#### Intervals

Every interval of $\mathbb{R}$, open, closed or half-open, bounded or not, is connected, as an exercise below proves. A
subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ that is not an interval contains $a < c < b$ with $a, b \in S$ and $c \notin S$, and then $S
\cap (-\infty, c)$, $S \cap (c, \infty)$ is a separation.
:::

The circle, the sphere, the torus and the coordinate spaces are connected, and the example shows how the circle behaves
when points are removed. Since a homeomorphism restricts to the spaces with a point removed, such behaviour tells spaces
apart (@exm-homeomorphism-square).

::: {#exm-connected-circle}
#### Circles and spheres

$S^1$, $S^2$, $T^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ are connected, as exercises below show. Removing one point from a circle leaves an
open arc, homeomorphic to an interval (@exm-homeomorphism-stereographic-circle) and so connected; removing two points
leaves two open arcs, a separation. Removing an interior point from $[0, 1]$ disconnects it, while removing a point from
the circle does not, so the circle is not homeomorphic to $[0, 1]$.
:::

A finite graph is a discrete model of a space, and connectedness of the graph is the combinatorial version of
connectedness of the space. @fig-components-graph shows a graph with two components and a six-cycle, a discrete
circle, with one or two vertices removed.

::: {#exm-connected-finite}
#### Finite models

A finite graph is a finite model of a space, its vertices the regions and its edges the adjacencies; its components are
the classes of vertices joined by chains of edges. The graph with edges $AB$, $BC$, $DE$ has two components, and the
six-cycle behaves like the circle under the removal of one or two vertices.

![Left, the graph with edges $AB$, $BC$, $DE$ and its two components. Middle and right, the six-cycle with one vertex
removed, still one component, and with two opposite vertices removed, two components.](figures/components_graph.svg){#fig-components-graph width=95%}
:::

A continuous function that never vanishes splits its domain into the parts where it is positive and negative. If both
parts are non-empty the domain is disconnected, and this is the commonest way to prove disconnectedness
[@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 4.1.1].

::: {#exm-connected-groups}
#### Spaces split by a sign

If $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous with no zero and takes both signs, then $\{f > 0\}$ and $\{f < 0\}$ are open
(@exm-continuous-level-sets) and form a separation. Thus the hyperbola $\{u^2 - v^2 = 1\}$ falls into the branches $u > 0$
and $u < 0$, and the plane without the $u$-axis into the half-planes $v > 0$ and $v < 0$.
:::

The energy level sets of a particle in a double well show connectedness at work in physics. Below the barrier the
particle is confined to one well or the other, and @fig-energy-components shows the two pieces of the level set.

::: {#exm-connected-energy-levels}
#### Energy levels of a double well

For $H(q, p) = p^2/2 + (q^2 - 1)^2$ the barrier at $q = 0$ has height $H(0, 0) = 1$. For $0 < E < 1$ the level set $\{H = E\}$
has no point with $q = 0$, since $H(0, p) \geq 1$, so the sign of $q$ separates it into a left and a right piece: a particle
with this energy stays in its well. For $E > 1$ the level set is a single closed curve around both wells.

![Level sets of $H = p^2/2 + (q^2 - 1)^2$ in the phase plane: two components at $E = 1/2$, one at $E = 3/2$, and the
level $E = 1$ through the top of the barrier, dashed.](figures/energy_components.svg){#fig-energy-components width=75%}
:::

The phase space of a pendulum is a cylinder, and its energy levels show the opposite pattern to the double well. Above
the top of the circle the pendulum rotates, and the two senses of rotation are two components.

::: {#exm-connected-pendulum}
#### Rotations of a pendulum

On the phase cylinder $S^1 \times \mathbb{R}$, with angle $\varphi$ from the bottom and $H = p^2/2 - \cos\varphi$, the level
$\{H = E\}$ for $E > 1$ has $p^2 = 2(E + \cos\varphi) > 0$, so $p \neq 0$ on it and the sign of $p$ separates the
anticlockwise rotations from the clockwise ones. For $-1 < E < 1$ the level is one oscillation loop around the bottom.
:::

Connectedness does not pass to intersections, and disjointness does not prevent a union from being connected. The
example records both facts with the simplest sets [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.1, Part A, Problems 1 and 12].

::: {#exm-connected-intersection-fails}
#### Intersections and unions

The circle and the vertical axis are connected, but their intersection $\{(0, 1), (0, -1)\}$ is two points, not
connected. The intervals $[0, 1]$ and $(1, 2)$ are disjoint, yet their union $[0, 2)$ is connected.
:::

Continuous images of connected sets are connected, but preimages need not be. The last example cuts the circle with a
connected interval of values and gets two arcs [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.1, Part A, Problem 19].

::: {#exm-connected-preimage}
#### Preimages can fall apart

For $f(u, v) = u$ on $S^1$, the preimage of the interval $(-\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ is $\{(u, v) \in S^1 : |u| < \tfrac12\}$, two
open arcs separated by the sign of $v$. A continuous map need not pull connected sets back to connected sets.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the components of the graphs of @exm-connected-finite with Sage's graph module. Removing
one and two vertices from the six-cycle mirrors the behaviour of the circle in @exm-connected-circle.

::: {#exr-connected-components}
#### Components of a finite model

Find the connected components of the graph with edges $AB$, $BC$, $DE$, and check what removing one or two vertices does
to a six-cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Vertices joined by a chain of edges lie in one component. $A$, $B$, $C$ are joined through $B$, and $D$, $E$ by their edge,
with no edge between the two groups: the components are $\{A, B, C\}$ and $\{D, E\}$. The six-cycle $0, 1, \dots, 5$ minus
the vertex $0$ is the chain $1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5$, one component; minus $0$ and $3$ it is $1 - 2$ and $4 - 5$, two components.

## SageMath

Sage builds the graphs and asks for their components.

```{.python .sage}
G = Graph({"A": ["B"], "B": ["C"], "C": [], "D": ["E"], "E": []})
print("connected:", G.is_connected(), "; components:", G.connected_components(sort=True))
H = graphs.CycleGraph(6)
H1 = H.copy(); H1.delete_vertex(0)
H2 = H.copy(); H2.delete_vertices([0, 3])
print("the six-cycle is connected:", H.is_connected())
print("one vertex removed, components:", H1.connected_components_number())
print("two opposite vertices removed, components:", H2.connected_components(sort=True))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
connected: False ; components: [['A', 'B', 'C'], ['D', 'E']]
the six-cycle is connected: True
one vertex removed, components: 1
two opposite vertices removed, components: [[1, 2], [4, 5]]
```
::::
:::

Four subsets of the plane are tested for connectedness, each defined by an inequality or an equation. For the
disconnected ones the separation is given by the sign of a continuous function, as in @exm-connected-groups
[@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.1, Part A, Problem 11].

::: {#exr-connected-decide}
#### Which are connected?

Decide which of $A = \{uv > 0\}$, $B = \{u^2 + v^2 \neq 1\}$, $C = \{u^2 - v^2 = 1\}$, $D = \{v = u^3\}$ are disconnected, and
give a separation for each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$A$: $u$ has no zero on $A$ and takes both signs, so $\{u > 0\} \cap A$ (the first quadrant) and $\{u < 0\} \cap A$ (the third)
separate it. $B$: $u^2 + v^2 - 1$ has no zero on $B$, separating the open disc from the outside of the circle. $C$: the sign
of $u$, as in @exm-connected-groups. $D$ is connected: it is the image of the line under the continuous map $t \mapsto (t,
t^3)$, which is connected by an exercise below; so only $A$, $B$, $C$ are disconnected.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates each separating function at two points of the set, one on each side.

```{.python .sage}
u, v = var("u v")
for name, g, pts in [("A", u, [(1, 1), (-1, -1)]), ("B", u^2 + v^2 - 1, [(0, 0), (2, 0)]), ("C", u, [(1, 0), (-1, 0)])]:
    print(name, ": separating function at two points of the set:", [g(u=a, v=b) for a, b in pts])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A : separating function at two points of the set: [1, -1]
B : separating function at two points of the set: [-1, 3]
C : separating function at two points of the set: [1, -1]
```
::::
:::

A separation of a space is the same as a continuous function to a two-point discrete space that takes both values. The
exercise asks for this reformulation, which is how connectedness is used in most proofs.

::: {#exr-connected-two-valued}
#### Two-valued functions

Let $\{0, 1\}$ carry the discrete topology. Prove that $X$ is connected if and only if every continuous $f : X \to \{0, 1\}$
is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $U$, $V$ is a separation, the function $f = 0$ on $U$ and $1$ on $V$ is continuous, since the preimages of the four subsets
of $\{0, 1\}$ are $\emptyset$, $U$, $V$, $X$, and it is not constant. Conversely, a continuous non-constant $f$ gives the
disjoint non-empty open sets $f^{-1}(\{0\})$ and $f^{-1}(\{1\})$ covering $X$, a separation.

## SageMath

Check on the four topologies of $\{1, 2\}$: Sage lists the maps to the discrete $\{0, 1\}$ that are continuous and reports
whether they are all constant.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
F = frozenset; X = (1, 2)
tops = {"indiscrete": [F(), F(X)], "Sierpinski": [F(), F([1]), F(X)], "discrete": [F(), F([1]), F([2]), F(X)]}
for name, T in tops.items():
    cont = [f for f in product([0, 1], repeat=2) if all(F(x for x in X if f[x - 1] in W) in T for W in [{0}, {1}])]
    print(name, ": continuous maps", cont, "; all constant:", all(f[0] == f[1] for f in cont))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
indiscrete : continuous maps [(0, 0), (1, 1)] ; all constant: True
Sierpinski : continuous maps [(0, 0), (1, 1)] ; all constant: True
discrete : continuous maps [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)] ; all constant: False
```
::::
:::

A connected subset cannot straddle a separation of the ambient space, and the exercise asks for the short proof. The fact
is the key step in the union and component arguments that follow [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.1, Part A, Problem 14].

::: {#exr-connected-one-side}
#### A connected set lies on one side

Let $U$, $V$ be a separation of $X$ and $S \subseteq X$ connected. Prove that $S \subseteq U$ or $S \subseteq V$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$S \cap U$ and $S \cap V$ are open in $S$ (@def-subspace-topology), disjoint, and their union is $S$. Since $S$ is connected
they are not both non-empty; if $S \cap V = \emptyset$ then $S \subseteq U$, and otherwise $S \cap U = \emptyset$ and $S \subseteq
V$.

## SageMath

Check on $X = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ with the separation by sign: Sage tests sample intervals and reports on which side
each lies.

```{.python .sage}
for a, b in [(1, 3), (-5, -1/2), (-1, 2)]:
    pts = [a + (b - a) * QQ(k) / 10 for k in range(11) if a + (b - a) * QQ(k) / 10 != 0]
    side = {sign(x) for x in pts}
    print((a, b), "minus 0: signs", sorted(side), "-> one side" if len(side) == 1 else "-> not an interval of X")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(1, 3) minus 0: signs [1] -> one side
(-5, -1/2) minus 0: signs [-1] -> one side
(-1, 2) minus 0: signs [-1, 1] -> not an interval of X
```
::::
:::

That intervals are connected is the base on which all other connectedness proofs rest. The proof uses the least upper
bound of the real numbers to find a point that neither part of a supposed separation can contain.

::: {#exr-connected-interval}
#### Intervals are connected

Prove that $[a, b]$ is connected, and deduce that every interval of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $U$, $V$ is a separation of $[a, b]$, with $a \in U$, and let $s = \sup\{x \in [a, b] : [a, x] \subseteq U\}$. Every $y < s$
lies below some $x$ with $[a, x] \subseteq U$, so $[a, s) \subseteq U$. If $s \in U$, the set $U$, open in $[a, b]$, contains $[s, s +
\delta) \cap [a, b]$ for some $\delta > 0$; then $[a, \min(s + \delta/2, b)] \subseteq U$, so $s = b$ by the choice of $s$, and $U = [a, b]$,
leaving $V$ empty. If $s \in V$, then $s > a$ and $V$ contains $(s - \delta, s]$ for some $\delta > 0$, which meets $[a, s) \subseteq U$,
contradicting $U \cap V = \emptyset$. Both cases are impossible. Any interval $I$ is the union of the closed intervals $[a, b]
\subseteq I$ containing a fixed point $c \in I$; a separation of $I$ would, by @exr-connected-one-side, put each of them on the
side of $c$, leaving the other side empty.

## SageMath

Check on the attempted split of $[0, 1]$ into $\{x^2 < 1/2\}$ and $\{x^2 \geq 1/2\}$: Sage computes the supremum of the first
part and shows that the second part is not open at it.

```{.python .sage}
s = sqrt(1/2); print("sup of {x^2 < 1/2} in [0, 1]:", s, "; s^2 =", s^2)
print("points s - 1/10^k lie in the first part:", all(bool((s - 1 / 10^k)^2 < 1/2) for k in range(1, 8)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sup of {x^2 < 1/2} in [0, 1]: sqrt(1/2) ; s^2 = 1/2
points s - 1/10^k lie in the first part: True
```
::::
:::

Continuous maps preserve connectedness, and the exercise asks for the proof by pulling back a separation of the image.
With the intervals of @exr-connected-interval this gives the intermediate value theorem.

::: {#exr-connected-image}
#### Continuous images of connected spaces

Prove that the image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected, and deduce the intermediate value
theorem for a continuous $f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $f(X)$ had a separation $U \cap f(X)$, $V \cap f(X)$ with $U$, $V$ open in the target, then $f^{-1}(U)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ would be
disjoint non-empty open sets covering $X$, a separation of $X$. A connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is an interval
(@exm-connected-intervals), so $f([0, 1])$ is an interval containing $f(0)$ and $f(1)$, hence every value between them.

## SageMath

Check on $f(x) = x^3 - x - 1/5$ on $[0, 2]$: Sage finds the value $0$, between $f(0)$ and $f(2)$, at a point of the interval.

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x"); f = x^3 - x - 1/5
print("f(0) =", f(x=0), "; f(2) =", f(x=2))
r = find_root(f, 0, 2); print("root in [0, 2]:", round(r, 6), "; f(root) ~", round(abs(f(x=r)), 12))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f(0) = -1/5 ; f(2) = 29/5
root in [0, 2]: 1.088034 ; f(root) ~ 0.0
```
::::
:::

The components of a space are built from the following fact about unions. The exercise asks for it and then for the
statement of @def-connected that the components partition the space [@lee2013introduction, Prop. A.39].

::: {#exr-connected-union}
#### Unions with a common point, and components

Prove that a union of connected subsets with a point in common is connected. Deduce that the components of a space are
disjoint and cover it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $S = \bigcup S_\alpha$ with $c \in S_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$, and let $U$, $V$ separate $S$, with $c \in U$. Each $S_\alpha$ lies on
one side (@exr-connected-one-side), the side of $c$, so $S \subseteq U$ and $V$ is empty: no separation exists. For $x \in X$, let
$C_x$ be the union of all connected subsets containing $x$; it is connected by the first part and contains $\{x\}$, so it is
the largest connected set containing $x$, a component. If $C_x$ and $C_y$ meet, $C_x \cup C_y$ is connected and contains
both, so $C_x = C_x \cup C_y = C_y$. Thus the components are disjoint and their union is $X$.

## SageMath

Check on the graph model: Sage joins a path through $1, 2, 3$ and a path through $3, 4, 5$, which share the vertex $3$, and
tests the union for connectedness.

```{.python .sage}
G1 = Graph([(1, 2), (2, 3)]); G2 = Graph([(3, 4), (4, 5)])
G = G1.union(G2)
print("pieces connected:", G1.is_connected(), G2.is_connected(), "; union connected:", G.is_connected())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
pieces connected: True True ; union connected: True
```
::::
:::

The connectedness of the circle, the sphere and the coordinate spaces, quoted in @exm-connected-circle, follows from the
two previous exercises. Each space is a continuous image of a connected space or a union of connected sets through a
point [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.1, Part B, Problem 1].

::: {#exr-connected-circle-sphere}
#### The line, the plane, the circle and the sphere

Prove that $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^2$ are connected, and deduce that the ellipse $\{u^2/4 + v^2/9 = 1\}$, the circle and
the sphere $S^2$ are connected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbb{R}$ is an interval, connected by @exr-connected-interval. $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the union of the lines $t \mapsto t\mathbf w$,
continuous images of $\mathbb{R}$, all through the origin, so it is connected by @exr-connected-image and
@exr-connected-union. The ellipse is the image of $\mathbb{R}$ under $t \mapsto (2\cos t, 3\sin t)$ and the circle under $t
\mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$. The sphere is the image of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi,
\sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$, continuous and onto; so all three are connected.

## SageMath

Sage checks that the three parametrisations land on the ellipse, the circle and the sphere.

```{.python .sage}
t, th, ph = var("t theta phi")
print("ellipse:", ((2 * cos(t))^2 / 4 + (3 * sin(t))^2 / 9).simplify_trig())
print("circle:", (cos(t)^2 + sin(t)^2).simplify_trig())
print("sphere:", ((sin(th) * cos(ph))^2 + (sin(th) * sin(ph))^2 + cos(th)^2).simplify_trig())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
ellipse: 1
circle: 1
sphere: 1
```
::::
:::

The double well of @exm-connected-energy-levels is examined quantitatively. The exercise asks for the separation of a
level set below the barrier and for the positions that each of its two pieces covers.

::: {#exr-connected-energy-levels}
#### The two wells

For $H(q, p) = p^2/2 + (q^2 - 1)^2$, show that $\{H = 1/2\}$ is disconnected, and find the interval of positions $q$ covered by
each of its two pieces.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

On the level set $q \neq 0$, since $H(0, p) = p^2/2 + 1 \geq 1$, and both signs occur, at $(\pm q_0, 0)$; so the sign of $q$
gives a separation (@exm-connected-groups). A point $(q, p)$ of the level set has $(q^2 - 1)^2 \leq 1/2$, that is $1 - 1/\sqrt2 \leq
q^2 \leq 1 + 1/\sqrt2$, and every such $q$ occurs with $p = \pm\sqrt{2(1/2 - (q^2 - 1)^2)}$. So the right piece covers $q \in
[\sqrt{1 - 1/\sqrt2}, \sqrt{1 + 1/\sqrt2}]$ and the left piece the negatives of these values.

## SageMath

Sage solves $(q^2 - 1)^2 = 1/2$ for the turning points and checks that $H(0, p) \geq 1$.

```{.python .sage}
q, p = var("q p")
tp = sorted(solve((q^2 - 1)^2 == 1/2, q), key=lambda s: s.rhs().n())
print("turning points:", [round(s.rhs().n(), 5) for s in tp])
print("H(0, p) - 1 =", (p^2 / 2 + (0 - 1)^2 - 1), ">= 0")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
turning points: [-1.30656, -0.5412, 0.5412, 1.30656]
H(0, p) - 1 = 1/2*p^2 >= 0
```
::::
:::

The two-sheeted hyperboloid is a surface in space that falls into two pieces. The exercise asks for both halves of the
statement that it has exactly two components, combining a sign separation with continuous images.

::: {#exr-connected-hyperboloid}
#### The two-sheeted hyperboloid

Show that $Q = \{(x, y, z) : z^2 - x^2 - y^2 = 1\}$ has exactly two components, the sheets $z > 0$ and $z < 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

On $Q$, $z^2 = 1 + x^2 + y^2 \geq 1$, so $z$ has no zero and takes both signs: the sheets are a separation
(@exm-connected-groups). The upper sheet is the image of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $(x, y) \mapsto (x, y, \sqrt{1 + x^2 + y^2})$,
continuous, so it is connected (@exr-connected-circle-sphere, @exr-connected-image), and so is the lower sheet. A connected
set containing points of both sheets would contradict @exr-connected-one-side, so the sheets are the components.

## SageMath

Sage checks that the parametrisation of the upper sheet satisfies the equation and that $z \geq 1$ on $Q$.

```{.python .sage}
x, y = var("x y"); z = sqrt(1 + x^2 + y^2)
print("z^2 - x^2 - y^2 =", (z^2 - x^2 - y^2).simplify_full())
print("min of z on the upper sheet, at x = y = 0:", z(x=0, y=0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
z^2 - x^2 - y^2 = 1
min of z on the upper sheet, at x = y = 0: 1
```
::::
:::
::::

A more concrete way for a space to be in one piece is that any two of its points can be joined by a continuous curve.
The next definition introduces paths and the spaces in which every pair of points is joined by one, and records that
this stronger property implies connectedness.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-path-connected}
#### Path-connected space

A **path** from $p$ to $q$ in a space $X$ is a continuous map $\gamma : [0, 1] \to X$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma(1) = q$.
A space is **path-connected** if any two of its points are joined by a path. A path-connected space is connected, as an
exercise below proves.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In a coordinate space the simplest path between two points is the straight segment. Every set that contains the segment
between any two of its points is therefore path-connected.

::: {#exm-path-convex}
#### Segments

For $p, q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the map $\gamma(t) = (1 - t)p + tq$ is continuous, with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma(1) = q$. So
$\mathbb{R}^n$, every interval, every ball $B_\varepsilon(c)$ and every box are path-connected: each contains the segment
between any two of its points.
:::

On the sphere the natural path between two points runs along a great circle. The zero-dimensional sphere, two points on
a line, is the one exception [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.2, Part A, Problem 17].

::: {#exm-path-sphere}
#### Spheres

Any two points of $S^2$ are joined by an arc of a great circle through them, and the same holds on $S^1$ and on every
sphere $S^n$, $n \geq 1$; these spaces are path-connected. The sphere $S^0 = \{-1, 1\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is not even
connected.
:::

Removing a point from a coordinate space of dimension at least two leaves it path-connected, since a path can go around
the hole. On the line the hole cuts the space in two [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.2, Part A, Problem 16].

::: {#exm-path-punctured}
#### Coordinate space minus a point

For $n \geq 2$, two points $p, q$ of $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}$ are joined by the segment unless $0$ lies on it; then they
are joined by two segments through a point $z$ off the line through $p$ and $q$. So $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}$ is
path-connected, while $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ is not connected (@exm-connected-real-subsets).
:::

In a finite graph a path is a sequence of adjacent vertices, and connectedness and joinability by such sequences
coincide. The example makes the point that the component computation of @exr-connected-components is exactly this.

::: {#exm-path-graph}
#### Finite models

In a graph, a path is a sequence of vertices each adjacent to the next, and the components found in
@exr-connected-components are the classes of vertices joined by such sequences. This is the combinatorial counterpart of
path-connectedness.
:::

A double pendulum moves on the torus of two angles, and a path between two configurations can be written down by
turning both angles at once. The torus is therefore path-connected.

::: {#exm-path-torus}
#### Two angles

Two configurations $(\alpha_1, \alpha_2)$ and $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$ of a double pendulum, given by angles, are joined by
$\gamma(t) = (c((1 - t)\alpha_1 + t\beta_1), c((1 - t)\alpha_2 + t\beta_2))$ in $S^1 \times S^1$, where $c(\varphi) = (\cos\varphi,
\sin\varphi)$. Each component of $\gamma$ is continuous, so $S^1 \times S^1$, and the torus surface $T^2$ homeomorphic to it
(@exm-homeomorphism-torus), are path-connected.
:::

A motion of a mechanical system is itself a path in its configuration space. For a pendulum swinging from one turning
point to the other, the path runs along an arc of the configuration circle.

::: {#exm-path-pendulum}
#### A swing of the pendulum

The motion of a pendulum during a time $T$, with angle $\varphi(s)$ continuous in $s \in [0, T]$, gives the path $t \mapsto
\ell(\sin\varphi(tT), -\cos\varphi(tT))$ in the configuration circle. A swing from $\varphi = -\varphi_0$ to $\varphi_0$ joins the two
turning points, and every position in between lies on the path.
:::

The orbit of a harmonic oscillator is an ellipse in the phase plane, traversed by the motion. Its parametrisation by
time is a path that visits every point of the energy level.

::: {#exm-path-oscillator}
#### The oscillator's orbit

For $E(x, p) = p^2/2m + kx^2/2$ and $E_0 > 0$, the map $t \mapsto (a\cos 2\pi t, b\sin 2\pi t)$, with $a = \sqrt{2E_0/k}$ and $b =
\sqrt{2mE_0}$, is a path onto the level set $\{E = E_0\}$; restricting it to subintervals joins any two states of the orbit,
so the orbit is path-connected.
:::

The graph of a continuous function on an interval is path-connected, since one can walk along it. This covers the graph
part of the topologist's sine curve of the next example [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.2, Part B, Problem 4].

::: {#exm-path-graph-function}
#### Graphs of continuous functions

If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous on an interval and $a, b \in I$, then $\gamma(t) = ((1 - t)a + tb, f((1 - t)a + tb))$ is a
path from $(a, f(a))$ to $(b, f(b))$ in the graph. So the graph of $\sin(1/x)$ over $(0, 1]$ is path-connected.
:::

The converse of the implication in @def-path-connected fails, and the standard witness is the topologist's sine curve of
@fig-sine-curve. It is connected, because the graph accumulates on the segment, but no path can reach the segment from
the graph.

::: {#exm-path-sine-curve}
#### The topologist's sine curve

$S = \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : 0 < x \leq 1\} \cup (\{0\} \times [-1, 1])$ is connected but not path-connected, as an exercise below
proves: near the segment the graph oscillates between $-1$ and $1$ infinitely often, so a path ending on the segment
would have to jump.

![The topologist's sine curve: the graph of $\sin(1/x)$ for $0 < x \leq 1$, oscillating ever faster as $x \to 0$, together with
the segment $\{0\} \times [-1, 1]$ that it accumulates on.](figures/sine_curve.svg){#fig-sine-curve width=75%}
:::

Paths in finite spaces behave unexpectedly. A continuous map from the interval onto two points exists as soon as one of
the points is not closed, and the Sierpiński space is path-connected.

::: {#exm-path-finite}
#### Paths in finite spaces

On $\{1, 2\}$ with $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}\}$, the map $\gamma(t) = 1$ for $t < 1$, $\gamma(1) = 2$ is continuous: the
preimage of $\{1\}$ is $[0, 1)$, open in $[0, 1]$. So the Sierpiński space is path-connected. The discrete two-point space has
no path between its points, being disconnected (@exm-connected-finite-small).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise writes down an explicit path along a great circle from the north pole to a point on the equator. The
check that it stays on the sphere is the Pythagorean identity.

::: {#exr-path-great-circle}
#### A path on the sphere

Write down a path on $S^2$ from the north pole to the point $(1, 0, 0)$ along a great circle, and check that it stays on the
sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\gamma(t) = (\sin\tfrac{\pi t}{2}, 0, \cos\tfrac{\pi t}{2})$ is continuous, a quarter of the great circle through the pole in the
$XZ$-plane, with $\gamma(0) = (0, 0, 1)$, $\gamma(1) = (1, 0, 0)$ and $|\gamma(t)|^2 = \sin^2\tfrac{\pi t}{2} + \cos^2\tfrac{\pi
t}{2} = 1$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the path at its ends and simplifies $|\gamma(t)|^2$.

```{.python .sage}
t = var("t")
g = vector([sin(pi * t / 2), 0, cos(pi * t / 2)])
print("gamma(0) =", g.subs(t=0), ", gamma(1) =", g.subs(t=1), ", |gamma|^2 =", (g * g).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
gamma(0) = (0, 0, 1) , gamma(1) = (1, 0, 0) , |gamma|^2 = 1
```
::::
:::

The segment of @exm-path-convex stays inside a ball, and the exercise asks for the inequality that proves it. The
computation then checks it on a specific ball and two specific points.

::: {#exr-path-segment-ball}
#### Balls contain their segments

Show that if $p, q \in B_r(c)$ then $(1 - t)p + tq \in B_r(c)$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$. Check it for $c = (0, 0)$, $r = 1$, $p = (0.6, 0)$,
$q = (0, -0.7)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(1 - t)p + tq - c = (1 - t)(p - c) + t(q - c)$, so by the triangle inequality $|(1 - t)p + tq - c| \leq (1 - t)|p - c| + t|q - c|
< (1 - t)r + tr = r$. For the given points the largest distance to the origin along the segment is at an end, $0.7 < 1$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $|\gamma(t)|^2$ along the segment and its maximum on $[0, 1]$.

```{.python .sage}
t = var("t")
p = vector(QQ, [6/10, 0]); q = vector(QQ, [0, -7/10])
g = (1 - t) * p + t * q; n2 = (g * g).expand()
print("|gamma(t)|^2 =", n2)
print("max on [0, 1] at the ends:", max(n2(t=0), n2(t=1)), "< 1; value at t = 1/2:", n2(t=1/2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|gamma(t)|^2 = 17/20*t^2 - 18/25*t + 9/25
max on [0, 1] at the ends: 49/100 < 1; value at t = 1/2: 17/80
```
::::
:::

The punctured plane of @exm-path-punctured needs a detour when the segment passes through the hole. The exercise asks for
an explicit path between two opposite points that avoids the origin.

::: {#exr-path-punctured-plane}
#### Going around the origin

Find a path in $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ from $(1, 0)$ to $(-1, 0)$, and check that it avoids the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The segment passes through $0$, so take the upper half circle $\gamma(t) = (\cos\pi t, \sin\pi t)$: it is continuous,
$\gamma(0) = (1, 0)$, $\gamma(1) = (-1, 0)$, and $|\gamma(t)| = 1 \neq 0$. Two segments through $z = (0, 1)$, as in
@exm-path-punctured, work as well.

## SageMath

Sage computes the ends of the half circle and its distance to the origin.

```{.python .sage}
t = var("t"); g = vector([cos(pi * t), sin(pi * t)])
print("ends:", g(t=0), g(t=1), "; |gamma|^2 =", (g * g).simplify_trig())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
ends: (1, 0) (-1, 0) ; |gamma|^2 = 1
```
::::
:::

The implication stated in @def-path-connected is proved here using the preservation of connectedness under continuous
maps. The converse fails, as @exm-path-sine-curve showed.

::: {#exr-path-connected-implies}
#### Path-connected implies connected

Prove that a path-connected space is connected, using @exr-connected-image.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $X = U \cup V$ with $U$, $V$ disjoint non-empty open sets; pick $p \in U$, $q \in V$ and a path $\gamma$ from $p$ to $q$. Its
image $\gamma([0, 1])$ is connected, as the image of the connected interval (@exr-connected-interval,
@exr-connected-image), yet $U \cap \gamma([0, 1])$ and $V \cap \gamma([0, 1])$ are disjoint, open in it, non-empty and cover it: a
contradiction.

## SageMath

Check on the path $\gamma(t) = (2t - 1, 0)$ from $(-1, 0)$ to $(1, 0)$ in the plane: Sage locates where it crosses the line
$u = 0$ that separates the two sides of the attempted split $\{u < 0\}$, $\{u > 0\}$, showing that the two sides do not cover
the path.

```{.python .sage}
t = var("t"); u = 2 * t - 1
t0 = solve(u == 0, t)[0].rhs()
print("crossing at t =", t0, "; gamma(t0) =", (u(t=t0), 0), "lies in neither side")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
crossing at t = 1/2 ; gamma(t0) = (0, 0) lies in neither side
```
::::
:::

Two paths that meet end to start can be run one after the other. The exercise asks for the continuity of the
concatenation and deduces that "joined by a path" is an equivalence relation.

::: {#exr-path-concatenate}
#### Running two paths in turn

If $\gamma_1$ is a path from $p$ to $q$ and $\gamma_2$ one from $q$ to $r$, show that $\gamma(t) = \gamma_1(2t)$ for $t \leq \tfrac12$
and $\gamma_2(2t - 1)$ for $t \geq \tfrac12$ is a path from $p$ to $r$. Deduce that "$p$ and $q$ are joined by a path" is an
equivalence relation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

On the closed sets $[0, \tfrac12]$ and $[\tfrac12, 1]$ the two formulas are continuous and agree at $t = \tfrac12$, where both give
$q$; so $\gamma$ is continuous by @exr-continuous-gluing, with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma(1) = r$. The constant path joins $p$ to
itself, $t \mapsto \gamma_1(1 - t)$ joins $q$ to $p$, and concatenation gives transitivity (@def-equivalence-relation).

## SageMath

Check on $\gamma_1(t) = (t, 0)$ and $\gamma_2(t) = (1, t)$: Sage evaluates both formulas at $t = \tfrac12$ and the
concatenation at its ends.

```{.python .sage}
g1 = lambda s: (s, 0); g2 = lambda s: (1, s)
g = lambda t: g1(2 * t) if t <= 1/2 else g2(2 * t - 1)
print("formulas at t = 1/2:", g1(2 * (1/2)), g2(2 * (1/2) - 1), "; ends:", g(0), g(1))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
formulas at t = 1/2: (1, 0) (1, 0) ; ends: (0, 0) (1, 1)
```
::::
:::

Continuous maps carry paths to paths, so they preserve path-connectedness. The exercise asks for the proof and applies
it to the torus surface in space [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.2, Part B, Problem 2].

::: {#exr-path-image}
#### Images of path-connected spaces

Prove that the image of a path-connected space under a continuous map is path-connected, and deduce that $T^2 \subset
\mathbb{R}^3$ of @exm-subspace-torus is path-connected as the image of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $f : X \to Y$ be continuous and $y_1 = f(x_1)$, $y_2 = f(x_2)$. A path $\gamma$ from $x_1$ to $x_2$ gives the path $f \circ \gamma$
from $y_1$ to $y_2$, continuous by @exr-continuous-composition and lying in $f(X)$. The map $(u, v) \mapsto ((2 + \cos v)\cos u,
(2 + \cos v)\sin u, \sin v)$ is continuous and onto $T^2$, and $\mathbb{R}^2$ is path-connected (@exm-path-convex), so $T^2$ is
path-connected.

## SageMath

Check on the segment from $(0, 0)$ to $(\pi, \pi/2)$ in the plane: Sage maps it to the torus and verifies that the image
satisfies the equation of $T^2$.

```{.python .sage}
t = var("t"); u, v = pi * t, pi / 2 * t
X = ((2 + cos(v)) * cos(u), (2 + cos(v)) * sin(u), sin(v))
print("ends:", [tuple(c(t=s) for c in X) for s in (0, 1)])
print("(sqrt(x^2+y^2) - 2)^2 + z^2 =", ((sqrt(X[0]^2 + X[1]^2) - 2)^2 + X[2]^2).simplify_full().canonicalize_radical().simplify_trig())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
ends: [(3, 0, 0), (-2, 0, 1)]
(sqrt(x^2+y^2) - 2)^2 + z^2 = 1
```
::::
:::

A path from inside a ball to outside it must cross the sphere, which is the intermediate value theorem applied to the
distance from the centre. In physics terms, a particle cannot leave a region without passing its boundary
[@cheung2024metric, Exercise 3.2, Part B, Problem 1].

::: {#exr-path-boundary-crossing}
#### Leaving the ball

Let $\gamma$ be a path in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $|\gamma(0)| < 1 < |\gamma(1)|$. Prove that $|\gamma(t)| = 1$ for some $t \in (0, 1)$, and
find such $t$ for $\gamma(t) = (2t, t^2)$ in the plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$g(t) = |\gamma(t)|$ is continuous, as the composition of $\gamma$ with the continuous $x \mapsto |x|$, and $g(0) < 1 < g(1)$, so
$g(t) = 1$ for some $t$ by the intermediate value theorem (@exr-connected-image). For $\gamma(t) = (2t, t^2)$: $|\gamma(t)|^2 =
4t^2 + t^4 = 1$ gives $t^2 = -2 + \sqrt5$, $t = \sqrt{\sqrt5 - 2} \approx 0.486$.

## SageMath

Sage solves $4t^2 + t^4 = 1$ and keeps the root in $(0, 1)$.

```{.python .sage}
R.<t> = QQ[]
r = [a for a, m in (t^4 + 4 * t^2 - 1).roots(AA) if 0 < a < 1]
print("roots in (0, 1):", r, "; equal to sqrt(sqrt(5) - 2):", r[0] == AA(sqrt(sqrt(5) - 2)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
roots in (0, 1): [0.4858682717566457?] ; equal to sqrt(sqrt(5) - 2): True
```
::::
:::

The path of @exm-path-finite in the Sierpiński space is checked here against all open sets. The exercise also shows that
no path joins the two points of the discrete two-point space.

::: {#exr-path-sierpinski}
#### Paths between two points

Verify that $\gamma(t) = 1$ for $t < 1$, $\gamma(1) = 2$ is continuous into $\{1, 2\}$ with $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}\}$. Show
that no path joins $1$ and $2$ in the discrete topology.
