:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The preimages of $\emptyset$, $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 2\}$ are $\emptyset$, $[0, 1)$ and $[0, 1]$, all open in $[0, 1]$, so $\gamma$ is
continuous. In the discrete topology a path $\gamma$ from $1$ to $2$ would make $\gamma^{-1}(\{1\})$ and $\gamma^{-1}(\{2\})$ a
separation of $[0, 1]$, impossible by @exr-connected-interval.

## SageMath

Sage records the preimages of the open sets under $\gamma$ as intervals, in both topologies.

```{.python .sage}
pre = {(): "empty", (1,): "[0, 1)", (2,): "{1}", (1, 2): "[0, 1]"}
for name, T in [("Sierpinski", [(), (1,), (1, 2)]), ("discrete", [(), (1,), (2,), (1, 2)])]:
    print(name, ":", [(W, pre[W]) for W in T], "; all open:", all(pre[W] != "{1}" for W in T))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
Sierpinski : [((), 'empty'), ((1,), '[0, 1)'), ((1, 2), '[0, 1]')] ; all open: True
discrete : [((), 'empty'), ((1,), '[0, 1)'), ((2,), '{1}'), ((1, 2), '[0, 1]')] ; all open: False
```
::::
:::

The topologist's sine curve of @exm-path-sine-curve is analysed in full. The connectedness uses the accumulation of the
graph on the segment, and the failure of path-connectedness uses the intermediate value theorem on the first coordinate
of a supposed path.

::: {#exr-path-sine-curve}
#### The topologist's sine curve

Prove that $S = G \cup L$, with $G = \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : 0 < x \leq 1\}$ and $L = \{0\} \times [-1, 1]$, is connected but not
path-connected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$G$ is path-connected (@exm-path-graph-function), hence connected (@exr-path-connected-implies). Let $U$, $V$ separate $S$;
$G$ lies on one side (@exr-connected-one-side), say $G \subseteq U$. A point $(0, y) \in L \cap V$ would have a ball whose trace
on $S$ lies in $V$; but the ball contains points $(x, \sin(1/x))$ with $x$ small and $\sin(1/x) = y$, which lie in $G \subseteq U$.
So $V = \emptyset$ and $S$ is connected. Suppose $\gamma = (x(t), y(t))$ is a path from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, \sin 1)$. The set
$\{t : x(t) = 0\}$ is closed; its largest element $t_0$ exists, and $x(t) > 0$ for $t > t_0$. By continuity at $t_0$ there is $\delta
> 0$ with $|y(t) - y(t_0)| < \tfrac12$ on $[t_0, t_0 + \delta]$. On that interval $x$ takes every value in $[0, x(t_0 + \delta)]$
(@exr-connected-image), in particular $1/(\pi/2 + 2k\pi)$ and $1/(3\pi/2 + 2k\pi)$ for large $k$, where $y = 1$ and $y = -1$; both
cannot lie within $\tfrac12$ of $y(t_0)$. So no such path exists.

## SageMath

Check on the points $x_k = 1/(\pi/2 + 2k\pi)$ and $x'_k = 1/(3\pi/2 + 2k\pi)$: Sage shows that they approach $0$ while $\sin(1/x)$
stays at $1$ and $-1$ on them.

```{.python .sage}
for k in [1, 10, 100]:
    a = 1 / (pi / 2 + 2 * k * pi); b = 1 / (3 * pi / 2 + 2 * k * pi)
    print("k =", k, ": x =", round(a.n(), 6), round(b.n(), 6), "; sin(1/x) =", sin(1 / a), sin(1 / b))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = 1 : x = 0.127324 0.090946 ; sin(1/x) = 1 -1
k = 10 : x = 0.015527 0.014805 ; sin(1/x) = 1 -1
k = 100 : x = 0.001588 0.00158 ; sin(1/x) = 1 -1
```
::::
:::

The last exercise returns to the pendulum of @exm-connected-pendulum. Each of the two pieces of a level set above the
top is shown to be path-connected, so the level set has exactly two components.

::: {#exr-path-pendulum-levels}
#### The rotating pendulum

On the phase cylinder with $H = p^2/2 - \cos\varphi$ and $E > 1$, show that each of the two pieces $\{H = E, p > 0\}$ and
$\{H = E, p < 0\}$ is path-connected, so that $\{H = E\}$ has exactly two components. Compute the range of $p$ on the upper piece.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The upper piece is the image of the circle under $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) \mapsto ((\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi), \sqrt{2(E +
\cos\varphi)})$, continuous since $E + \cos\varphi > 0$; as $S^1$ is path-connected (@exm-path-sphere), so is the upper piece
(@exr-path-image), and likewise the lower one. The sign of $p$ separates them (@exm-connected-pendulum), and a connected
set lies on one side (@exr-connected-one-side), so they are the two components. On the upper piece $p$ runs from
$\sqrt{2(E - 1)}$ at the top to $\sqrt{2(E + 1)}$ at the bottom.

## SageMath

Sage computes the extreme momenta for $E = 2$ and checks that $E + \cos\varphi$ stays positive.

```{.python .sage}
phi = var("phi"); E = 2
p = sqrt(2 * (E + cos(phi)))
print("p at the top (phi = pi):", p(phi=pi), "; at the bottom (phi = 0):", p(phi=0))
print("min of E + cos(phi):", E - 1, "> 0")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
p at the top (phi = pi): sqrt(2) ; at the bottom (phi = 0): sqrt(6)
min of E + cos(phi): 1 > 0
```
::::
:::
::::

The Hausdorff count on three points closes the section. Like @prp-finite-topologies it rests on the enumeration of
@exr-finite-topologies, and the examples below explain why the answer is one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-hausdorff-topologies}
#### Hausdorff topologies on three points

Of the $29$ topologies on a three-element set, exactly one, the discrete topology, is Hausdorff.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a two-element set the enumeration of @exr-hausdorff-check-finite found the same pattern, a single Hausdorff topology
among four. The example records it as the first instance of the finite case.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-two-points}
#### Two points

Of the $4$ topologies on two points, only the discrete one is Hausdorff (@exr-hausdorff-check-finite).
:::

The one Hausdorff topology on three points is the discrete one, with all eight subsets open. The example lists the
separating sets for each of the three pairs of points.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-three-discrete}
#### The discrete topology on three points

On $\{1, 2, 3\}$ with all $8$ subsets open, the pairs $\{1, 2\}$, $\{1, 3\}$, $\{2, 3\}$ are separated by the singletons: $\{1\}$
and $\{2\}$, $\{1\}$ and $\{3\}$, $\{2\}$ and $\{3\}$.
:::

A topology can separate some pairs and not others. In the next example two of the points are separated, and the third
cannot be separated from either.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-three-near-miss}
#### A near miss

For $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}, X\}$ on $X = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the points $1$ and $2$ are separated by $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$. The
only neighbourhood of $3$ is $X$, which meets everything, so $3$ is separated from neither.
:::

A topology made of a partition into open blocks separates points of different blocks only. The points inside one block
are indistinguishable by open sets.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-three-partition}
#### A partition topology

For $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2, 3\}, X\}$, the points $1$ and $2$ are separated by $\{1\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$, and so are $1$ and $3$; but
every open set containing $2$ contains $3$, so $2$ and $3$ are not separated.
:::

The pattern on two and three points holds on every finite set: the discrete topology is the only Hausdorff one. The
example states the general fact, which an exercise below proves from the closedness of points.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-discrete-general}
#### The general finite case

On any finite set the discrete topology is the only Hausdorff one: a finite Hausdorff space is discrete.
:::

A finite set of physical labels, such as the three states $m = -1, 0, 1$ of a spin-one particle, can carry many topologies.
Only one of them lets all three labels be told apart by open sets.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-spin-labels}
#### Spin labels

On the set $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ of the values of $m$ for spin one, $29$ topologies are possible, and the discrete one is the only
topology in which any two values have disjoint neighbourhoods. It is also the topology the labels inherit as a subset of
$\mathbb{R}$.
:::

A finite subset of a coordinate space inherits the discrete topology, which is consistent with the count. Three
positions of a particle on a line, at three sites of a lattice, give the simplest case.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-subspace-finite}
#### Three sites on a line

The sites $\{-1, 0, 1\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ with the subspace topology: $\{0\} = (-\tfrac12, \tfrac12) \cap \{-1, 0, 1\}$ is open, and
likewise $\{-1\}$ and $\{1\}$, so the topology is discrete, the Hausdorff one, as @exm-hausdorff-subspace requires.
:::

The separation conditions on three points form a chain of decreasing counts. Of the $29$ topologies, $19$ can tell every
pair of points apart by some open set (@exr-topology-t0-count), and only one separates every pair by disjoint ones.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-chain}
#### A chain of conditions

On three points: $29$ topologies; $19$ in which, for any two points, some open set contains one and not the other; $1$ in
which every point is closed; and $1$ Hausdorff. On a finite set the last two conditions coincide.
:::

Finiteness is what makes the Hausdorff topology unique. On an infinite set there are many, including the usual and the
discrete topologies on the line.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-infinite}
#### Infinite spaces

On an infinite set there are many Hausdorff topologies, for instance the usual one on $\mathbb{R}$ and the discrete one, which
differ; finiteness is what collapses the count to one.
:::

Quotients of finite Hausdorff spaces remain Hausdorff, in contrast with the line modulo the rationals. The reason is that
every subset of a discrete space is open, so every set of classes has an open preimage.

::: {#exm-hausdorff-finite-quotient}
#### Quotients of finite spaces

Gluing two of the three points of the discrete space $\{1, 2, 3\}$ gives a two-point quotient in which both classes are
open, since every preimage is open: the discrete two-point space, again Hausdorff. Compare @exm-hausdorff-quotient, where
an infinite Hausdorff space has an indiscrete quotient.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise tests four given topologies on three points directly against the definition. It is a check of the
three examples above and of one more topology.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-three-list}
#### Four topologies on three points

Decide which of $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}, X\}$, $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}, X\}$, $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2, 3\}, X\}$ and the
discrete topology on $X = \{1, 2, 3\}$ are Hausdorff, and list the pairs each one separates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

In the chain $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}, X\}$ every non-empty open set contains $1$, so no pair is separated. The second
separates only $1$, $2$ (@exm-hausdorff-three-near-miss), the third separates $1$, $2$ and $1$, $3$
(@exm-hausdorff-three-partition), and the discrete topology separates all three pairs; only the last is Hausdorff.

## SageMath

Sage tests each pair of points for disjoint open sets.

```{.python .sage}
F = frozenset; X = F([1, 2, 3])
Ts = [[F(), F([1]), F([1, 2]), X], [F(), F([1]), F([2]), F([1, 2]), X], [F(), F([1]), F([2, 3]), X],
      [F(s) for s in Subsets([1, 2, 3])]]
for T in Ts:
    sep = [(a, b) for a, b in [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)] if any(a in U and b in V and not U & V for U in T for V in T)]
    print(len(T), "open sets: separated pairs", sep, "; Hausdorff:", len(sep) == 3)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
4 open sets: separated pairs [] ; Hausdorff: False
5 open sets: separated pairs [(1, 2)] ; Hausdorff: False
4 open sets: separated pairs [(1, 2), (1, 3)] ; Hausdorff: False
8 open sets: separated pairs [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)] ; Hausdorff: True
```
::::
:::

The general statement of @exm-hausdorff-discrete-general is proved here: a finite Hausdorff space is discrete. The
argument passes through the closedness of points from @exr-hausdorff-points-closed, and the result is compared with the
enumeration.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-finite}
#### Which finite topologies are Hausdorff?

Explain why the only Hausdorff topology on a finite set is the discrete one, and compare with the count of
@exr-finite-topologies.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

In a Hausdorff space every point is closed (@exr-hausdorff-points-closed), so in a finite space every subset, a finite
union of points, is closed, and its complement, an arbitrary subset, is open: the topology is discrete. Conversely the
discrete topology is Hausdorff (@exm-hausdorff-discrete-indiscrete). The enumeration of @exr-finite-topologies finds
$29$ topologies on three points, and exactly one Hausdorff topology among them, the discrete one, in agreement.

## SageMath

Check on four points: Sage enumerates the topologies on $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ through their smallest neighbourhoods, as in the
proof of @prp-finite-topologies, and counts the Hausdorff ones.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
X = [0, 1, 2, 3]; P = [(x, y) for x in X for y in X if x != y]
count, haus = 0, 0
for bits in product([0, 1], repeat=len(P)):
    R = {p for p, b in zip(P, bits) if b}
    if all((x, z) in R for (x, y) in R for (y2, z) in R if y == y2 and x != z):
        count += 1
        haus += (len(R) == 0)      # Hausdorff iff every smallest neighbourhood is a point
print("topologies on four points:", count, "; Hausdorff:", haus)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
topologies on four points: 355 ; Hausdorff: 1
```
::::
:::

A weaker separation condition than Hausdorff asks only that every point be closed, and the exercise counts the
three-point topologies satisfying it. On a finite set the two conditions turn out to agree.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-count-t1}
#### Topologies with closed points

Count the topologies on three points in which every single point is closed, and compare with the Hausdorff count.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If all points are closed in a finite space, every subset is a finite union of points, hence closed, and so every subset is
open: the topology is discrete. So exactly one of the $29$ topologies has all points closed, the discrete one, which is
also the only Hausdorff one.

## SageMath

Sage tests which of the $29$ topologies contain the complement of each point.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import combinations
F = frozenset; X = [1, 2, 3]
subs = [F(c) for r in range(4) for c in combinations(X, r)]
T29 = [T for T in ({subs[i] for i in range(8) if m >> i & 1} for m in range(256))
       if F() in T and F(X) in T and all(A | B in T and A & B in T for A in T for B in T)]
t1 = [T for T in T29 if all(F(X) - {p} in T for p in X)]
print("topologies:", len(T29), "; with all points closed:", len(t1), "; that one has", len(t1[0]), "open sets")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
topologies: 29 ; with all points closed: 1 ; that one has 8 open sets
```
::::
:::

The two-point topology with a single open singleton is the smallest in which separation fails, and the exercise asks
for an inventory of its neighbourhoods, its limits and its closed points. Non-unique limits and a non-closed point appear
together, as @exr-hausdorff-points-closed and @exr-hausdorff-limits-unique predict they must in a non-Hausdorff space.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-sierpinski}
#### The Sierpiński space

For the topology $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}\}$ on $\{1, 2\}$, list the neighbourhoods of each point, decide whether limits of
sequences (@exm-hausdorff-limits) are unique, and which points are closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Neighbourhoods of $1$: $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 2\}$; of $2$: only $\{1, 2\}$. The constant sequence $1, 1, 1, \dots$ converges to $1$ and
also to $2$, since every neighbourhood of $2$ contains $1$: limits are not unique. The point $2$ is closed, its complement
$\{1\}$ being open, and the point $1$ is not, since $\{2\}$ is not open.

## SageMath

Sage lists the neighbourhoods, tests convergence of the constant sequence to each point, and tests the closedness of each
point.

```{.python .sage}
F = frozenset; X = F([1, 2]); T = [F(), F([1]), X]
nb = {p: [sorted(U) for U in T if p in U] for p in X}
print("neighbourhoods:", nb)
print("constant sequence 1 converges to:", [p for p in X if all(1 in U for U in T if p in U)])
print("closed points:", [p for p in X if X - {p} in T])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
neighbourhoods: {1: [[1], [1, 2]], 2: [[1, 2]]}
constant sequence 1 converges to: [1, 2]
closed points: [2]
```
::::
:::

The next exercise measures how far each topology on three points is from Hausdorff by counting the separated pairs.
The distribution shows that only the discrete topology reaches three.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-pairs-separated}
#### Counting separated pairs

For each of the $29$ topologies on three points, count the pairs of points that have disjoint neighbourhoods, and tabulate
how many topologies separate $0$, $1$, $2$ or $3$ pairs.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Two points are separated exactly when their smallest neighbourhoods $U_x$, $U_y$ of the proof of @prp-finite-topologies are
disjoint. Three separated pairs force all $U_x$ to be points: $1$ topology, the discrete one. If exactly $\{x, y\}$ and $\{x,
z\}$ are separated, then $U_x = \{x\}$, while $U_y \in \{\{y\}, \{y, z\}\}$ and $U_z \in \{\{z\}, \{y, z\}\}$ meet: $3$ choices for
each of the $3$ points $x$, so $9$ topologies. If only $\{x, y\}$ is separated, then $U_x = \{x\}$, $U_y = \{y\}$ (a larger one
would separate $z$ from one of them), and $U_z$ meets both, so $U_z = X$: $3$ topologies. The other $29 - 13 = 16$ separate no
pair.

## SageMath

Sage counts the separated pairs in each of the $29$ topologies.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import combinations
from collections import Counter
F = frozenset; X = [1, 2, 3]
subs = [F(c) for r in range(4) for c in combinations(X, r)]
T29 = [T for T in ({subs[i] for i in range(8) if m >> i & 1} for m in range(256))
       if F() in T and F(X) in T and all(A | B in T and A & B in T for A in T for B in T)]
sep = lambda T: sum(any(a in U and b in V and not U & V for U in T for V in T) for a, b in combinations(X, 2))
print(sorted(Counter(sep(T) for T in T29).items()))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[(0, 16), (1, 3), (2, 9), (3, 1)]
```
::::
:::

A finite subset of a coordinate space gets the discrete topology, as @exm-hausdorff-subspace-finite showed for three
sites. The exercise asks for the proof in general.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-finite-subspace}
#### Finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$

Prove that a finite subset $F \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with the subspace topology is discrete, and check it for $F = \{0, 1/3, 1\}
\subset \mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$F$ is Hausdorff (@exm-hausdorff-subspace) and finite, hence discrete (@exr-hausdorff-finite). Directly: for $p \in F$ let
$r$ be the smallest distance from $p$ to another point of $F$; then $B_r(p) \cap F = \{p\}$, so $\{p\}$ is open in $F$, and every
subset of $F$ is a union of such points.

## SageMath

Sage computes the radius $r$ for each point of $F$ and the trace of the ball.

```{.python .sage}
Fs = [0, 1/3, 1]
for p in Fs:
    r = min(abs(p - q) for q in Fs if q != p)
    print("p =", p, ": r =", r, "; ball trace:", [q for q in Fs if abs(q - p) < r])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
p = 0 : r = 1/3 ; ball trace: [0]
p = 1/3 : r = 1/3 ; ball trace: [1/3]
p = 1 : r = 2/3 ; ball trace: [1]
```
::::
:::

In the language of the proof of @prp-finite-topologies, a topology on a finite set is a reflexive and transitive relation.
The exercise identifies the relation of a Hausdorff topology.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-preorder}
#### Hausdorff in terms of the relation

With $x \preceq y \iff x \in U_y$ as in the proof of @prp-finite-topologies, prove that a topology on a finite set is Hausdorff iff
$x \preceq y$ only for $x = y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If the relation is equality, every $U_y = \{y\}$ is open and the topology is discrete, hence Hausdorff. Conversely, if $x
\preceq y$ with $x \neq y$, then $x$ lies in every open set containing $y$, as $U_y$ is the smallest such set, so every
neighbourhood of $y$ meets every neighbourhood of $x$ (both contain $x$), and the topology is not Hausdorff.

## SageMath

Check on the $29$ topologies of three points: Sage computes each relation and compares "relation is equality" with
"Hausdorff".

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import combinations
F = frozenset; X = [1, 2, 3]
subs = [F(c) for r in range(4) for c in combinations(X, r)]
T29 = [T for T in ({subs[i] for i in range(8) if m >> i & 1} for m in range(256))
       if F() in T and F(X) in T and all(A | B in T and A & B in T for A in T for B in T)]
def trivial(T):
    U = {y: F.intersection(*[V for V in T if y in V]) for y in X}
    return all(U[y] == F([y]) for y in X)
haus = lambda T: all(any(a in U and b in V and not U & V for U in T for V in T) for a, b in combinations(X, 2))
print("criterion agrees on all 29:", all(trivial(T) == haus(T) for T in T29))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
criterion agrees on all 29: True
```
::::
:::

Adding open sets can only help to separate points, so a topology finer than a Hausdorff one is Hausdorff. The exercise
asks for this and checks it against the three-point count, where the discrete topology has nothing finer.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-finer}
#### Finer topologies

Let $\tau_1 \subseteq \tau_2$ be topologies on $X$ with $\tau_1$ Hausdorff. Prove that $\tau_2$ is Hausdorff, and list the
topologies on three points that contain a given topology $\tau_1$ when $\tau_1$ is the partition topology $\{\emptyset, \{1\},
\{2, 3\}, X\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Disjoint sets $U \ni p$, $V \ni q$ of $\tau_1$ are also in $\tau_2$, so they separate $p$ and $q$ for $\tau_2$ as well. On three
points the only Hausdorff topology is discrete and nothing is finer; the topologies containing the partition topology
must contain $\{1\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$, and they are the partition topology itself, the two obtained by adding $\{2\}$ or
$\{3\}$ together with the unions this forces, and the discrete topology. Only the last is Hausdorff, as the partition
topology does not separate $2$ and $3$ (@exm-hausdorff-three-partition).

## SageMath

Sage lists the topologies on three points containing the partition topology and tests each for the Hausdorff property.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import combinations
F = frozenset; X = [1, 2, 3]
subs = [F(c) for r in range(4) for c in combinations(X, r)]
T29 = [T for T in ({subs[i] for i in range(8) if m >> i & 1} for m in range(256))
       if F() in T and F(X) in T and all(A | B in T and A & B in T for A in T for B in T)]
T1 = {F(), F([1]), F([2, 3]), F(X)}
haus = lambda T: all(any(a in U and b in V and not U & V for U in T for V in T) for a, b in combinations(X, 2))
for T in sorted((T for T in T29 if T1 <= T), key=len):
    print(sorted(sorted(U) for U in T), "Hausdorff:", haus(T))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[[], [1], [1, 2, 3], [2, 3]] Hausdorff: False
[[], [1], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3], [2], [2, 3]] Hausdorff: False
[[], [1], [1, 2, 3], [1, 3], [2, 3], [3]] Hausdorff: False
[[], [1], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3], [1, 3], [2], [2, 3], [3]] Hausdorff: True
```
::::
:::

Maps into a finite Hausdorff space are severely restricted when the domain is connected. The exercise combines the
proposition with the two-valued criterion of @exr-connected-two-valued.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-finite-connected-maps}
#### Maps to a finite Hausdorff space

Show that a map from a space $X$ to a finite Hausdorff space is continuous if and only if the preimage of each point is open,
and that a continuous map from a connected space to a finite Hausdorff space is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The target $Y$ is discrete (@exr-hausdorff-finite), so its points are open and a continuous map has open preimages of
points. Conversely, every subset of $Y$ is a union of points, so its preimage is a union of open preimages of points, and the
map is continuous. If $X$ is connected and $f : X \to Y$ continuous takes a value $y$, the
sets $f^{-1}(\{y\})$ and $f^{-1}(Y \setminus \{y\})$ are open and disjoint and cover $X$; the first is non-empty, so the second is
empty and $f$ is constant (@exr-connected-two-valued).

## SageMath

Check on $X = [0, 1]$ and the discrete $\{1, 2, 3\}$: Sage takes the step function equal to $1$ on $[0, \tfrac12)$ and $2$ on $[\tfrac12,
1]$ and finds that the preimage of $\{2\}$ contains its left end point $\tfrac12$ but no points just before it, so it is not open.

```{.python .sage}
f = lambda t: 1 if t < 1/2 else 2
print("f(1/2) =", f(1/2), "; f(1/2 - 1/10^k) for k = 1..5:", [f(1/2 - 1 / 10^k) for k in range(1, 6)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f(1/2) = 2 ; f(1/2 - 1/10^k) for k = 1..5: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
```
::::
:::

The last exercise brings the three properties of the section together on finite spaces. Every finite space is compact,
and a finite Hausdorff space is connected only when it is a single point.

::: {#exr-hausdorff-finite-all-three}
#### Finite spaces and the three properties

Show that every finite space is compact, and that a finite Hausdorff space with at least two points is disconnected.
Among the $29$ topologies on three points, count the connected ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A finite space is compact by @exm-compact-finite. A finite Hausdorff space is discrete (@exr-hausdorff-finite), and a
discrete space with two or more points is disconnected (@exm-connected-finite-small). A topology on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is
disconnected iff some open set other than $\emptyset$ and $X$ has an open complement; testing the $29$ topologies leaves
$19$ connected ones.

## SageMath

Sage tests each of the $29$ topologies for an open set with open complement.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import combinations
F = frozenset; X = [1, 2, 3]
subs = [F(c) for r in range(4) for c in combinations(X, r)]
T29 = [T for T in ({subs[i] for i in range(8) if m >> i & 1} for m in range(256))
       if F() in T and F(X) in T and all(A | B in T and A & B in T for A in T for B in T)]
conn = [T for T in T29 if not any(U and U != F(X) and F(X) - U in T for U in T)]
print("connected topologies on three points:", len(conn))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
connected topologies on three points: 19
```
::::
:::
::::

## Metric spaces {#sec-metric-spaces}

The open sets of @def-open-set were cut out by one number, the distance $|x - p|$, and much of the topology of this
chapter used nothing else. A metric keeps exactly that number and forgets the coordinates: a set with a distance
function obeying three axioms. It gives the topologies of $\mathbb{R}^n$, of the circle and the sphere, and of spaces
of functions a concrete form, in which an open set is a union of balls and a limit is a point approached in distance.
It also adds one property that a topology alone cannot express. A sequence whose terms come close to each other
should come close to a point, and a space in which this always happens is complete. Completeness is the property the
analysis chapters need: it makes the real line a continuum without gaps, it makes spaces of functions usable, and it
gives the contraction mapping theorem, which solves equations by iteration and with which this section ends.

For more on this topic, see @cheung2024metric [Secs. 1.1, 2.1-2.2, 4.2], @lee2013introduction [App. A, Example A.5,
p. 598] and @keskivakkuri2022mathematical [Sec. 4.1.1, pp. 100-101].

### Metrics

The definition lists the three properties of the distance between two points of space that every later argument
uses. A distance is never negative and vanishes only between a point and itself, it does not depend on the order of
the two points, and a detour through a third point is never shorter than the direct way.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-metric-space}
#### Metric space

A **metric** on a set $X$ is a map $d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$

1. $d(x, y) \geq 0$, with $d(x, y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$;
2. $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$ (**symmetry**);
3. $d(x, z) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, z)$ (the **triangle inequality**).

A set with a metric is a **metric space** $(X, d)$, and $d(x, y)$ is the **distance** between $x$ and $y$. The
**open ball** of radius $\varepsilon > 0$ about $p \in X$ is $B_\varepsilon(p) = \{x \in X : d(x, p) < \varepsilon\}$. A
subset $Y \subseteq X$ with the restriction of $d$ to $Y \times Y$ is again a metric space, a **metric subspace** of $X$.
:::
::::

The axioms are those of @lee2013introduction [Example A.5] and @cheung2024metric [Def. 1.1.1]. On $\mathbb{R}^n$ with
$d(x, y) = |x - y|$ the ball $B_\varepsilon(p)$ is the ball of @def-open-set, so the notation does not clash. When two
metrics on one set are compared, the ball is named with its metric, as in "the $d_1$-ball".

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The real line is the first metric space, and the only fact behind it is the inequality $|a + b| \leq |a| + |b|$ for real
numbers. Every other example of the section imitates it in some way.

::: {#exm-metric-real-line}
#### The real line

On $\mathbb{R}$ put $d(x, y) = |x - y|$. It is non-negative and vanishes only for $x = y$, and $|x - y| = |y - x|$. With
$a = x - y$ and $b = y - z$, the inequality $|a + b| \leq |a| + |b|$ reads $|x - z| \leq |x - y| + |y - z|$. Its ball
$B_\varepsilon(p)$ is the open interval $(p - \varepsilon, p + \varepsilon)$.
:::

The opposite extreme gives every pair of distinct points the same distance. The discrete metric exists on every set,
and it shows that a metric need not measure anything geometric [@cheung2024metric, Example 1.1.2(ii)].

::: {#exm-metric-discrete}
#### The discrete metric

On any set $X$ put $d(x, y) = 0$ if $x = y$ and $d(x, y) = 1$ otherwise. The first two axioms are clear. In the
triangle inequality the left side is $0$ or $1$, and if it is $1$ then $x \neq z$, so $y$ differs from $x$ or from $z$ and
the right side is at least $1$. The ball $B_\varepsilon(p)$ is $\{p\}$ for $\varepsilon \leq 1$ and all of $X$ for
$\varepsilon > 1$.
:::

On a finite set a metric is a symmetric table of distances with zeros on the diagonal, and the only axiom left to check
is the triangle inequality for every triple. The table shows how a single long side breaks it
[@cheung2024metric, Example 1.1.2(i)].

::: {#exm-metric-finite-table}
#### A metric given by a table

On $X = \{a, b, c\}$ let $d(a, b) = 2$, $d(a, c) = 3$, $d(b, c) = 4$. Each side of the triangle is at most the sum of the
other two, $4 \leq 2 + 3$ being the tightest case, so $d$ is a metric. Changing $d(a, b)$ to $1$ and $d(a, c)$ to $2$
while keeping $d(b, c) = 4$ breaks it: $d(b, c) = 4 > 3 = d(b, a) + d(a, c)$.
:::

The Euclidean distance on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the metric of @def-open-set. Its triangle inequality needs one algebraic
step beyond the real line, the inequality of Cauchy and Schwarz, which is proved here from a sum of squares.

::: {#exm-metric-space-euclidean}
#### The Euclidean metric

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ let $d_2(x, y) = |x - y| = \big(\sum_i (x_i - y_i)^2\big)^{1/2}$. For $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the
identity $\big(\sum_i a_i^2\big)\big(\sum_j b_j^2\big) - \big(\sum_i a_i b_i\big)^2 = \sum_{i < j}(a_i b_j - a_j b_i)^2 \geq 0$
gives $\sum_i a_i b_i \leq |a|\,|b|$, hence $|a + b|^2 = |a|^2 + 2\sum_i a_i b_i + |b|^2 \leq (|a| + |b|)^2$. With
$a = x - y$ and $b = y - z$ this is the triangle inequality $d_2(x, z) \leq d_2(x, y) + d_2(y, z)$.
:::

The same set carries other natural metrics, and their balls have other shapes. The taxicab and the max metrics are the
two most used besides the Euclidean one [@cheung2024metric, Example 1.1.2(viii)-(ix)], and @fig-metric-balls draws
the three unit balls in the plane.

::: {#exm-metric-taxicab-max}
#### The taxicab and the max metrics

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ let $d_1(x, y) = \sum_i |x_i - y_i|$ and $d_\infty(x, y) = \max_i |x_i - y_i|$. Both satisfy the triangle
inequality coordinate by coordinate, from $|x_i - z_i| \leq |x_i - y_i| + |y_i - z_i|$. The three metrics are comparable:
$$
d_\infty(x, y) \leq d_2(x, y) \leq d_1(x, y) \leq n\, d_\infty(x, y).
$$
In the plane the unit $d_1$-ball is a diamond, the $d_2$-ball a disc and the $d_\infty$-ball a square, nested as in the
figure.

![Unit balls about the origin of the plane for the taxicab metric $d_1$ (diamond), the Euclidean metric $d_2$ (disc)
and the max metric $d_\infty$ (square).](figures/metric_balls.svg){#fig-metric-balls width=50%}
:::

A row of $N$ spins, each up or down, is a finite set with a natural metric: the number of spins that must be flipped to
turn one configuration into another. This Hamming distance is the taxicab metric restricted to configurations written
as strings of $0$s and $1$s.

::: {#exm-metric-hamming}
#### Flipping spins

Write a configuration of $N$ spins as $s = (s_1, \dots, s_N)$ with $s_i \in \{0, 1\}$, and let $d(s, t)$ be the number of $i$
with $s_i \neq t_i$. Since $|s_i - t_i|$ is $1$ exactly when $s_i \neq t_i$, this is $d_1(s, t)$ on $\{0, 1\}^N \subset
\mathbb{R}^N$, a metric subspace of $(\mathbb{R}^N, d_1)$. For $N = 3$, $d(\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow, \uparrow\downarrow\downarrow) = 2$, and the
ball of radius $3/2$ about a configuration holds it and the $3$ configurations one flip away.
:::

The circle can be given two metrics: the length of the chord, inherited from the plane, and the length of the shorter
arc, measured inside the circle. The second is the distance a bead on a ring travels, and it is computed from the
angles of the two points [@cheung2024metric, Example 1.1.2(vi) and Example 1.1.10(iii)].

::: {#exm-metric-circle-arc}
#### Arc length on the circle

For points $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$ and $(\cos\beta, \sin\beta)$ of $S^1$ the shorter arc between them has length
$$
d(\alpha, \beta) = \min_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} |\alpha - \beta - 2\pi k| \in [0, \pi],
$$
which does not change when $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is shifted by a multiple of $2\pi$. The chord has length
$\sqrt{(\cos\alpha - \cos\beta)^2 + (\sin\alpha - \sin\beta)^2} = 2\sin(d/2)$. The north and south poles are at arc
distance $\pi$ and chord distance $2$.
:::

The sphere carries the same two metrics, and the intrinsic one is the angle between two directions. Physics measures it
whenever it compares directions: the angular separation of two stars, or the angle between two spin axes
[@cheung2024metric, Example 1.1.2(vii)].

::: {#exm-metric-sphere-angle}
#### The angle between two directions

For unit vectors $u, v \in S^2$ the **great-circle distance** is the angle $\theta(u, v) \in [0, \pi]$ between them, the
length of the shorter arc of a great circle through $u$ and $v$. It is related to the chord by $|u - v| = 2\sin(\theta/2)$,
so $\cos\theta = 1 - |u - v|^2/2 = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3$. That $\theta$ satisfies the triangle inequality is a fact of
spherical geometry, which this chapter uses but does not prove. The north pole and a point of the equator are at angle
$\pi/2$; antipodal points are at angle $\pi$.
:::

Functions can be points of a metric space too, with the largest gap between two graphs as their distance. Two motions
of an oscillator are then close when they never differ by much, at any time of the interval watched
[@cheung2024metric, Example 1.1.2(xiii)-(xiv)].

::: {#exm-metric-bounded-functions}
#### Bounded functions and the sup metric

For a set $S$, let $\ell_\infty(S)$ be the set of bounded functions $f : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$d_\infty(f, g) = \sup_{t \in S} |f(t) - g(t)|$. The supremum exists because $f - g$ is bounded, and the triangle
inequality follows from $|f(t) - h(t)| \leq d_\infty(f, g) + d_\infty(g, h)$ for every $t$. Two oscillations $x(t) = \cos t$ and
$y(t) = A\cos t$ on $S = [0, 2\pi]$ are at distance $|1 - A|$, the gap at $t = 0$. On a finite set $S = [n]$ this is the max
metric of @exm-metric-taxicab-max.
:::

Formulas that look like distances can fail the axioms, and a distance can be bent without breaking them. Squaring
$|x - y|$ breaks the triangle inequality, while its square root keeps it [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.1, Part A,
Problems 3-5].

::: {#exm-metric-failures}
#### What is not a metric

On $\mathbb{R}$, $(x - y)^2$ is not a metric: $(0 - 2)^2 = 4 > 1 + 1 = (0 - 1)^2 + (1 - 2)^2$. On $\mathbb{R}^2$,
$\min(|x_1 - y_1|, |x_2 - y_2|)$ is not a metric, since it vanishes between $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 5)$. A table on $\{a, b\}$
with $d(a, b) = 1$ and $d(b, a) = 2$ satisfies the first axiom and the triangle inequality but is not symmetric. In
contrast, $\sqrt{|x - y|}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ with the same balls as $|x - y|$, only with squared radii.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the axioms on finite tables, the case in which every triple can be listed. It asks which of
three tables on three points are metrics, and why the others fail.

::: {#exr-metric-table-check}
#### Which tables are metrics?

On $\{a, b, c\}$, decide which tables are metrics: (i) $d(a, b) = 1$, $d(a, c) = 2$, $d(b, c) = 3$; (ii) $d(a, b) = 1$,
$d(a, c) = 2$, $d(b, c) = 4$; (iii) $d(a, b) = 1$, $d(b, a) = 2$, $d(a, c) = d(c, a) = d(b, c) = d(c, b) = 1$. All diagonal
entries are $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

(i) is a metric: the entries are positive off the diagonal and symmetric, and the three triangle inequalities
$1 \leq 2 + 3$, $2 \leq 1 + 3$, $3 \leq 1 + 2$ hold, the last with equality (the three points lie "on a line"). (ii) is not:
$d(b, c) = 4 > 1 + 2 = d(b, a) + d(a, c)$, so the triangle inequality of @def-metric-space fails. (iii) is not, because
$d(a, b) \neq d(b, a)$ breaks symmetry, although every triangle inequality holds there [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.1,
Part A, Problem 1].

## SageMath

Sage tests all three axioms on each table by running through every triple of points.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
X = "abc"
def table(ab, ba, ac, bc):
    d = {(x, x): 0 for x in X}
    d.update({("a", "b"): ab, ("b", "a"): ba, ("a", "c"): ac, ("c", "a"): ac, ("b", "c"): bc, ("c", "b"): bc})
    return d
def is_metric(d):
    pos = all((d[x, y] > 0) == (x != y) for x, y in product(X, X))
    sym = all(d[x, y] == d[y, x] for x, y in product(X, X))
    tri = all(d[x, z] <= d[x, y] + d[y, z] for x, y, z in product(X, X, X))
    return pos, sym, tri
for name, d in [("(i)", table(1, 1, 2, 3)), ("(ii)", table(1, 1, 2, 4)), ("(iii)", table(1, 2, 1, 1))]:
    print(name, "positivity, symmetry, triangle:", is_metric(d))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(i) positivity, symmetry, triangle: (True, True, True)
(ii) positivity, symmetry, triangle: (True, True, False)
(iii) positivity, symmetry, triangle: (True, False, True)
```
::::
:::

The second exercise computes the three metrics of @exm-metric-taxicab-max for one pair of points of the plane. The
numbers show the chain of inequalities between them in a concrete case.

::: {#exr-metric-three-distances}
#### Three distances between two points

Compute $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ between $x = (1, 2)$ and $y = (4, -2)$, and check $d_\infty \leq d_2 \leq d_1 \leq 2d_\infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The coordinate differences are $3$ and $4$ in absolute value. So $d_1 = 3 + 4 = 7$, $d_2 = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ and
$d_\infty = \max(3, 4) = 4$. The chain reads $4 \leq 5 \leq 7 \leq 8$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the three distances from the coordinate differences.

```{.python .sage}
x = vector(QQ, [1, 2]); y = vector(QQ, [4, -2]); a = [abs(c) for c in x - y]
d1, d2, dinf = sum(a), sqrt(sum(c^2 for c in a)), max(a)
print("d1 =", d1, " d2 =", d2, " dinf =", dinf)
print("chain holds:", dinf <= d2 <= d1 <= 2 * dinf)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
d1 = 7  d2 = 5  dinf = 4
chain holds: True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise counts the configurations of a spin chain at a given Hamming distance from a fixed one, the metric of
@exm-metric-hamming. The count is the number of ways to choose which spins to flip.

::: {#exr-metric-hamming-count}
#### Configurations at distance $k$

For $N$ spins, show that exactly $\binom{N}{k}$ configurations are at Hamming distance $k$ from a given one, and find the
number of points in the ball of radius $5/2$ about a configuration of $N = 6$ spins.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A configuration at distance $k$ from $s$ differs from it in exactly $k$ positions, and it is determined by the set of
those positions, since each differing spin has only one other value. So the configurations at distance $k$ correspond
to the $k$-element subsets of $[N]$, of which there are $\binom{N}{k}$. The ball of radius $5/2$ consists of the
configurations at distance $0$, $1$ or $2$: $1 + 6 + 15 = 22$ of them for $N = 6$.

## SageMath

Sage lists all $64$ configurations of six spins and counts them by their distance from the all-up configuration.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
N = 6; s = (0,) * N
dist = lambda a, b: sum(1 for i in range(N) if a[i] != b[i])
counts = [sum(1 for t in product([0, 1], repeat=N) if dist(s, t) == k) for k in range(N + 1)]
print("counts by distance:", counts, " binomials:", [binomial(N, k) for k in range(N + 1)])
print("ball of radius 5/2:", sum(1 for t in product([0, 1], repeat=N) if dist(s, t) < 5/2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
counts by distance: [1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1]  binomials: [1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1]
ball of radius 5/2: 22
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise compares the two metrics of the circle in @exm-metric-circle-arc. It asks for the chord in terms of
the arc and shows that the chord is never longer.

::: {#exr-metric-arc-chord}
#### Arc and chord

Show that the chord between two points of $S^1$ at arc distance $\theta$ is $2\sin(\theta/2)$, and that it is at most
$\theta$. Compute both for the points at angles $0$ and $2\pi/3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Rotating both points by the same angle changes neither distance, so take them at angles $0$ and $\theta \in [0, \pi]$.
The squared chord is $(1 - \cos\theta)^2 + \sin^2\theta = 2 - 2\cos\theta = 4\sin^2(\theta/2)$, so the chord is
$2\sin(\theta/2)$, as $\sin(\theta/2) \geq 0$. From $\sin t \leq t$ for $t \geq 0$ the chord is at most $2(\theta/2) = \theta$.
For the angles $0$ and $2\pi/3$, $\theta = 2\pi/3 \approx 2.094$ and the chord is $2\sin(\pi/3) = \sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the chord from the coordinates and compares it with $2\sin(\theta/2)$ and with the arc.

```{.python .sage}
th = 2 * pi / 3
P, Q = vector([1, 0]), vector([cos(th), sin(th)])
chord = (P - Q).norm().simplify_full()
print("chord =", chord, " 2 sin(theta/2) =", 2 * sin(th / 2), " arc =", th)
print("chord <= arc:", bool(chord <= th), " numerically:", N(chord, digits=5), N(th, digits=5))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
chord = sqrt(3)  2 sin(theta/2) = sqrt(3)  arc = 2/3*pi
chord <= arc: True  numerically: 1.7320 2.0944
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise proves that the square root of the distance on the line is again a metric. It shows how the triangle
inequality survives a concave change of scale [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.1, Part A, Problem 3].

::: {#exr-metric-sqrt}
#### The square root of a metric

Prove that $\rho(x, y) = \sqrt{|x - y|}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$, and that its balls are $B^\rho_\varepsilon(p) =
B_{\varepsilon^2}(p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\rho$ is non-negative, vanishes only for $x = y$ and is symmetric, because $|x - y|$ has these properties
(@exm-metric-real-line). For the triangle inequality,
$\rho(x, z)^2 = |x - z| \leq |x - y| + |y - z| = \rho(x, y)^2 + \rho(y, z)^2 \leq (\rho(x, y) + \rho(y, z))^2$, and taking the
non-negative square root gives $\rho(x, z) \leq \rho(x, y) + \rho(y, z)$. Finally $\sqrt{|x - p|} < \varepsilon$ if and
only if $|x - p| < \varepsilon^2$.

## SageMath

Check on random rational triples: Sage tests the triangle inequality for $\rho$ on $2000$ triples.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(1)
rho = lambda x, y: sqrt(abs(x - y))
trip = [[QQ.random_element(100, 100) for _ in range(3)] for _ in range(2000)]
print("triangle inequality on 2000 triples:", all(bool(rho(x, z) <= rho(x, y) + rho(y, z)) for x, y, z in trip))
print("squaring breaks it:", (0 - 2)^2, ">", (0 - 1)^2 + (1 - 2)^2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
triangle inequality on 2000 triples: True
squaring breaks it: 4 > 2
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise derives the reverse triangle inequality, which says that distances to a fixed point change by at
most the distance moved. It is the estimate behind the continuity of distance functions.

::: {#exr-metric-reverse-triangle}
#### The reverse triangle inequality

Prove that $|d(x, z) - d(y, z)| \leq d(x, y)$ for all $x, y, z$ in a metric space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The triangle inequality gives $d(x, z) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, z)$, so $d(x, z) - d(y, z) \leq d(x, y)$. Exchanging $x$ and $y$
and using symmetry, $d(y, z) - d(x, z) \leq d(y, x) = d(x, y)$. The two bounds together say $|d(x, z) - d(y, z)| \leq
d(x, y)$.

## SageMath

Check on $(\mathbb{R}^2, d_1)$: Sage tests the inequality on $1000$ random rational triples.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(2)
d1 = lambda x, y: sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(x, y))
pt = lambda: [QQ.random_element(20, 20) for _ in range(2)]
trip = [(pt(), pt(), pt()) for _ in range(1000)]
print("reverse triangle inequality:", all(abs(d1(x, z) - d1(y, z)) <= d1(x, y) for x, y, z in trip))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
reverse triangle inequality: True
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise shows that the axioms of @def-metric-space are not independent: non-negativity follows from the
others. It is a short proof that uses each of the other axioms once [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.1, Part A,
Problem 2].

::: {#exr-metric-positivity-redundant}
#### Non-negativity comes free

Let $d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y$, symmetry and the triangle inequality. Prove that
$d(x, y) \geq 0$ for all $x, y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the triangle inequality with $z = x$, then symmetry, $0 = d(x, x) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, x) = 2d(x, y)$. Hence
$d(x, y) \geq 0$.

## SageMath

Check on all symmetric tables on three points with entries in $\{-2, \dots, 2\}$: Sage finds that every table satisfying
the other axioms has no negative entry.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
X = range(3); pairs = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]
ok = 0; bad = 0
for vals in product(range(-2, 3), repeat=3):
    d = {(i, i): 0 for i in X}
    for (i, j), v in zip(pairs, vals):
        d[i, j] = d[j, i] = v
    zero = all((d[i, j] == 0) == (i == j) for i in X for j in X)
    tri = all(d[i, k] <= d[i, j] + d[j, k] for i in X for j in X for k in X)
    if zero and tri:
        ok += 1; bad += any(v < 0 for v in vals)
print("tables satisfying the other axioms:", ok, " with a negative entry:", bad)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
tables satisfying the other axioms: 8  with a negative entry: 0
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise builds new metrics from two given ones, and shows that one natural construction fails. The sum and
the maximum of two metrics are metrics, but the minimum need not be [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 1.1, Part A,
Problem 6].

::: {#exr-metric-combinations}
#### Sums, maxima and minima of metrics

Let $d$ and $d'$ be metrics on $X$. Prove that $d + d'$ and $\max(d, d')$ are metrics, and find metrics on three points
whose minimum is not one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Non-negativity, the zero condition and symmetry pass to $d + d'$ and $\max(d, d')$ at once. Adding the two triangle
inequalities gives that of $d + d'$. For the maximum, $d(x, z) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, z) \leq \max(d, d')(x, y) +
\max(d, d')(y, z)$, and the same bound holds for $d'(x, z)$, so it holds for their maximum. For the minimum take
$X = \{p, q, r\}$ with $d(p, q) = 10$, $d(p, r) = 1$, $d(q, r) = 10$ and $d'(p, q) = 10$, $d'(p, r) = 10$, $d'(q, r) = 1$.
Both are metrics, but $m = \min(d, d')$ has $m(p, q) = 10 > 2 = m(p, r) + m(r, q)$.

## SageMath

Sage checks the triangle inequality for $d$, $d'$, their sum, maximum and minimum on the three points.

```{.python .sage}
from itertools import product
X = "pqr"
def sym(t):
    d = {(x, x): 0 for x in X}
    for (a, b), v in t.items():
        d[a, b] = d[b, a] = v
    return d
d = sym({("p", "q"): 10, ("p", "r"): 1, ("q", "r"): 10}); e = sym({("p", "q"): 10, ("p", "r"): 10, ("q", "r"): 1})
tri = lambda f: all(f(x, z) <= f(x, y) + f(y, z) for x, y, z in product(X, X, X))
for name, f in [("d", lambda x, y: d[x, y]), ("d'", lambda x, y: e[x, y]), ("sum", lambda x, y: d[x, y] + e[x, y]),
                ("max", lambda x, y: max(d[x, y], e[x, y])), ("min", lambda x, y: min(d[x, y], e[x, y]))]:
    print(name, "triangle inequality:", tri(f))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
d triangle inequality: True
d' triangle inequality: True
sum triangle inequality: True
max triangle inequality: True
min triangle inequality: False
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise caps a metric at $1$. The capped metric has the same small balls as the original one, which matters
later, because the topology depends only on small balls.

::: {#exr-metric-capped}
#### A metric capped at one

Prove that $\bar d(x, y) = \min(d(x, y), 1)$ is a metric for every metric $d$, and that $\bar d$ and $d$ have the same balls of
every radius $\varepsilon \leq 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The first two axioms pass from $d$ to $\bar d$. For the triangle inequality, if $\bar d(x, y) = 1$ or $\bar d(y, z) = 1$ the
right side is at least $1 \geq \bar d(x, z)$. Otherwise $\bar d(x, y) = d(x, y)$ and $\bar d(y, z) = d(y, z)$, and
$\bar d(x, z) \leq d(x, z) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, z)$. For $\varepsilon \leq 1$, $\min(d(x, p), 1) < \varepsilon$ holds exactly
when $d(x, p) < \varepsilon$, so the balls agree.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{R}$ with $|x - y|$: Sage tests the triangle inequality for $\bar d$ on random triples and compares two
balls of radius $1/2$ on a grid.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(3)
db = lambda x, y: min(abs(x - y), 1)
trip = [[QQ.random_element(10, 4) for _ in range(3)] for _ in range(2000)]
print("triangle inequality:", all(db(x, z) <= db(x, y) + db(y, z) for x, y, z in trip))
grid = [QQ(k) / 20 for k in range(-60, 61)]
print("same ball of radius 1/2:", [x for x in grid if db(x, 0) < 1/2] == [x for x in grid if abs(x) < 1/2])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
triangle inequality: True
same ball of radius 1/2: True
```
::::
:::

The last exercise derives the arc metric of the circle from the quotient $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ of
@def-quotient-set. It shows that the minimum over representatives is well defined on classes and satisfies the
triangle inequality, so the circle is a metric space in its own right.

::: {#exr-metric-circle-quotient}
#### The metric of $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$

For classes $[\alpha], [\beta]$ of $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ put $d([\alpha], [\beta]) = \min_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} |\alpha - \beta -
2\pi k|$. Prove that $d$ is well defined and is a metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The minimum exists: the numbers $|\alpha - \beta - 2\pi k|$ grow without bound in $|k|$, so only finitely many are below
$2\pi$. Replacing $\alpha$ by $\alpha + 2\pi m$ shifts $k$ by $m$ and does not change the set of values over which the
minimum is taken, and likewise for $\beta$, so $d$ depends only on the classes. It is non-negative, and $d = 0$ means
$\alpha - \beta = 2\pi k$ for some $k$, that is $[\alpha] = [\beta]$. Symmetry follows from $|\alpha - \beta - 2\pi k| =
|\beta - \alpha - 2\pi(-k)|$. For the triangle inequality choose $k$ and $l$ attaining $d([\alpha], [\beta])$ and
$d([\beta], [\gamma])$; then
$$
d([\alpha], [\gamma]) \leq |\alpha - \gamma - 2\pi(k + l)| \leq |\alpha - \beta - 2\pi k| + |\beta - \gamma - 2\pi l| =
d([\alpha], [\beta]) + d([\beta], [\gamma]).
$$

## SageMath

Check on angles that are rational multiples of $\pi$: Sage verifies that $d$ ignores shifts by $2\pi$ and satisfies the
triangle inequality on random triples.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(4)
def d(a, b):
    t = (a - b) / 2
    return 2 * min(abs(t - k) for k in range(floor(t) - 1, floor(t) + 3))
r = lambda: QQ.random_element(30, 7)
trip = [(r(), r(), r()) for _ in range(1000)]
print("well defined:", all(d(a + 2 * m, b) == d(a, b) for a, b, _ in trip[:200] for m in (-3, 1, 5)))
print("triangle inequality:", all(d(a, c) <= d(a, b) + d(b, c) for a, b, c in trip))
print("d(0, 3pi/2) = pi times", d(0, 3/2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
well defined: True
triangle inequality: True
d(0, 3pi/2) = pi times 1/2
```
::::
:::
::::

### The metric topology

A metric decides which sets have room around each of their points, exactly as @def-open-set did with the Euclidean
distance. The proposition says that these sets form a topology in the sense of @def-topological-space, that balls are
open in it, and that it always separates points, so every metric space is a Hausdorff space (@def-hausdorff).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-metric-topology}
#### The metric topology

Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space, and call $U \subseteq X$ **open** if for every $p \in U$ some ball $B_\varepsilon(p)$ lies in
$U$. Then:

1. these sets form a topology on $X$, the **metric topology**;
2. every open ball $B_\varepsilon(p)$ is open;
3. $X$ with the metric topology is Hausdorff.

For $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $d_2$ the metric topology is the topology of @def-open-set.
:::
::::

*Proof.* (1) $\emptyset$ has no points to check, and every ball lies in $X$. If $p$ lies in a union of open sets, it lies in one
of them, $U$, and a ball about $p$ inside $U$ lies in the union. If $p \in U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_m$ with balls
$B_{\varepsilon_i}(p) \subseteq U_i$, the ball of radius $\min_i \varepsilon_i$ lies in every $U_i$.

(2) For $x \in B_\varepsilon(p)$ put $\delta = \varepsilon - d(x, p) > 0$. If $d(y, x) < \delta$ then $d(y, p) \leq d(y, x) +
d(x, p) < \varepsilon$, so $B_\delta(x) \subseteq B_\varepsilon(p)$.

(3) For $p \neq q$ let $r = d(p, q)/2 > 0$. A point $x$ in $B_r(p) \cap B_r(q)$ would give $d(p, q) \leq d(p, x) + d(x, q) <
2r = d(p, q)$, so the two balls are disjoint, and they are open by (2).

For $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $d_2$ the definition of an open set is word for word that of @def-open-set.

The proposition is the construction of @lee2013introduction [Example A.5] and @keskivakkuri2022mathematical
[Sec. 4.1.1, p. 101], and the Hausdorff property is the argument of @exm-hausdorff-rn with $|p - q|$ replaced by
$d(p, q)$. From now on a metric space is a topological space with this topology, and so a subset of it is open,
closed, compact or connected in the sense of the earlier sections.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the line, the balls are open intervals and the open sets are the usual ones. This is the case the proposition
generalises, and it fixes the meaning of "open" for every later subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-line}
#### The line

For $d(x, y) = |x - y|$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $B_\varepsilon(p) = (p - \varepsilon, p + \varepsilon)$, so $U$ is open when every
point of $U$ has an open interval about it inside $U$. This is @def-open-set for $n = 1$: $(0, 1)$ is open, $[0, 1]$
is closed and $[0, 1)$ is neither (@exm-open-intervals).
:::

The discrete metric gives the discrete topology, because a small enough ball is a single point. It is the metric
counterpart of the topology in which every subset is open.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-discrete}
#### The discrete metric gives the discrete topology

For the discrete metric of @exm-metric-discrete, $B_{1/2}(p) = \{p\}$, so every singleton is open, and every subset is a
union of singletons. The metric topology is the discrete topology of @exm-topology-discrete.
:::

A finite metric space behaves in the same way, whatever its table. The smallest distance between distinct points is a
radius whose balls are single points.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-finite}
#### Finite metric spaces are discrete

Let $X$ be finite and $\delta$ the smallest of the distances $d(p, q)$, $p \neq q$. Then $B_\delta(p) = \{p\}$ for every
$p$, and the metric topology is discrete. Of the $29$ topologies on three points (@prp-finite-topologies) only the
discrete one comes from a metric.
:::

Different metrics can give the same topology. On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the three metrics of @exm-metric-taxicab-max do,
because each of their balls contains a ball of the others with a smaller radius, as @fig-metric-balls shows for the
unit balls.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-equivalent}
#### Three metrics, one topology

The chain $d_\infty \leq d_2 \leq d_1 \leq n\,d_\infty$ gives
$B^{d_1}_\varepsilon(p) \subseteq B^{d_2}_\varepsilon(p) \subseteq B^{d_\infty}_\varepsilon(p) \subseteq
B^{d_1}_{n\varepsilon}(p)$. So a set that contains a ball of one metric about each of its points contains a ball of
each other metric about it, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ have the same open sets: those of @def-open-set.
:::

Rescaling a metric, or capping it, does not change the topology either. Only small balls enter the definition of
an open set, and these are the same up to their radii.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-scaled}
#### Rescaled and capped metrics

For $c > 0$ the metric $c\,d$ has $B^{cd}_\varepsilon(p) = B^d_{\varepsilon/c}(p)$, and the capped metric
$\min(d, 1)$ of @exr-metric-capped has the same balls of radius at most $1$. Both give the topology of $d$. The second
shows that every metric topology comes from a metric with all distances at most $1$.
:::

The arc metric of the circle gives the subspace topology inherited from the plane. Each arc-ball is a chord-ball, with
a radius computed from the relation between arc and chord.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-circle}
#### The two metrics of the circle

By @exm-metric-circle-arc the chord is $2\sin(\theta/2)$ when the arc is $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, and $2\sin(\theta/2)$
increases with $\theta$. So for $\varepsilon \leq \pi$ the arc-ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about a point is the set of
points at chord distance less than $2\sin(\varepsilon/2)$, a ball of the plane cut down to $S^1$. Both metrics give the
subspace topology of $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ (@exm-subspace-circle).
:::

The same holds on the sphere, and there it has a reading from astronomy. An angle-ball about a direction is the cone of
directions within that angle, such as the field of view of a telescope pointed at a star.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-sphere}
#### Fields of view

For $u \in S^2$ and $0 < \varepsilon \leq \pi$, the directions within angle $\varepsilon$ of $u$ are those with
$|v - u| < 2\sin(\varepsilon/2)$, by @exm-metric-sphere-angle. For the north pole $u = (0, 0, 1)$ they are the points with
$v_3 > \cos\varepsilon$, an open polar cap. A telescope with a field of view of half-angle $0.5°$ sees the cap of
directions within $0.5°$ of its axis, an open set of $S^2$ in the subspace topology (@exm-subspace-sphere).
:::

The Hamming metric on spin configurations is a finite metric, so its topology is discrete. Its balls of half-integer
radius still carry information: they collect the configurations reached by a given number of flips.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-hamming}
#### Balls of spin configurations

On $\{0, 1\}^N$ with the Hamming metric of @exm-metric-hamming, the smallest distance is $1$, so the topology is
discrete (@exm-metric-topology-finite). The ball of radius $k + \tfrac12$ about $s$ holds the $\sum_{j \leq k}\binom{N}{j}$
configurations at most $k$ flips from $s$; for $N = 4$ and $k = 1$ these are $5$ configurations.
:::

In $\ell_\infty(S)$ a ball is a band around a graph, and a set of functions is open if it contains a band around each
of its members. For the motions of an oscillator, a ball is a tolerance on the trajectory over the whole interval
watched.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-bands}
#### Bands around a graph

In $\ell_\infty([0, 2\pi])$ with $d_\infty$ the ball $B_\varepsilon(f)$ is the set of bounded $g$ with $|g(t) - f(t)| <
\varepsilon'$ for all $t$ and some $\varepsilon' < \varepsilon$: the graphs inside a band of half-width $\varepsilon$ about the
graph of $f$, staying a positive gap away from its edges. The trajectories $A\cos t$ in the ball of radius $0.1$ about
$\cos t$ are those with $|A - 1| < 0.1$ (@exm-metric-bounded-functions).
:::

Not every topology comes from a metric, and the Hausdorff property of the proposition is the first obstruction. A
topology that cannot separate two points has no metric behind it.

::: {#exm-metric-topology-not-metric}
#### Topologies without a metric

The indiscrete topology on a set with at least two points and the Sierpiński space (@exm-topology-sierpinski) are not
Hausdorff (@exm-hausdorff-discrete-indiscrete, @exm-hausdorff-finite), so by the proposition no metric gives them. The
cofinite topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is not Hausdorff either (@exm-hausdorff-cofinite), so it is not a metric topology
although every point of it is closed.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise finds a ball inside a ball, the step (2) of the proof, for the max metric of the plane. The radius
is the room left between the point and the edge of the square.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-room}
#### Room inside a square

In $(\mathbb{R}^2, d_\infty)$, find the largest $\delta$ with $B_\delta((0.9, 0.5)) \subseteq B_1((0, 0))$, and compare with the
radius $\varepsilon - d(x, p)$ of the proof.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$B_1((0, 0))$ is the open square $|y_1| < 1$, $|y_2| < 1$, and $B_\delta((0.9, 0.5))$ is the square $|y_1 - 0.9| < \delta$,
$|y_2 - 0.5| < \delta$. It lies inside exactly when $0.9 + \delta \leq 1$ and $0.5 + \delta \leq 1$, so the largest $\delta$ is
$0.1$. The proof's radius is $1 - d_\infty((0.9, 0.5), (0, 0)) = 1 - 0.9 = 0.1$, the same.

## SageMath

Sage computes the proof's radius and tests the corners of the smaller square against the larger one.

```{.python .sage}
dinf = lambda x, y: max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(x, y))
x = (QQ(9) / 10, QQ(1) / 2); delta = 1 - dinf(x, (0, 0))
corners = [(x[0] + s * delta, x[1] + t * delta) for s in (-1, 1) for t in (-1, 1)]
print("delta =", delta, " corner distances from 0:", [dinf(c, (0, 0)) for c in corners])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
delta = 1/10  corner distances from 0: [4/5, 4/5, 1, 1]
```
::::
:::

The second exercise shows that closed balls are closed. The argument is the complement version of step (2), with the
triangle inequality used the other way round.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-closed-ball}
#### Closed balls are closed

Prove that $\{x : d(x, p) \leq \varepsilon\}$ is closed in every metric space, and that the sphere $\{x : d(x, p) = \varepsilon\}$
is closed too.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $d(y, p) > \varepsilon$ and $\delta = d(y, p) - \varepsilon$. If $d(z, y) < \delta$, then $d(z, p) \geq d(y, p) - d(y, z) >
\varepsilon$ by the triangle inequality, so $B_\delta(y)$ misses the closed ball. Hence the complement is open and the
closed ball is closed. The sphere is the closed ball minus the open ball $B_\varepsilon(p)$, that is, the intersection of
the closed ball with the complement of an open set, an intersection of two closed sets (@exr-topology-closed-axioms).

## SageMath

Check in $(\mathbb{R}^2, d_1)$ for the closed unit ball: Sage takes points outside it and verifies that the radius
$\delta$ of the proof keeps a grid of nearby points outside.

```{.python .sage}
d1 = lambda x, y: abs(x[0] - y[0]) + abs(x[1] - y[1])
ok = True
for y in [(QQ(3) / 4, QQ(1) / 2), (QQ(-1), QQ(1) / 10), (QQ(0), QQ(-11) / 10)]:
    delta = d1(y, (0, 0)) - 1
    near = [(y[0] + delta * i / 10, y[1] + delta * j / 10) for i in range(-9, 10) for j in range(-9, 10) if abs(i) + abs(j) < 10]
    ok = ok and all(d1(z, (0, 0)) > 1 for z in near)
    print("y =", y, " delta =", delta)
print("nearby points stay outside:", ok)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
y = (3/4, 1/2)  delta = 1/4
y = (-1, 1/10)  delta = 1/10
y = (0, -11/10)  delta = 1/10
nearby points stay outside: True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise computes all balls of the discrete metric. They come in only two sizes, and the computation also
shows that the closed ball of radius $1$ is not the closure of the open ball of radius $1$.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-discrete-balls}
#### Balls of the discrete metric

For the discrete metric on a set $X$ with at least two points, find $B_r(p)$ and $\{x : d(x, p) \leq r\}$ for every $r > 0$.
Show that the closed ball of radius $1$ is $X$, while the open ball $B_1(p) = \{p\}$ is already closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Distances are $0$ and $1$. So $B_r(p) = \{p\}$ for $r \leq 1$ and $X$ for $r > 1$, while the closed ball is $\{p\}$ for
$r < 1$ and $X$ for $r \geq 1$. In the discrete topology (@exm-metric-topology-discrete) every set is closed, so
$B_1(p) = \{p\}$ is closed and equals its closure, whereas the closed ball of radius $1$ is all of $X$. In $\mathbb{R}^n$
the two agree, so this is a feature of metric spaces in general [@cheung2024metric, Sec. 1.2].

## SageMath

Sage lists the balls of the discrete metric on four points for a few radii.

```{.python .sage}
X = [1, 2, 3, 4]; d = lambda x, y: 0 if x == y else 1
for r in [1/2, 1, 3/2]:
    print("r =", r, " open:", [x for x in X if d(x, 1) < r], " closed:", [x for x in X if d(x, 1) <= r])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
r = 1/2  open: [1]  closed: [1]
r = 1  open: [1]  closed: [1, 2, 3, 4]
r = 3/2  open: [1, 2, 3, 4]  closed: [1, 2, 3, 4]
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise proves the inclusions of balls behind @exm-metric-topology-equivalent. It derives them from the
chain of inequalities between the three metrics and concludes that the topologies agree.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-nested}
#### Nested balls of three metrics

Prove $d_\infty \leq d_2 \leq d_1 \leq n\,d_\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, deduce $B^{d_1}_\varepsilon(p) \subseteq B^{d_2}_\varepsilon(p)
\subseteq B^{d_\infty}_\varepsilon(p) \subseteq B^{d_1}_{n\varepsilon}(p)$, and conclude that the three metric topologies coincide.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $a_i = |x_i - y_i|$ and $m = \max_i a_i$. Then $m^2 \leq \sum_i a_i^2 \leq \big(\sum_i a_i\big)^2$, since the square of
a sum of non-negative numbers contains their squares; this is $d_\infty \leq d_2 \leq d_1$. And $\sum_i a_i \leq nm$. If
$d_1(x, p) < \varepsilon$ then $d_2(x, p) < \varepsilon$, and so on down the chain, which gives the first two inclusions;
$d_\infty(x, p) < \varepsilon$ gives $d_1(x, p) < n\varepsilon$. So if $U$ contains a ball of one of the metrics about each of
its points, it contains a ball of each of the others, with radius $\varepsilon$ or $\varepsilon/n$, and the three families of
open sets of @prp-metric-topology are equal.

## SageMath

Check on random points of $\mathbb{Q}^3$: Sage tests the chain of inequalities, comparing squares to stay exact.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(5)
ok = True
for _ in range(2000):
    a = [abs(QQ.random_element(50, 9)) for _ in range(3)]
    m, s2, s1 = max(a), sum(c^2 for c in a), sum(a)
    ok = ok and m^2 <= s2 <= s1^2 and s1 <= 3 * m
print("dinf <= d2 <= d1 <= 3 dinf on 2000 points:", ok)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
dinf <= d2 <= d1 <= 3 dinf on 2000 points: True
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise reads @prp-metric-topology together with @exr-hausdorff-points-closed. In a metric space every
finite set is closed, and the exercise asks for a direct proof with balls.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-finite-closed}
#### Finite sets are closed

Prove directly from balls that a finite subset $F$ of a metric space is closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $y \notin F$. If $F$ is empty its complement is $X$, which is open. Otherwise let $\delta = \min_{x \in F} d(x, y)$, a
minimum of finitely many positive numbers, so $\delta > 0$. The ball $B_\delta(y)$ contains no point of $F$. So the
complement of $F$ is open and $F$ is closed. Alternatively, every point is closed because $X$ is Hausdorff
(@exr-hausdorff-points-closed), and a finite union of closed sets is closed.

## SageMath

Check on $F = \{0, 1/2, 1\} \subset \mathbb{R}$: Sage computes the radius $\delta$ for a few points outside $F$ and confirms
that the ball misses $F$.

```{.python .sage}
F = [0, 1/2, 1]
for y in [1/4, 2/3, -1, 101/100]:
    delta = min(abs(x - y) for x in F)
    print("y =", y, " delta =", delta, " ball misses F:", all(abs(x - y) >= delta for x in F))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
y = 1/4  delta = 1/4  ball misses F: True
y = 2/3  delta = 1/6  ball misses F: True
y = -1  delta = 1  ball misses F: True
y = 101/100  delta = 1/100  ball misses F: True
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise translates continuity from open sets into distances. It shows that for maps between metric spaces
the definition @def-continuous-map is the familiar condition with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-epsilon-delta}
#### Continuity with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$

Let $f : X \to Y$ be a map of metric spaces. Prove that $f$ is continuous if and only if for every $p \in X$ and
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $d_Y(f(x), f(p)) < \varepsilon$ whenever $d_X(x, p) < \delta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $f$ is continuous. The ball $B_\varepsilon(f(p))$ is open (@prp-metric-topology), so its preimage is open and
contains $p$, hence contains some $B_\delta(p)$; this is the condition. Conversely, let $V \subseteq Y$ be open and
$p \in f^{-1}(V)$. Some $B_\varepsilon(f(p)) \subseteq V$, and the condition gives $\delta$ with $f(B_\delta(p)) \subseteq
B_\varepsilon(f(p)) \subseteq V$. So $B_\delta(p) \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$, the preimage is open, and $f$ is continuous.

## SageMath

Check on $f(x) = x^2$ at $p = 3$ with $\varepsilon = 1/10$: Sage tests the choice $\delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/7)$ on a fine
grid of the interval $(p - \delta, p + \delta)$.

```{.python .sage}
p, eps = 3, 1/10
delta = min(1, eps / 7)
grid = [p + delta * k / 1000 for k in range(-999, 1000)]
print("delta =", delta, " all |x^2 - 9| < eps:", all(abs(x^2 - 9) < eps for x in grid))
print("largest gap:", max(abs(x^2 - 9) for x in grid).n(digits=5))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
delta = 1/70  all |x^2 - 9| < eps: True
largest gap: 0.085832
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise shows that the distance to a fixed point is a continuous function. It combines the reverse
triangle inequality of @exr-metric-reverse-triangle with the criterion just proved.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-distance-continuous}
#### Distance functions are continuous

For a point $p$ of a metric space $X$, prove that $x \mapsto d(x, p)$ is continuous from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$, and deduce again
that closed balls are closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @exr-metric-reverse-triangle, $|d(x, p) - d(y, p)| \leq d(x, y)$, so $\delta = \varepsilon$ works in
@exr-metric-topology-epsilon-delta. The closed ball is the preimage of the closed set $(-\infty, \varepsilon]$ under this
continuous function, and preimages of closed sets under continuous maps are closed (@exr-continuous-closed-preimage).

## SageMath

Check on $(\mathbb{R}^2, d_\infty)$ with $p = (1, -2)$: Sage tests $|d(x, p) - d(y, p)| \leq d(x, y)$ on random pairs.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(6)
dinf = lambda x, y: max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(x, y)); p = (1, -2)
pt = lambda: (QQ.random_element(30, 7), QQ.random_element(30, 7))
print("1-Lipschitz on 2000 pairs:", all(abs(dinf(x, p) - dinf(y, p)) <= dinf(x, y) for x, y in ((pt(), pt()) for _ in range(2000))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
1-Lipschitz on 2000 pairs: True
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise proves that a compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded. It is one direction of the
Heine-Borel theorem of @exr-compact-heine-borel, now in any metric space, and the bounded part uses only a cover by
balls.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-compact-closed-bounded}
#### Compact sets are closed and bounded

Call $S \subseteq X$ **bounded** if it lies in some ball. Prove that a compact subset $K$ of a metric space is bounded and
closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $K$ is empty there is nothing to prove; otherwise fix $p \in K$. The open balls $B_k(p)$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, cover $X$
and so cover $K$; their traces on $K$ are an open cover of $K$ (@def-subspace-topology). Finitely many suffice, and as
they are nested $K \subseteq B_m(p)$ for the largest $m$ used. For closedness let $q \notin K$. The balls $B_{r(x)}(x)$
with $r(x) = d(x, q)/2$, $x \in K$, cover $K$, and finitely many, about $x_1, \dots, x_m$, suffice. Let $r = \min_i r(x_i)$.
If $y \in B_r(q)$ and $y \in B_{r(x_i)}(x_i)$, then $d(x_i, q) \leq d(x_i, y) + d(y, q) < 2r(x_i) = d(x_i, q)$, which is
impossible. So $B_r(q)$ misses $K$, the complement of $K$ is open and $K$ is closed.

## SageMath

Check on $K = \{0\} \cup \{1/k\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, which is compact (@exm-compact-sequence-set): Sage computes the
radius $r$ of the proof for $q = -1/10$ from the finitely many balls that cover $K$ and confirms that $B_r(q)$ misses $K$.

```{.python .sage}
q = -1/10
r0 = abs(0 - q) / 2                                  # the ball about 0 has radius 1/20 and contains every 1/k with 1/k < 1/20 + 1/10
centres = [0] + [1 / k for k in range(1, 7)]         # 1/k for k >= 7 lie in the ball about 0
r = min(abs(x - q) / 2 for x in centres)
K = [0] + [1 / k for k in range(1, 200)]
print("all of K covered:", all(any(abs(y - x) < abs(x - q) / 2 for x in centres) for y in K))
print("r =", r, " B_r(q) misses K:", all(abs(y - q) >= r for y in K), " K in B_2(0):", all(abs(y) < 2 for y in K))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
all of K covered: True
r = 1/20  B_r(q) misses K: True  K in B_2(0): True
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise asks for the open caps of the sphere around the pole in two descriptions, by angle and by height.
It joins the angle metric of @exm-metric-sphere-angle with the subspace topology of @def-subspace-topology.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-polar-cap}
#### Directions near the pole

Show that the directions within angle $\pi/4$ of the north pole $n = (0, 0, 1)$ are the points of $S^2$ with $v_3 > 1/\sqrt2$,
and that this set is open in $S^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $v \in S^2$, $|v - n|^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2 + (v_3 - 1)^2 = 2 - 2v_3$, so $\cos\theta(v, n) = 1 - |v - n|^2/2 = v_3$ by
@exm-metric-sphere-angle. Since $\cos$ decreases on $[0, \pi]$, $\theta < \pi/4$ exactly when $v_3 > \cos(\pi/4) = 1/\sqrt2$.
The set $\{v_3 > 1/\sqrt2\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is open as the preimage of an open interval under a coordinate function
(@exm-continuous-projections), and its trace on $S^2$ is open in the subspace topology.

## SageMath

Sage checks the identity $|v - n|^2 = 2 - 2v_3$ on the sphere and the height at angle $\pi/4$.

```{.python .sage}
th, ph = var("th ph")
v = vector([sin(th) * cos(ph), sin(th) * sin(ph), cos(th)]); n = vector([0, 0, 1])
print("|v - n|^2 - (2 - 2 v3) =", ((v - n) * (v - n) - (2 - 2 * v[2])).simplify_full())
print("height at angle pi/4:", cos(pi / 4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
|v - n|^2 - (2 - 2 v3) = 0
height at angle pi/4: 1/2*sqrt(2)
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines the Hausdorff property of @prp-metric-topology with the quotient of
@exm-quotient-collapse-interval. It shows that the line with $[-1, 1]$ collapsed to a point is Hausdorff, by giving it a
metric.

::: {#exr-metric-topology-collapse}
#### A metric on a collapsed line

With the map $c$ of @exm-quotient-collapse-interval, $c(x) = x + 1$ for $x < -1$, $0$ on $[-1, 1]$ and $x - 1$ for $x > 1$,
define $\rho([x], [y]) = |c(x) - c(y)|$ on the quotient of $\mathbb{R}$ that collapses $[-1, 1]$ to a point. Show that $\rho$
is a well defined metric, so that this quotient is Hausdorff.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$c$ is constant on $[-1, 1]$ and injective elsewhere, with $c(x) < 0$ for $x < -1$ and $c(x) > 0$ for $x > 1$. So $c(x) =
c(y)$ exactly when $[x] = [y]$, and $\rho$ is well defined on classes and vanishes only on equal classes. It is symmetric
and satisfies the triangle inequality because $|a - b|$ does on $\mathbb{R}$. By @prp-metric-topology the quotient with the
metric topology of $\rho$ is Hausdorff. By @exr-quotient-collapse-interval, $\bar c$ is a homeomorphism from the quotient
topology onto $\mathbb{R}$, and $\rho$ is the distance of $\mathbb{R}$ carried back by $\bar c$, so this metric topology is
the quotient topology.

## SageMath

Check on a grid of rational points: Sage confirms that $\rho$ vanishes exactly on pairs in the same class and satisfies the
triangle inequality.

```{.python .sage}
c = lambda x: x + 1 if x < -1 else (0 if x <= 1 else x - 1)
same = lambda x, y: x == y or (-1 <= x <= 1 and -1 <= y <= 1)
pts = [QQ(k) / 4 for k in range(-12, 13)]
print("rho = 0 iff same class:", all((c(x) == c(y)) == same(x, y) for x in pts for y in pts))
print("triangle inequality:", all(abs(c(x) - c(z)) <= abs(c(x) - c(y)) + abs(c(y) - c(z)) for x in pts for y in pts for z in pts))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rho = 0 iff same class: True
triangle inequality: True
```
::::
:::
::::

### Convergent sequences

A sequence approaches a point when its distance to the point becomes and stays as small as one likes. The definition
says this with one number $\varepsilon$ for "as small as one likes" and one index $N$ for "from some term on", and it is
the form of convergence that every later estimate in the analysis chapters checks.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-metric-convergence}
#### Convergent sequence

A **sequence** in a set $X$ is a map $\mathbb{N} \to X$, $k \mapsto x_k$, written $(x_k)$. In a metric space $(X, d)$ it
**converges** to $p \in X$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for all
$k \geq N$. Then $p$ is a **limit** of $(x_k)$, and one writes $x_k \to p$ or $\lim_{k \to \infty} x_k = p$. A sequence
that converges to no point is **divergent**.
:::
::::
