covering argument of the proof, applied to a sequence that need not be Cauchy.

::: {#exr-compact-complete-subsequence}
#### Convergent subsequences in compact spaces

Prove that every sequence $(x_k)$ in a compact metric space $X$ has a convergent subsequence.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Call $p$ a cluster point if every ball about $p$ contains $x_k$ for infinitely many $k$. If there were none, each $p$ would
have a ball $U_p$ containing $x_k$ for only finitely many $k$; finitely many $U_p$ cover $X$, so only finitely many indices
would remain, which is impossible. So a cluster point $p$ exists. Choose $k_1$ with $x_{k_1} \in B_1(p)$, then $k_2 > k_1$ with
$x_{k_2} \in B_{1/2}(p)$, and so on, which is possible because each ball contains infinitely many terms. Then $d(x_{k_m}, p) < 1/m$
and $x_{k_m} \to p$.

## SageMath

Check on $x_k = \cos k$ in $[-1, 1]$: Sage picks indices $k_m$ with $|\cos k_m - 1| < 1/m$, a subsequence converging to $1$.

```{.python .sage}
ks = []; k = 0
for m in range(1, 7):
    k = next(j for j in range(k + 1, 10^6) if abs(cos(RDF(j)) - 1) < 1 / m)
    ks.append(k)
print("indices:", ks, " values:", [N(cos(RDF(j)), digits=6) for j in ks])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
indices: [1, 6, 7, 12, 13, 19]  values: [0.540302, 0.960170, 0.753902, 0.843854, 0.907447, 0.988705]
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise proves that an absolutely convergent series of reals converges. It is the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ in
the form used for series.

::: {#exr-compact-complete-absolute-series}
#### Absolute convergence

Let $\sum_m |a_m|$ have bounded partial sums. Prove that $s_k = \sum_{m \leq k} a_m$ converges, and apply it to $a_m = (-1)^m/m^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The partial sums $t_k = \sum_{m \leq k}|a_m|$ increase and are bounded, so they converge (@exr-compact-complete-monotone) and are
Cauchy. For $j > k$, $|s_j - s_k| = |\sum_{m = k + 1}^{j} a_m| \leq t_j - t_k$, so $(s_k)$ is Cauchy, and it converges because $\mathbb{R}$
is complete. For $a_m = (-1)^m/m^2$ the absolute partial sums are below $2$ (@exr-metric-cauchy-find-n), and the sum is
$-\pi^2/12$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the partial sums for large $k$ and compares with $-\pi^2/12$.

```{.python .sage}
for k in [10, 100, 1000]:
    s = sum(QQ((-1)^m) / m^2 for m in range(1, k + 1))
    print("k =", k, " s_k + pi^2/12 =", (RealField(100)(s) + RealField(100)(pi)^2 / 12).n(digits=4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = 10  s_k + pi^2/12 = 0.004505
k = 100  s_k + pi^2/12 = 0.00004950
k = 1000  s_k + pi^2/12 = 4.995e-7
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise computes the total time of the bouncing ball of @exm-metric-convergence-bouncing. The bounce times form a
geometric series, its partial sums are Cauchy, and completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ gives the moment the ball comes to rest.

::: {#exr-compact-complete-bouncing-time}
#### When the bouncing stops

A ball dropped from height $h_0$ hits the floor after $t_0 = \sqrt{2h_0/g}$, and each bounce with coefficient $e$ lasts $2e^m t_0$
for the $m$-th rebound. Show that the total time $T = t_0(1 + 2\sum_{m \geq 1} e^m)$ is finite and equals $t_0(1 + e)/(1 - e)$, and
compute it for $h_0 = 1\,\mathrm{m}$, $e = 0.8$, $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The partial sums of $\sum_m e^m$ have steps $e^{m}$, so they are Cauchy (@exr-metric-cauchy-geometric-steps) and converge in $\mathbb{R}$,
to $e/(1 - e)$ by the geometric sum formula and $e^m \to 0$. So $T = t_0(1 + 2e/(1 - e)) = t_0(1 + e)/(1 - e)$. With the data,
$t_0 = \sqrt{2/9.81} \approx 0.452\,\mathrm{s}$ and $T = 9t_0 \approx 4.06\,\mathrm{s}$: infinitely many bounces in a finite time.

## SageMath

Sage computes $t_0$, the closed form and a long partial sum.

```{.python .sage}
t0 = sqrt(2 / 9.81); e = 0.8
print("t0 =", N(t0, digits=4), " T =", N(t0 * (1 + e) / (1 - e), digits=4))
print("partial sum (200 bounces):", N(t0 * (1 + 2 * sum(e^m for m in range(1, 201))), digits=4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
t0 = 0.4515  T = 4.064
partial sum (200 bounces): 4.064
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines the proposition with the product of @exr-complete-product and the quotient metric of
@exr-metric-circle-quotient. It shows that the torus of two angles is complete, and finds the limit of a sequence of its
points.

::: {#exr-compact-complete-torus}
#### The torus of two angles

Give $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ the max of the two arc metrics. Prove that it is complete, and find the
limit of $([2\pi - 1/k], [\pi + 2^{-k}])$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With the arc metric, $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ is the circle $S^1$ with its arc metric (@exm-metric-circle-arc), complete by
@exm-compact-complete-spheres, so the product is complete by @exr-complete-product. The first coordinates are at arc
distance $1/k$ from $[0]$ and the second at $2^{-k}$ from $[\pi]$ (@exr-metric-convergence-circle-angles), so the max distance to
$([0], [\pi])$ is $\max(1/k, 2^{-k}) = 1/k \to 0$, and the limit is $([0], [\pi])$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the product distance of the points to $([0], [\pi])$ for a few $k$.

```{.python .sage}
def arc(a, b):
    t = (a - b) / (2 * pi)
    return min(abs(a - b - 2 * pi * m) for m in range(floor(t) - 1, floor(t) + 3))
for k in [1, 10, 100]:
    print("k =", k, " distance:", max(arc(2 * pi - 1 / k, 0), arc(pi + 2^(-k), pi)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = 1  distance: 1
k = 10  distance: 1/10
k = 100  distance: 1/100
```
::::
:::
::::

### The contraction mapping theorem

Many equations of physics can be written as $x = f(x)$, a point that a map leaves where it is. If $f$ brings every two
points closer by a fixed factor, iterating it from any start produces a Cauchy sequence, and completeness supplies the
limit. The theorem says that this limit is the only solution, and it bounds the error after each step.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-contraction-mapping}
#### Contraction mapping theorem

Let $(X, d)$ be a non-empty complete metric space and $f : X \to X$ a **contraction**: there is $c \in [0, 1)$ with
$d(f(x), f(y)) \leq c\,d(x, y)$ for all $x, y \in X$. Then $f$ has exactly one **fixed point**, a point $p$ with $f(p) = p$. For
every $x_0 \in X$ the iterates $x_{k + 1} = f(x_k)$ converge to $p$, with
$$
d(x_k, p) \leq \frac{c^k}{1 - c}\, d(x_1, x_0).
$$
:::
::::

*Proof.* By induction, $d(x_{k + 1}, x_k) = d(f(x_k), f(x_{k - 1})) \leq c\,d(x_k, x_{k - 1}) \leq \dots \leq c^k d(x_1, x_0)$. By
@exr-metric-cauchy-geometric-steps with $C = d(x_1, x_0)$ and $r = c$, $d(x_j, x_k) \leq c^k d(x_1, x_0)/(1 - c)$ for $j > k$, and
$(x_k)$ is Cauchy. As $X$ is complete, $x_k \to p$ for some $p \in X$. A contraction is continuous, with $\delta = \varepsilon$ in
@exr-metric-topology-epsilon-delta when $c > 0$ and trivially when $c = 0$, so $x_{k + 1} = f(x_k) \to f(p)$
(@exr-metric-convergence-continuous); as $x_{k + 1} \to p$ too, $f(p) = p$ by @exr-metric-convergence-unique. If $q$ is another fixed
point, $d(p, q) = d(f(p), f(q)) \leq c\,d(p, q)$, so $(1 - c)d(p, q) \leq 0$ and $p = q$. Finally, $d(x_k, p) \leq d(x_k, x_j) + d(x_j, p)
\leq c^k d(x_1, x_0)/(1 - c) + d(x_j, p)$ for every $j > k$, and $d(x_j, p)$ is as small as one likes for large $j$; so the
bound holds.

This is Banach's fixed point theorem, in the form of @cheung2024metric [Thm. 4.2.6], with the error bound of their
Example 4.2.8. Two hypotheses carry the proof: completeness, which provides the limit, and the factor $c < 1$, which makes
the steps shrink geometrically. The examples show that neither can be dropped, and that a self-map is required too.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest contraction halves every distance, and its iterates are explicit. Shifting it shows that the fixed point
is wherever the map is anchored, and that a subspace must be mapped into itself [@cheung2024metric, Examples 4.2.2 and
4.2.5].

::: {#exm-contraction-halving}
#### Halving

$f(x) = x/2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $|f(x) - f(y)| = |x - y|/2$, fixed point $0$ and iterates $x_k = x_0/2^k$. The map $g(x) = 1 + x/2$ is
also a contraction with $c = 1/2$; on the complete set $[2, \infty)$ it is a self-map, since $x \geq 2$ gives $g(x) \geq 2$, and its
fixed point is $2$. On $(2, \infty)$ it is a self-map without a fixed point, because $(2, \infty)$ is not complete.
:::

An affine map of the line with slope of absolute value less than one is a contraction. Its fixed point and its iterates
can be written down, which shows the error bound of the theorem at work.

::: {#exm-contraction-affine}
#### Affine maps

$f(x) = ax + b$ with $|a| < 1$ has $c = |a|$ and fixed point $p = b/(1 - a)$. The iterates satisfy $x_k - p = a^k(x_0 - p)$, so the
error shrinks by exactly $|a|$ at each step. For $a = 1/3$, $b = 2$ and $x_0 = 0$, $p = 3$ and $x_k = 3 - 3^{1 - k}$.
:::

The equation $\cos x = x$ has no solution in closed form, and the iteration finds it. @fig-cobweb-cos draws the iterates as
a staircase between the graph of $\cos$ and the diagonal, spiralling into the fixed point.

::: {#exm-contraction-cos}
#### Iterating the cosine

On $[0, 1]$, $\cos$ takes values in $[\cos 1, 1] \subset [0, 1]$. For $x, y \in [0, 1]$, $\cos x - \cos y = -2\sin\frac{x + y}{2}\sin\frac{x -
y}{2}$, and with $|\sin u| \leq |u|$ and $0 \leq \frac{x + y}{2} \leq 1$ this gives $|\cos x - \cos y| \leq \sin 1 \cdot |x - y|$. So $\cos$ is a
contraction of the complete space $[0, 1]$ with $c = \sin 1 \approx 0.841$, and its fixed point is $p \approx 0.739085$.

![The iterates $x_{k + 1} = \cos x_k$ from $x_0 = 0$, drawn as steps between the graph of $\cos$ and the diagonal $y = x$,
converging to the fixed point $p \approx 0.739$.](figures/cobweb_cos.svg){#fig-cobweb-cos width=60%}
:::

Newton's iteration for $\sqrt2$ is a contraction of $[1, 2]$. The theorem applies in $\mathbb{R}$, but not in the rationals,
where the same map has no fixed point; this is completeness at work.

::: {#exm-contraction-newton-sqrt2}
#### Newton's iteration as a contraction

$f(x) = (x + 2/x)/2$ maps $[1, 2]$ into itself: $f(x) \geq \sqrt2$ because $x^2 + 2 \geq 2\sqrt2 x$, and $f(x) \leq 3/2$ because $x^2 - 3x + 2 =
(x - 1)(x - 2) \leq 0$. Further $f(x) - f(y) = (x - y)(1/2 - 1/(xy))$, and $xy \in [1, 4]$ gives $|1/2 - 1/(xy)| \leq 1/2$, so $c = 1/2$. The
fixed point is $\sqrt2$. On $\mathbb{Q} \cap [1, 2]$, $f$ is the same contraction and has no fixed point (@exm-complete-rationals).
:::

Contractions of the plane are found in the same way, with the max metric making the estimate one line per coordinate.
The example solves two linear equations by iteration.

::: {#exm-contraction-plane}
#### A contraction of the plane

$f(x, y) = (y/2, x/3 + 1)$ on $(\mathbb{R}^2, d_\infty)$ satisfies $d_\infty(f(x, y), f(x', y')) = \max(|y - y'|/2, |x - x'|/3) \leq
d_\infty((x, y), (x', y'))/2$. The space is complete (@prp-compact-metric-complete), so the fixed point is unique: $x = y/2$ and
$y = x/3 + 1$ give $y = 6/5$, $x = 3/5$.
:::

Kepler's equation gives the position of a planet on its ellipse at a given time, and it is the classic fixed-point
problem of celestial mechanics. The eccentricity is the contraction constant, so the iteration is fast for nearly
circular orbits.

::: {#exm-contraction-kepler}
#### Kepler's equation

For an orbit of eccentricity $e \in [0, 1)$, the eccentric anomaly $E$ at mean anomaly $M$ solves $E = M + e\sin E$. With
$\sin u - \sin v = 2\cos\frac{u + v}{2}\sin\frac{u - v}{2}$ and $|\sin w| \leq |w|$, $|\sin u - \sin v| \leq |u - v|$, so $E \mapsto M + e\sin E$ is a
contraction of $\mathbb{R}$ with $c = e$. There is exactly one $E$ for each $M$. For the Earth, $e \approx 0.0167$, and each iteration gains
almost two digits.
:::

The Picard iteration turns a differential equation into a fixed-point problem for functions. The example takes the
simplest equation, $y' = y$ with $y(0) = 1$, written as $y(t) = 1 + \int_0^t y(s)\,ds$, and checks the solution by
substitution.

::: {#exm-contraction-picard}
#### The Picard iteration for $y' = y$

On polynomials $y$ on $[0, 1/2]$ let $(Ty)(t) = 1 + \int_0^t y(s)\,ds$. Then $|(Ty)(t) - (Tz)(t)| \leq t\,d_\infty(y, z)$, so
$d_\infty(Ty, Tz) \leq \tfrac12 d_\infty(y, z)$. From $y_0 = 1$ the iterates are $y_k(t) = \sum_{m \leq k} t^m/m!$, the partial sums of
@exm-metric-cauchy-exponential, which converge to $e^t$ in $\ell_\infty([0, 1/2])$. Substitution gives $1 + \int_0^t e^s\,ds = 1 +
(e^t - 1) = e^t$, so $e^t$ is a fixed point, and the contraction estimate, valid for all continuous $y$, makes it the only
continuous one.
:::

An infinite ladder of resistors is a circuit equal to a part of itself. Its resistance $R$ is a fixed point of the map that
adds one rung, and the map is a contraction.

::: {#exm-contraction-ladder}
#### An infinite resistor ladder

A ladder of $1\,\Omega$ resistors, with one in series and one across at each rung, has resistance $R = 1 + R/(1 + R)$, the
series resistor followed by the parallel combination of $1\,\Omega$ and the rest of the ladder. The map $f(R) = 2 - 1/(1 + R)$ sends
$[1, 2]$ into $[3/2, 5/3]$, and $|f(R) - f(S)| = |R - S|/((1 + R)(1 + S)) \leq |R - S|/4$. Its fixed point solves $R^2 - R - 1 = 0$:
$R = (1 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618\,\Omega$.
:::

Shrinking every distance is not enough; the shrinking must be by a fixed factor. A map can bring every two points closer
and still have no fixed point [@cheung2024metric, Examples 4.2.3 and 4.2.5(iii)].

::: {#exm-contraction-distance-decreasing}
#### Distance-decreasing but not a contraction

$f(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + 1}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $|f(x) - f(y)| = |x - y|\,|x + y|/(f(x) + f(y)) < |x - y|$ for $x \neq y$, since $|x| < f(x)$. But the
ratio tends to $1$ as $x, y \to \infty$, and $f(x) > |x| \geq x$, so $f$ has no fixed point. The translation $x \mapsto x + 1$, with ratio exactly
$1$, has none either.
:::

The last example removes the other hypotheses one at a time. A contraction of an incomplete space, or a map that leaves
the space, can miss its fixed point [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 4.2, Part A, Problems 5-6].

::: {#exm-contraction-hypotheses}
#### Completeness and self-maps

$x \mapsto x/2$ is a contraction of $(0, 1]$, which is not complete, and has no fixed point there. On $[1, \infty)$ the same formula
is not a self-map, since $1 \mapsto 1/2$, and again there is no fixed point. And $x \mapsto 1/(1 + x)$ maps $[0, 1]$ into itself with
ratio $1/((1 + x)(1 + y))$, which is not bounded below $1$ near $0$; it is not a contraction of $[0, 1]$, although it has the fixed
point $(\sqrt5 - 1)/2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise iterates an affine contraction by hand. It compares the actual error with the bound of the theorem,
which is sharp up to the factor $1/(1 - c)$.

::: {#exr-contraction-affine}
#### Iterating $x \mapsto x/3 + 2$

From $x_0 = 0$, compute $x_1, \dots, x_4$ for $f(x) = x/3 + 2$, the fixed point, and the error bound of the theorem for $k = 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 8/3$, $x_3 = 26/9$, $x_4 = 80/27$, and $p = 3$ by @exm-contraction-affine. The actual error is $3 - 80/27 = 1/27$. The
bound is $c^4 d(x_1, x_0)/(1 - c) = (1/81) \cdot 2/(2/3) = 1/27$; here it is attained.

## SageMath

Sage iterates exactly and prints the errors and the bounds.

```{.python .sage}
f = lambda x: x / 3 + 2; c = QQ(1) / 3; x = QQ(0); x1 = f(x)
for k in range(5):
    print("k =", k, " x_k =", x, " error =", 3 - x, " bound =", c^k * abs(x1) / (1 - c))
    x = f(x)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = 0  x_k = 0  error = 3  bound = 3
k = 1  x_k = 2  error = 1  bound = 1
k = 2  x_k = 8/3  error = 1/3  bound = 1/3
k = 3  x_k = 26/9  error = 1/9  bound = 1/9
k = 4  x_k = 80/27  error = 1/27  bound = 1/27
```
::::
:::

The second exercise counts the iterations of the cosine needed for six correct digits, from the bound and in fact. The
bound is pessimistic because $\sin 1$ overestimates the local contraction near the fixed point.

::: {#exr-contraction-cos-steps}
#### How many iterations for the cosine?

For $x_{k + 1} = \cos x_k$ with $x_0 = 0$, find the least $k$ for which the bound of the theorem with $c = \sin 1$ guarantees
$|x_k - p| < 10^{-6}$, and the least $k$ for which it actually holds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$d(x_1, x_0) = 1$, so the bound is $(\sin 1)^k/(1 - \sin 1) < 10^{-6}$, that is $k > \ln\big(10^{6}/(1 - \sin 1)\big)/\ln(1/\sin 1) \approx 90.7$, so
$k = 91$. In fact the error near $p$ shrinks by about $\sin p \approx 0.674$ per step, since by @exm-contraction-cos the ratio
$|\cos x - \cos y|/|x - y|$ is close to $\sin\frac{x + y}{2}$ for nearby $x, y$, and $33$ iterations suffice.

## SageMath

Sage finds the fixed point numerically and both iteration counts.

```{.python .sage}
R = RealField(60); p = find_root(lambda x: cos(x) - x, 0, 1); c = sin(R(1))
kb = next(k for k in range(1, 500) if c^k / (1 - c) < 1e-6)
x = R(0); k = 0
while abs(x - p) >= 1e-6:
    x = cos(x); k += 1
print("p =", N(p, digits=8), " bound needs k =", kb, " actually k =", k)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
p = 0.73908513  bound needs k = 91  actually k = 33
```
::::
:::

The third exercise solves Kepler's equation for a strongly eccentric orbit. The contraction constant is the eccentricity,
so the iteration still converges, though more slowly than for the Earth.

::: {#exr-contraction-kepler}
#### Solving Kepler's equation

For $e = 1/2$ and $M = 1$, iterate $E_{k + 1} = 1 + \tfrac12\sin E_k$ from $E_0 = M$, find $E$ to eight digits, and give the number of
steps the bound of the theorem requires for $10^{-8}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @exm-contraction-kepler the map is a contraction of $\mathbb{R}$ with $c = 1/2$. Here $d(E_1, E_0) = \tfrac12\sin 1 \approx 0.421$, and the
bound is $2^{-k} \cdot 0.421/(1/2) = 0.841 \cdot 2^{-k} < 10^{-8}$ for $k \geq 27$. The iterates converge to $E \approx 1.49870113$.

## SageMath

Sage iterates $30$ times and checks Kepler's equation at the result.

```{.python .sage}
R = RealField(60); M = R(1); E = M
for k in range(30):
    E = M + sin(E) / 2
kb = next(k for k in range(1, 100) if 2^(-k) * sin(R(1)) < 1e-8)
print("E =", N(E, digits=9), " |residual| < 1e-15:", abs(E - M - sin(E) / 2) < 1e-15, " bound needs k =", kb)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
E = 1.49870113  |residual| < 1e-15: True  bound needs k = 27
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise computes the resistance of the ladder of @exm-contraction-ladder by iteration. Each iterate is the
resistance of a finite ladder, so the sequence has a physical meaning term by term.

::: {#exr-contraction-ladder}
#### Finite ladders

Show that the iterates $R_{k + 1} = 1 + R_k/(1 + R_k)$ from $R_1 = 1$ are ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers, and estimate
$|R_6 - (1 + \sqrt5)/2|$ with the bound of the theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$R_1 = 1$ is one resistor; $R_{k + 1}$ adds one rung. Write $R_k = F_{2k}/F_{2k - 1}$ with the Fibonacci numbers $F_1 = F_2 = 1$. Then
$R_{k + 1} = (1 + 2R_k)/(1 + R_k) = (F_{2k - 1} + 2F_{2k})/(F_{2k - 1} + F_{2k}) = (F_{2k + 1} + F_{2k})/F_{2k + 1} = F_{2k + 2}/F_{2k + 1}$, and $R_1 =
F_2/F_1$. So $R_k = 1, 3/2, 8/5, 21/13, 55/34, 144/89, \dots$ With $c = 1/4$, $x_0 = R_1 = 1$ and $x_1 = R_2 = 3/2$, the bound for
$R_6 = x_5$ is $4^{-5}(1/2)/(3/4) = 1/1536 \approx 6.5 \cdot 10^{-4}$; the true error is about $1.2 \cdot 10^{-4}$.

## SageMath

Sage iterates exactly and compares with the Fibonacci ratios and the golden ratio.

```{.python .sage}
R = QQ(1); rs = [R]
for _ in range(5):
    R = 1 + R / (1 + R); rs.append(R)
print("iterates:", rs)
print("Fibonacci ratios:", [fibonacci(2 * k) / fibonacci(2 * k - 1) for k in range(1, 7)])
print("error of R_6:", N(abs(rs[-1] - golden_ratio), digits=3), " bound:", N(QQ(1) / 4^5 * (QQ(1) / 2) / (QQ(3) / 4), digits=3))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
iterates: [1, 3/2, 8/5, 21/13, 55/34, 144/89]
Fibonacci ratios: [1, 3/2, 8/5, 21/13, 55/34, 144/89]
error of R_6: 0.000122  bound: 0.000651
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise proves that $\cos(\cos x)$ is a contraction of the whole line. The estimate of @exm-contraction-cos is
applied twice, once on $[-1, 1]$ [@cheung2024metric, Exercise 4.2, Part A, Problem 3].

::: {#exr-contraction-cos-cos}
#### $\cos\circ\cos$ on the line

Prove $|\cos a - \cos b| \leq \sin 1 \cdot |a - b|$ for $a, b \in [-1, 1]$, and deduce that $x \mapsto \cos(\cos x)$ is a contraction of $\mathbb{R}$ with
$c = \sin 1$. What is its fixed point?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\cos a - \cos b = -2\sin\frac{a + b}{2}\sin\frac{a - b}{2}$. For $a, b \in [-1, 1]$, $|\frac{a + b}{2}| \leq 1$, so $|\sin\frac{a + b}{2}| \leq \sin 1$,
as $\sin$ increases on $[0, 1]$ and is odd; and $|\sin\frac{a - b}{2}| \leq |a - b|/2$. Hence $|\cos a - \cos b| \leq \sin 1\,|a - b|$. With
$a = \cos x$, $b = \cos y$ and $|\cos x - \cos y| \leq |x - y|$ (the same identity with $|\sin| \leq 1$),
$|\cos\cos x - \cos\cos y| \leq \sin 1\,|x - y|$. $\mathbb{R}$ is complete, so there is one fixed point; the fixed point $p$ of $\cos$ is
one, since $\cos\cos p = \cos p = p$. So it is $p \approx 0.739085$.

## SageMath

Check on random pairs of reals: Sage tests the contraction estimate and iterates $\cos\circ\cos$ from $x_0 = 5$.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(8)
pairs = [(RDF.random_element(-20, 20), RDF.random_element(-20, 20)) for _ in range(5000)]
print("estimate holds:", all(abs(cos(cos(x)) - cos(cos(y))) <= sin(1.0) * abs(x - y) + 1e-15 for x, y in pairs))
x = RDF(5)
for _ in range(60):
    x = cos(cos(x))
print("limit:", N(x, digits=7))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
estimate holds: True
limit: 0.7390851
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise proves that a contraction is continuous, a step of the proof, and shows that it is even more:
uniformly continuous, with one $\delta$ for all points.

::: {#exr-contraction-continuous}
#### Contractions are continuous

Prove that a contraction $f : X \to X$ is continuous, and that $\delta = \varepsilon$ works in @exr-metric-topology-epsilon-delta at every point
simultaneously.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $d(x, p) < \varepsilon$ then $d(f(x), f(p)) \leq c\,d(x, p) \leq d(x, p) < \varepsilon$, whatever $p$. So the condition of
@exr-metric-topology-epsilon-delta holds with $\delta = \varepsilon$ at every point, and $f$ is continuous. In terms of balls,
$f(B_\varepsilon(p)) \subseteq B_\varepsilon(f(p))$ for every $p$ and every $\varepsilon$.

## SageMath

Check on $\cos$ on $[0, 1]$: Sage tests that points within $\varepsilon = 10^{-2}$ have images within $\varepsilon$, on a grid of pairs.

```{.python .sage}
eps = 1e-2
grid = [i / 400 for i in range(401)]
print("delta = eps works:", all(abs(cos(RDF(x)) - cos(RDF(y))) < eps for x in grid for y in grid if abs(x - y) < eps))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
delta = eps works: True
```
::::
:::


The seventh exercise extends the theorem to maps that contract only after two steps. The cosine on the whole line is such
a map, by @exr-contraction-cos-cos, although it is not a contraction itself.

::: {#exr-contraction-power}
#### A power that contracts

Let $X$ be complete and $f : X \to X$ such that $f \circ f$ is a contraction. Prove that $f$ has exactly one fixed point. Show that $\cos$
is not a contraction of $\mathbb{R}$, and deduce that $\cos x = x$ has exactly one real solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the theorem $g = f \circ f$ has a unique fixed point $p$. Then $g(f(p)) = f(g(p)) = f(p)$, so $f(p)$ is a fixed point of $g$, and
$f(p) = p$. Every fixed point of $f$ is a fixed point of $g$, so it is $p$. The cosine is not a contraction of $\mathbb{R}$: for
$x = \pi/2 - h$, $y = \pi/2 + h$, $|\cos x - \cos y| = 2\sin h$, and $2\sin h/(2h) \to 1$ as $h \to 0$, so no $c < 1$ works. But
$\cos\circ\cos$ is a contraction of $\mathbb{R}$ (@exr-contraction-cos-cos), so $\cos$ has exactly one fixed point on the line,
the $p \approx 0.739$ of @exm-contraction-cos.

## SageMath

Sage computes the ratio $\sin h/h$ for small $h$, and solves $\cos x = x$ on a wide interval by locating sign changes of
$\cos x - x$ on a grid.

```{.python .sage}
print("ratios near pi/2:", [N(sin(h) / h, digits=6) for h in (0.1, 0.01, 0.001)])
g = lambda x: cos(RDF(x)) - RDF(x)
grid = [RDF(i) / 100 for i in range(-2000, 2001)]
print("sign changes of cos x - x on [-20, 20]:", sum(1 for a, b in zip(grid, grid[1:]) if g(a) * g(b) < 0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
ratios near pi/2: [0.998334, 0.999983, 1.00000]
sign changes of cos x - x on [-20, 20]: 1
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise replaces the factor $c < 1$ by compactness. On a compact space a map that strictly decreases every
distance has a unique fixed point, found as the minimum of the continuous function $d(x, f(x))$.

::: {#exr-contraction-compact}
#### Distance-decreasing maps of compact spaces

Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $f : X \to X$ with $d(f(x), f(y)) < d(x, y)$ for $x \neq y$. Prove that $f$ has exactly one fixed
point. Show that $\sin$ on $[0, 1]$ is such a map but not a contraction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$f$ is continuous, as in @exr-contraction-continuous. The function $h(x) = d(x, f(x))$ satisfies $|h(x) - h(y)| \leq d(x, y) + d(f(x),
f(y)) \leq 2d(x, y)$ by two uses of @exr-metric-reverse-triangle, so it is continuous and attains its minimum at some $m$
(@exr-compact-image). If $f(m) \neq m$, then $h(f(m)) = d(f(m), f(f(m))) < d(m, f(m)) = h(m)$, contradicting minimality; so $f(m) = m$.
Two fixed points $p \neq q$ would give $d(p, q) = d(f(p), f(q)) < d(p, q)$. For $\sin$ on $[0, 1]$, $|\sin x - \sin y| = 2|\cos\frac{x +
y}{2}|\,|\sin\frac{x - y}{2}| < |x - y|$ for $x \neq y$, since $\cos\frac{x + y}{2} < 1$ unless $x = y = 0$ and $|\sin u| < |u|$ for $u \neq
0$. The ratio $\sin x/x$ tends to $1$ as $x \to 0$, so $\sin$ is not a contraction; its fixed point is $0$.

## SageMath

Sage iterates $\sin$ from $x_0 = 1$ and shows the slow approach to $0$, roughly like $\sqrt{3/k}$.

```{.python .sage}
x = RDF(1)
for k in range(1, 10001):
    x = sin(x)
    if k in (10, 100, 1000, 10000):
        print("k =", k, " x_k =", N(x, digits=4), " sqrt(3/k) =", N(sqrt(3 / k), digits=4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
k = 10  x_k = 0.4630  sqrt(3/k) = 0.5477
k = 100  x_k = 0.1689  sqrt(3/k) = 0.1732
k = 1000  x_k = 0.05459  sqrt(3/k) = 0.05477
k = 10000  x_k = 0.01731  sqrt(3/k) = 0.01732
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise runs the Picard iteration of @exm-contraction-picard for the decay equation $y' = -y$, $y(0) = 1$. The
iterates are the partial sums of $e^{-t}$, and the solution is checked by substitution.

::: {#exr-contraction-picard-decay}
#### The Picard iteration for decay

On $[0, 1/2]$ let $(Ty)(t) = 1 - \int_0^t y(s)\,ds$. Show that $T$ halves sup distances, compute the iterates from $y_0 = 1$, verify
by substitution that $e^{-t}$ is a fixed point, and bound $d_\infty(y_k, e^{-t})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|(Ty)(t) - (Tz)(t)| = |\int_0^t (z - y)\,ds| \leq t\,d_\infty(y, z) \leq \tfrac12 d_\infty(y, z)$. By induction $y_k(t) = \sum_{m \leq k}(-t)^m/m!$,
since $1 - \int_0^t \sum_{m \leq k}(-s)^m/m!\,ds = 1 + \sum_{m \leq k}(-t)^{m + 1}/(m + 1)!$. Substitution: $1 - \int_0^t e^{-s}\,ds = 1 - (1 -
e^{-t}) = e^{-t}$. As $y_k$ and $e^{-t}$ are continuous on $[0, 1/2]$, the contraction estimate gives $d_\infty(y_k, e^{-t}) =
d_\infty(T y_{k - 1}, T e^{-t}) \leq 2^{-k} d_\infty(y_0, e^{-t}) = 2^{-k}(1 - e^{-1/2}) \approx 0.39 \cdot 2^{-k}$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the iterates symbolically, checks the fixed point by substitution and measures the sup error on a grid.

```{.python .sage}
t, s = var("t s")
y = SR(1)
for k in range(1, 5):
    y = 1 - integrate(y.subs(t=s), s, 0, t)
print("y_4 =", y.expand())
print("T(exp(-t)) - exp(-t) =", (1 - integrate(exp(-s), s, 0, t) - exp(-t)).simplify_full())
grid = [i / 200 for i in range(101)]
print("sup error of y_4:", N(max(abs(y.subs(t=u) - exp(-u)) for u in grid), digits=3), " bound:", N(2^(-4) * (1 - exp(-1/2)), digits=3))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
y_4 = 1/24*t^4 - 1/6*t^3 + 1/2*t^2 - t + 1
T(exp(-t)) - exp(-t) = 0
sup error of y_4: 0.000244  bound: 0.0246
```
::::
:::

The last exercise solves an integral equation by contraction, combining the theorem with the sup metric of
@exm-metric-bounded-functions. The iterates stay in a family of multiples of one function, which reduces the problem to a
contraction of the line [@cheung2024metric, Example 4.2.8].

::: {#exr-contraction-integral-equation}
#### An integral equation

On $[0, 1]$ consider $f(x) = \tfrac12\int_0^1 xy f(y)\,dy + x$, and let $(Tf)(x)$ be the right side. Show that $T$ halves sup distances
between continuous functions, that $T(cx) = (1 + c/6)x$, and find the solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$|(Tf)(x) - (Tg)(x)| \leq \tfrac12\int_0^1 xy\,|f(y) - g(y)|\,dy \leq \tfrac12 d_\infty(f, g)$, since $0 \leq xy \leq 1$. For $f(y) = cy$,
$\tfrac12\int_0^1 xy \cdot cy\,dy = cx/6$, so $T(cx) = (1 + c/6)x$. The map $c \mapsto 1 + c/6$ is a contraction of the complete space
$\mathbb{R}$ with constant $1/6$, with fixed point $c = 6/5$. So $f(x) = 6x/5$ solves the equation, as substitution confirms: $\tfrac12 \cdot
\tfrac65\int_0^1 xy^2\,dy + x = x/5 + x$. A second continuous solution $g$ would give $d_\infty(f, g) \leq \tfrac12 d_\infty(f, g)$, so there is
none. From $f_0 = 0$ the iterates are $x, \tfrac76 x, \tfrac{43}{36}x, \dots$

## SageMath

Sage iterates the coefficients exactly and checks the solution by substitution.

```{.python .sage}
x, y = var("x y")
c = QQ(0); cs = []
for _ in range(5):
    c = 1 + c / 6; cs.append(c)
print("coefficients:", cs)
f = 6 * x / 5
print("T f - f =", (integrate(x * y * f.subs(x=y), y, 0, 1) / 2 + x - f).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
coefficients: [1, 7/6, 43/36, 259/216, 1555/1296]
T f - f = 0
```
::::
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-sets-topology-exercises}

For more on this topic, see @gasinski2014exercises [Def. 2.76, Prop. 2.83, Thm. 2.84] and @lee2013introduction [Thm. A.30, Prop. A.45, Lemma A.52].

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises combine the sections of this chapter: quotients, the quotient topology, compactness, the Hausdorff
property and the metrics of the last section.

The first shows that a quotient of a non-compact space can be compact, by using the compactness of a closed
interval and the continuity of the quotient map. It also asks for the Hausdorff property of the quotient circle,
which has to be checked because quotients can lose it, as @exm-hausdorff-quotient showed.

::: {#exr-circle-quotient-compact}
#### The circle as a compact quotient of a non-compact space

Show that $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ with the quotient topology is compact and Hausdorff although $\mathbb{R}$ is
not compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbb{R}$ is not compact (@exm-compact-complete-converse). The quotient map $\pi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ is
continuous (@def-quotient-topology), and its restriction to $[0, 2\pi]$ is still surjective, since every class has a
representative in $[0, 2\pi)$. A continuous image of a compact space is compact (@exr-compact-image), and $[0, 2\pi]$ is
compact (@exr-compact-closed-interval), so the quotient is compact. For the Hausdorff property, let $[\varphi] \neq
[\varphi']$ with $0 \leq \varphi < \varphi' < 2\pi$, $d = \varphi' - \varphi$, and $\varepsilon = \min(d, 2\pi - d)/2 > 0$. The sets
$U = \bigcup_k (\varphi - \varepsilon + 2\pi k, \varphi + \varepsilon + 2\pi k)$ and $V$, defined in the same way around $\varphi'$, are
open in $\mathbb{R}$ and unions of classes, so their images are open in the quotient. They are disjoint, because a common
point would put $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ within $2\varepsilon \leq \min(d, 2\pi - d)$ of each other modulo $2\pi$, while their
distance modulo $2\pi$ is exactly $\min(d, 2\pi - d)$ and the intervals are open.

## SageMath

Check on the classes of $\varphi = 1$ and $\varphi' = 5$: Sage computes $\varepsilon$ and tests on a fine grid of $[0, 2\pi)$ that no
point lies in both sets $U$ and $V$, measuring distances modulo $2\pi$.

```{.python .sage}
a, b = RDF(1), RDF(5); dd = b - a; tp = 2 * RDF(pi)
eps = min(dd, tp - dd) / 2
mod_dist = lambda x, y: min(abs(x - y - tp * k) for k in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2))
grid = [tp * i / 20000 for i in range(20000)]
both = [x for x in grid if mod_dist(x, a) < eps and mod_dist(x, b) < eps]
print("eps =", N(eps, digits=4), " grid points in both U and V:", len(both))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
eps = 1.142  grid points in both U and V: 0
```
::::
:::

The second exercise proves the criterion that turns a continuous bijection into a homeomorphism. It uses the
compactness of closed subsets (@exr-compact-closed-subset), of continuous images (@exr-compact-image) and the
closedness of compact subsets of a metric space (@exr-metric-topology-compact-closed-bounded), and applies them to the
interval with its endpoints glued.

::: {#exr-interval-quotient-homeomorphism}
#### Gluing the ends of an interval

Prove that a continuous bijection $F : K \to Y$ from a compact space onto a metric space is a homeomorphism. Deduce that the
quotient of $[0, 2\pi]$ by $0 \sim 2\pi$ is homeomorphic to $S^1$ via $[\varphi] \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

It suffices to show that $F$ sends closed sets to closed sets: then for $C$ closed in $K$, $(F^{-1})^{-1}(C) = F(C)$ is closed,
and $F^{-1}$ is continuous by @exr-continuous-closed-preimage. A closed $C \subseteq K$ is compact (@exr-compact-closed-subset), so
$F(C)$ is compact (@exr-compact-image), and a compact subset of a metric space is closed
(@exr-metric-topology-compact-closed-bounded). For the circle, $g(\varphi) = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is continuous on $[0, 2\pi]$
and takes the same value only at $0$ and $2\pi$, so it descends to a continuous bijection $\bar g$ from the quotient onto
$S^1$, continuous by @def-quotient-topology because $\bar g \circ \pi = g$ is. The quotient is compact, as the image of the
compact $[0, 2\pi]$ under $\pi$, and $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a metric space. So $\bar g$ is a homeomorphism.

## SageMath

Check on the closed set $C = [\pi/2, \pi]$ of the quotient: Sage computes its image under $\bar g$, an arc, and confirms that the
image is the set of points of $S^1$ with $u \leq 0 \leq v$, a closed set of the plane, and that $g$ identifies only $0$ and $2\pi$
on a grid.

```{.python .sage}
tp = 2 * RDF(pi)
img = [(cos(t), sin(t)) for t in [RDF(pi) / 2 + RDF(pi) / 2 * i / 400 for i in range(401)]]
print("image in {u <= 0 <= v}:", all(u <= 1e-12 and v >= -1e-12 for u, v in img))
pts = [tp * i / 600 for i in range(601)]
same = [(i, j) for i in range(601) for j in range(i + 1, 601)
        if abs(cos(pts[i]) - cos(pts[j])) < 1e-9 and abs(sin(pts[i]) - sin(pts[j])) < 1e-9]
print("identified pairs of grid indices:", same)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
image in {u <= 0 <= v}: True
identified pairs of grid indices: [(0, 600)]
```
::::
:::

The third exercise joins descent of maps from @def-quotient-set with continuity in the quotient topology from
@def-quotient-topology. A function constant on classes descends, and the exercise shows that the descended function
is continuous exactly when the original one is, which turns every periodic continuous function into a continuous
function on the circle.

::: {#exr-descend-continuity}
#### Descending maps and continuity

A map $f : X \to Y$ constant on the classes of $\sim$ descends to $\bar f : X/{\sim} \to Y$. Show that $\bar f$ is
continuous if and only if $f$ is, and apply it to $\cos : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $\pi : X \to X/{\sim}$ be the quotient map, so $f = \bar f \circ \pi$. If $\bar f$ is continuous so is $f$, as a composition of
continuous maps (@exr-continuous-composition). Conversely, for $V$ open in $Y$, $\pi^{-1}(\bar f^{-1}(V)) = f^{-1}(V)$ is open,
which by @def-quotient-topology means that $\bar f^{-1}(V)$ is open: $\bar f$ is continuous. $\cos$ is continuous and
$2\pi$-periodic, so it descends to a continuous function on $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, which the homeomorphism with $S^1$
(@exm-quotient-circle-top) turns into the first coordinate of a point of the circle. The same argument makes every
periodic continuous function a continuous function on the circle, the functions of @exr-descend.

## SageMath

Check on $f(\varphi) = \cos\varphi + \sin 2\varphi$: Sage confirms that $f$ is constant on classes, $f(\varphi + 2\pi k) = f(\varphi)$, and
that the descended function agrees with $u + 2uv$ on the circle, where $(u, v) = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$.

```{.python .sage}
phi, k = var("phi k")
assume(k, "integer")
f = cos(phi) + sin(2 * phi)
print("f(phi + 2 pi k) - f(phi) =", (f.subs(phi=phi + 2 * pi * k) - f).simplify_full())
u, v = cos(phi), sin(phi)
print("f - (u + 2uv) =", (f - (u + 2 * u * v)).simplify_trig())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f(phi + 2 pi k) - f(phi) = 0
f - (u + 2uv) = 0
```
::::
:::
::::
